items.title: Amazon's Plan to Index the World's Online Shopping Data
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Amazon is considering a "World Product Graph" that would index information about products sold across the internet in an effort to keep shoppers and AI agents from turning to Google, Reddit or other sources for product research. The proposed database could also improve Amazon's AI shopping assistant by addressing inaccurate or incomplete answers and allowing it to use cheaper models.
 
"Amazon cannot be the go-destination for every shopping mission if customers must leave to research product relationships on Google, brand websites, and review sites," according to an internal Amazon document. "These answers exist, but the only way to find them has been to leave Amazon for painstaking research on brand websites, third party review sites and tech forums." Reuters could not determine if or when this plan may be implemented, though the document, written like a press release, has an aspirational future release date of October 1, 2027.
 
Amazon said in a statement: "Draft, outdated documents often paint an incomplete picture and the existence of a brainstorming document such as this one doesn't necessarily reflect our current plans. We're constantly working on new ideas and technologies to make Amazon's product catalog comprehensive, accurate, and helpful for customers."

items.title: Windows 0-Day Dropped By Disgruntled Researcher Hands Hackers System Rights
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System, which Microsoft describes as a "general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode." By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System.
 
[...] Researcher Will Dormann said in an interview that he has been able to reproduce the exploit and that it works as described, but not on all versions of Windows 11. But there's a catch, he said. "The requirements are important in that it seems to require Windows 26H2, and one that has existed for more than 90 days, it seems," he explained. "That is, you can't just take a new 26H2 system and install updates and have it work." For a system to be vulnerable, Dormann said, the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication\Mode
value must be 0 or 1." Of the many machines Dormann uses, only a single one met this requirement. Microsoft said in a statement that it was investigating the vulnerability and had no evidence it was being exploited in the wild. The company also said Defender blocks potential exploitation attempts.

items.title: FAA Lifts Nationwide Ground Stop for All Aircraft [UPDATE]
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Longtime Slashdot readers cold fjord and sinij share news that the FAA grounded flights nationwide after a communications failure disrupted air traffic control centers across the country. By Friday evening, the outage had resulted in nearly 5,000 flight cancellations and roughly 10,000 delays, with no timeline for restoring normal operations. Rumors are swirling that this could be related to the FAA's newly deployed SMART AI system or Microsoft's recent global outage, but both the agency and Microsoft said they had no indication that their technology was responsible. Business Insider reports: US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said just after 4:15 pm. Eastern time that the nationwide flight traffic halt came "following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers." "FAA technicians are investigating the issue," he said in a post on X. The outage comes the same week as the FAA deployed SMART, a new AI tool to help air traffic control. ASI, the company that makes the SMART system for the FAA, said that Friday's issues weren't "based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC."
 
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a press conference Friday, when asked if the AI system might be related to the outage: "That's what we're looking at." Microsoft, which faced massive issues across its services this week, also said that it had "no indication" the ground stop was related to any Microsoft services. Meanwhile, the FAA said that the ground stop was due to "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." UPDATE 1:33 UTC: Secretary Mullin and Secretary Duffy are currently briefing members of the press on the issue.
 
UPDATE 1:46 UTC: The FAA has lifted the nationwide ground stop after more than four hours. Officials said the disruption appears to have stemmed from a network router issue that cascaded nationwide, with no evidence of a cyberattack or connection to Microsoft's recent outage. Airlines warned that disruptions could continue in Saturday.

items.title: SpaceX Falls Short of Historic Double Starship Catch
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
SpaceX's 15th Starship test flight successfully reached orbit Friday, but its historic attempt to catch both stages at the launch tower was derailed when the Super Heavy booster malfunctioned, forcing controllers to abort its return before it exploded after splashing down in the Gulf of Mexico. The upper-stage Starship did, however, successfully deploy 26 Starlink satellites and is scheduled to complete 15 orbits before attempting an unprecedented tower catch on Saturday. If successful, it would mark the first time a spacecraft has returned from orbit to land vertically at a launch tower. The Bakersfield Californian reports: The original goal was to retrieve every single piece of the rocket for the purpose of future recycling, something yet to be achieved anywhere in the world. Musk sees this leading to the kind of fast and consistent launch rates necessary for building moon bases and sending people to Mars. Shortly after reaching orbit, Starship dropped off 26 of the company's most advanced Starlink satellites. The plan is for Starship to complete 15 laps around the world at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) before heading back to the launch site for Saturday's grand finale.
 
SpaceX had already made three booster grabs at the company's sprawling Starbase near the U.S.-Mexico border. That made Friday's miss all the more surprising. "Well, that certainly isn't the news that we had hoped to hear for today," observed SpaceX launch commentator Kate Tice, adding that it was in line with the many rigorous safety checks to protect the pad. No explanation was provided for what went wrong. This was the first attempt to capture the upgraded version of the booster that stretches 236 feet (72 meters) -- the production model for moon and Mars expeditions. It will also be the first time the company attempts to catch the spacecraft, which spans 171 feet (52 meters). Together, they form the world's biggest and most powerful rocket -- an astounding 407 feet (124 meters) in height.
 
The spacecraft portion of the 14 previous Starships ended up in the ocean, either by design at flight's end or by accident in a stream of flaming wreckage. During the first full-scale test flight in 2023, multiple engines failed to ignite and the tumbling rocket's self-destruct system was activated. The last test, in September, was the first to reach orbit, but SpaceX did not try to recover any of the rocket stages. You can watch a recorded livestream of the launch on YouTube.

items.title: Lego's BrickLink Marketplace Back Online After Week-Long Outage Caused By 'Cyber Incident'
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
LEGO's BrickLink marketplace is back online after a week-long outage caused by what the company described as a "cyber incident," during which an unauthorized third party accessed some user data. Details about exactly what data was accessed remain unclear. The site went offline on November 5 and remained unavailable until November 12, preventing users from buying or selling LEGO sets and parts during the busy holiday shopping season. According to Brick Fanatics, LEGO initially described the outage as "necessary work" before confirming that the platform had suffered a security incident.
 
In an email to users, LEGO acknowledged that "some of the information associated with your account was accessed and disclosed by an unauthorized party," including potentially usernames and IP addresses. However, the company insisted that "your password, postal address, and financial information were not disclosed." Those assurances have since come under scrutiny following reports of convincing phishing emails containing detailed personal and purchase information.
 
The outage also dealt a significant blow to independent sellers who rely on BrickLink for income. Simon Webster, who operates stores on both BrickLink and rival marketplace Brick Owl, reported that his overall sales revenue fell 52% over a four-day period, even as sales through Brick Owl rose 79%. "Their comms are amateur at the best of times, but surely they should be able to send an email to let sellers and buyers alike know what is happening and what they're doing to rectify it," Webster said. "But no, we're all left in the dark."
 
The incident has renewed concerns about BrickLink's aging infrastructure. Founded in 2000 and acquired by LEGO in 2019, the marketplace reportedly runs on a complex collection of interconnected systems that makes modernization difficult. The Brick Fanatics report questions whether the 25-year-old platform remains fit for purpose and whether prolonged outages and security concerns could push sellers toward competing marketplaces like Brick Owl.

items.title: RevOps Is Quietly Becoming an Engineering Job
items.author: Malek Damiri
items.content:
Over the last two weeks, I've written here about a calendar table that knows November 1 has 25 hours, a customer health score that barely beats a coin flip, a 1961 warehouse formula that finds dead deals in a CRM, a Slack report that checks its own numbers before it posts, an exam for AI agents, a macOS job that died because of where it kept its log file, and why 3x pipeline coverage is a guess.

My title is Head of Revenue Operations. Very little of that shows up in a RevOps job description.

I started in supply chain, moved into revenue operations, and taught myself SQL along the way. For most of that time, the job looked the way people describe it: own the CRM, build the reports, run the forecast, keep sales and finance looking at the same numbers. That's still the job. But the way it gets done has changed, and I think it's changing faster than the job descriptions.

The data moved into the warehouse. RevOps used to live inside the CRM and its report builder. Now the numbers that matter, from billing, product usage, payments, and the CRM itself, land in Snowflake or BigQuery. The person who reconciles them needs SQL, not a report wizard.

An AI coding agent will write the script that syncs the CRM, builds the workbook, or posts the report in minutes. That's the real shift. When code is cheap, more of RevOps becomes code, and someone has to run it.

Running it is the part that didn't get cheaper. A script is easy. A script that runs at 7:45 every morning for two years, survives a laptop update, posts nothing when the data is wrong, and tells someone when it didn't run at all: that's operations engineering. And it's increasingly a RevOps problem, because the scripts are about revenue and nobody else owns them.

If you work in RevOps, sales ops, or finance ops and you're wondering where to invest, here's my list, roughly in order of how often each one has saved me.

Not just SELECT and GROUP BY. Grain, joins that duplicate rows, window functions, time zones. Most wrong numbers I've chased came down to a join or a day boundary. (These six Snowflake patterns cover the ones I reach for every week.)

One scheduler, and how it fails. cron, launchd, GitHub Actions, Airflow. Pick the one you'll actually use and learn what it does when things go wrong. Every scheduler has a way to fail silently. Know yours.

Version control for anything that produces a number. If it ends up in front of a CFO, it goes in git. "Which version of the query made that slide?" should have an answer.

Testing numbers, not just code. Reconciliations, check cells, golden questions with known answers. Code that runs is not code that's right.

Somewhere to break things that isn't production, and a deliberate step between the two.

Writing definitions down. Every metric needs a written definition that sales and finance have both agreed to. It's the least technical item on this list, and the one that prevents the most arguments.

Give them a sandbox, an exam, and a short list of things they're never allowed to touch. Then let them do a lot of the typing.

The risk in all of this is that RevOps turns into a shadow data engineering team: pipelines nobody else understands, a dozen scheduled jobs on one laptop, and a single person who knows how any of it works. That version is worse than not automating at all.

So draw a line. Data engineering owns the platform: ingestion, the warehouse, the infrastructure everyone shares. RevOps owns the business logic and the last mile: the definitions, the reconciliations, the reports, and the small automations that move revenue numbers to the people who use them.

And give the last mile an exit. When a RevOps automation becomes important enough that its failure would hurt the company, it graduates to the platform, with real monitoring, an owner on call, and a second person who understands it.

The job description hasn't caught up.

Most RevOps postings still ask for CRM administration, reporting, and strong analytical skills. Those matter. But the people I see doing this job well now are also comfortable in a terminal, can read a stack trace without panic, and treat a scheduled job like a product with users.

The title still says operations. More and more, the work says engineering. The people who do well will be the ones who take both words seriously.

I'm Malek Damiri, head of revenue operations in Atlanta. I write about revenue operations and the systems behind it at malekdamiri.com.

items.title: I Put a 42-Desk Design Studio Inside My Coding Agent
items.author: Aditya Reddy
items.content:
The part after the first design.

In October, I pointed Desk Studio at its own launch card. Three roughs, one pick, three polish rounds, scored 8.4, then 8.5, then 8.9, signed off at 8.9 for $1.34 at list price. And I could see every one of those steps while it happened, which is the whole reason the tool exists.

Before it, a follow-up like "make the headline bigger" would come back from my coding agent as a whole new design. New layout, new colors, sometimes new copy. Was the headline fixed? Couldn't tell, cause everything else moved too.

So Desk Studio splits the job up like a small studio. Rough options first, then one gets picked with notes, a cheaper desk polishes it, a script checks the real pixels, and a senior desk signs it off or sends it back. I still use it on my own projects.

There are 42 desks. The Design Manager runs in your own session and hands out work. The other 41 run as subagents, things like a Typographer, an Art Director, a UI Designer, or an Email Designer. Each one is just a markdown brief in the repo, so if you want to know how the Art Director decides, you open and read it.

They're grouped into three tiers, and each tier is on a model that suits what it does.

the pick, the notes, the sign-off

the roughs, research, type, tokens, copy

every polish round, the making

It all runs locally. The desks reach models through whatever CLI you're already logged into, , or , or an API key if you'd rather. Apart from those model calls and a few web lookups from the research desks, nothing leaves your machine.

In Claude Code it's a plugin. For Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot, Windsurf or OpenCode it's one line in the project:

# Claude Code
/plugin install desk --marketplace adityareddy-dev/deskstudio

# Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot, Windsurf, OpenCode
npx deskstudio add

Then you just ask like you normally would:

/desk:design a launch card for LinkedIn

# or run the job yourself from a terminal
npx --package deskstudio desk-run design "a launch card for LinkedIn"

The files land in with a short note on who did what, the scores and the cost.

Every visual job takes the same path.

  1. The UI Designer makes three different directions on the senior model, from the brief, your brand file and the standard for that kind of piece.
  2. The Art Director looks at the renders, picks one (or mixes two) and writes notes.
  3. A builder desk works from those notes plus a screenshot of the current render. Rounds are cheap, so this is where the back and forth happens.
  4. A script renders the file in Chrome at every size and checks the pixels. No model.
  5. The Creative Director scores eight axes: hierarchy, typography, spacing, colour, composition, originality, brand fit and copy.

To pass, every axis needs 8 or more and the average needs 8.5. Fail-proof, and it goes back to the builder with the screenshot. A builder that misses the same note twice hands the file up to a senior, and a senior that misses twice gets one round with the Art Director. After the round cap, the job comes back marked under the bar, with a note on which axis fell short, so it won't quietly ship something that didn't pass.

Here's a real terminal run of exactly that, on OpenAI models this time. Proof caught a type-scale problem in round 2, the builder fixed it, and round 3 still came back under the bar cause originality only got a 6. The last lines say what's missing.

Splitting out the pick was deliberate. Once a direction is picked, every round after that is a fix to that one design, so a note like "type sizes, not layout" means the next round touches type sizes and nothing else. When every round is a fresh design, there's nothing steady to measure against, which was the whole problem in the first place.

Proof has no model in it for a similar reason. Contrast against the real pixels, text spilling out of a box, a headline sitting in a platform's crop zone, a script checks all that the same way every time and it costs nothing. The models get to spend their judgment on the stuff a script can't see.

One real job, start to finish.

This is the launch card for Desk Studio itself, retold from its job record.

The UI Designer made three roughs: an editorial split, a type-only one, and a framed one. The Art Director went with rough 2, the type-only one, and wrote why: "headline reads first at both sizes, only amber is the small lamp, fixes are type sizes not layout."

You can overrule that. Every rough has a button, and if you use it, the pick goes on record as yours instead of the Art Director's.

After that, the builder polished, proof ran every round, and the Creative Director scored each one.

under the 8.5 bar, back to polish

originality 7, under the bar, back to polish

Round 3 got a 9 on seven axes and an 8 on originality, so 8.9 on average. This is the file it signed off.

The whole job came to $1.34 at list price.

the pick and three sign-offs

About 60% of that went to judgment and 40% to making, and the three polish rounds together were ten cents. That's what the tiers are for. If you're on a subscription, it's a list-price estimate of usage, not an extra bill.

The proof step, up close.

Before the Creative Director ever sees a file, proof renders it in Chrome at each target size and checks:

  • text contrast against the actual pixels behind it
  • colours inside the brand palette and type on the brand scale
  • that every required line of copy is actually there
  • carousel slides matching each other, and reading time and flashes in motion pieces

You can also run proof on its own against any HTML file:

desk-proof check hero.html --brand .desk/DESIGN.md --sizes phone,desktop

Watching it on the dashboard.

1.1 rebuilt the dashboard into the floor you can leave open while a job runs. It only listens on , and the URL carries a token.

# Claude Code
/desk:dashboard setup
/desk:dashboard start

# any other agent or a plain terminal
npx --package deskstudio desk-dashboard setup
npx --package deskstudio desk-dashboard start

The strip at the top is the job. In this capture of the launch card, it's sitting on round 2's sign-off; round 1 came in at 8.4, $0.77 is spent so far, and it's 17m 25s in.

holds the job before the next step, and ends it there. Neither one cuts a desk off halfway.

Below that is the floor, with a room per tier and a Proof booth. Each desk is a little bot that wakes up while that desk is working and goes back to sleep after. A ×3 on a desk means three of them are running at once, which is what you see during the roughs. Every room's sign shows its model, and swaps the whole tier.

Clicking a desk opens its panel. The UI Designer's panel here says it's on and has done 4 runs on this job, 887k tokens, $0.45. You can switch just that desk to another model, for this job or as the default, or leave it a note that goes into its next prompt.

On the right is who's working right now, and under it the studio log in plain words. One line from this job reads "Creative Director scored round 1: 8.4, under the bar", and the polish for round 2 starts on the very next line.

The roles and cost panel is where the tiers make sense. The builders went through 2.9 million tokens on this job, and that still came to ten cents. The slowest single run was the Creative Director's round 2 sign-off at 11 minutes 25 seconds, which tells you where the time actually goes.

Since 1.0.2, a job's event log also exports as an OpenTelemetry trace, with role timings, tokens and cost, so a design job can sit in the same tracing tool as the rest of your stuff.

The repo keeps a gallery of 17 signed-off pieces with their renders, scores and costs. Most are for four made-up brands, one's for a real site whose brand the studio found in the project, and three are for Desk Studio itself.

Ops dashboard for Northlight

Pitch deck for Northlight

The scores come from the studio's own model reviewers. They're useful for comparing rounds of one job, not as a benchmark against anything else. The standalone runner only takes for social cards right now, and the rest of the commands are Claude Code skills. The briefs install into other agents fine, though not every command works the same way there yet.

Free, MIT licensed, and it runs on the CLI login or API key you already have.

npx deskstudio add
npx --package deskstudio desk-dashboard setup
npx --package deskstudio desk-dashboard start

Then ask your agent for a launch card and keep the floor open. The code, docs, and full gallery are on GitHub, and there's a 50-second film on deskstudio.ai.

What I use most is the rounds view. I pull up round 1 next to round 3 and check if the thing I asked for is the thing that changed.

items.title: CI Failure Triage Needs Evidence Before It Needs a Classifier
items.author: Saqib Jan
items.content:
If you have ever owned a CI pipeline and cleared a wall of red builds before standup, you might recognize this routine. A nightly run finishes with thirty-seven failed tests, and by the time anyone looks, thirty have passed on a rerun and picked up a tag while the other seven get tickets.

Nobody records why the thirty failed in the first place, so the same failures come back the next night under the same label. And it is easy to see why teams settle into this, because a rerun clears the build in minutes while finding the real cause of thirty failures could take the whole team a day.

That gap is where a new class of AI models starts to look tempting. Shawn Gordon’s recent HackerNoon explainer introduces , a decision model from TypeSafe AI that writes nothing and only picks an answer. It chooses from up to 255 options or returns a yes or no probability in about half a second. TypeSafe also says those probabilities are calibrated, so an answer given at 80 percent confidence should be right about 80 percent of the time.

Sorting a failed test into a product defect, environment noise, or an agent error is a three-option choice question, which makes it look like a natural fit. But when Mastra, the company behind an open-source framework for building AI agents in TypeScript, tested Jev on a related triage job, the results were poor.

Jev labeled 78 of Mastra’s own GitHub issues as urgent, high, or low, using only each issue’s title and body, and only about 10 of its answers matched an engineer’s judgment. Mastra concluded that the model could not see the evidence that priority depends on, and Gordon put the risk plainly in his explainer. “A consistently wrong classifier that runs cheaply is just a faster way to tag things badly.”

CI triage has the same trap, because a model can sort failures well only when the pipeline has kept the evidence that separates one category from another. So the evidence has to come first and the classifier second.

Three Failure Categories Need Three Different Owners

Most pipelines record a failed test as one status, and that single status hides three kinds of failure that need different fixes from different teams.

, Director of Engineering at (formerly LambdaTest), draws that line before any fix starts. “We should ideally treat these failures into three different categories,” explains. “Whether it is a product defect, like an actual defect in the product. Or if it is environmental noise, maybe a network issue, a latency problem, a backend API that went down. Or very importantly now, since agentic pipelines are involved, whether it is an agent error.”

He also gives a working definition for the third category, which is the one teams find hardest to name. “If the agent’s reasoning or actions are inconsistent, that is the point where we can clearly say it is an agent error,” says. “We have to put them in different buckets.”

Each bucket leaves a different trail, and that trail is what a classifier will eventually read. A reproduces on the same commit under the same conditions and usually traces back to a recent change in the application. shows up as timeouts or 5xx responses from a dependency, and it tends to hit unrelated tests in the same time window.

An happens in a healthy environment and with an unchanged commit, while the agent’s steps differ from the last passing run. So the first practical move is to write those signals down as rules for each bucket and to name an owner for each one. The feature team takes defects, the platform team takes noise, and whoever owns the prompt and the model takes agent errors.

Parallel Runs Hide a Fourth Category Inside the Noise

Three buckets cover most failures, but some failures look like environment noise only because of how the suite runs.

, also Director of Engineering at , sees this most often when teams move from local runs to large parallel grids. “The most common and unanticipated failure is shared state across parallel workers,” highlights. “Locally, one or two tests run in parallel, and everything works, but in the cloud with 200 parallel workers you suddenly see tests depending on specific execution order.” The usual causes are global fixtures or singletons that several tests change at once, race conditions in test data setup, and ordering dependencies that nobody noticed while the suite ran one test at a time.

These failures are . And a classifier that only knows three labels will file them as environment noise, because they come and go without any change to the code. The fix is to add a fourth label and give the classifier the one signal that separates it, which is whether the test still fails with a single worker.

Rerunning each failure once with one worker inside the triage job costs a few seconds and turns an ambiguous failure into a clear one. And the repair itself belongs in the test, through per-worker test data and idempotent setup and teardown, and not in the infrastructure.

Capture the Agent’s Steps Along With the Result

Agent errors are the hardest bucket to fill correctly, because the evidence is in decisions the agent made and not in any log the pipeline already keeps.

, Director of , built his team’s approach around those decisions. His team captures a trace of every action an agent takes, with full context, in a cryptographically secure audit system. It then uses separate agent evaluators to review those traces for logic errors that have happened or might happen next.

“The steps that the non-deterministic system takes to get to an output are as important to test as the outputs themselves,” explains. “By examining a detailed trace of the steps an agent takes and the tools it leverages to generate an output, you can get deep insight into where decisions are brittle and anticipate errors before they happen.”

That trace is also the missing input for automated triage. After its test, advised letting an agent gather the evidence first and letting the classifier judge what it gathered, and CI works the same way. A triage job can attach an to every failure before any model sees it.

The bundle carries the commit, the model and prompt versions, dependency health at the start of the run, the retry outcome, and a diff of the agent’s steps against the last passing run.

{
  "test": "checkout > applies promo code",
  "commit": "9f3c2e1",
  "model": "provider-model-2026-09-15",
  "prompt_version": "checkout-agent@14",
  "attempts": [
    {"status": "failed", "workers": 8},
    {"status": "passed", "workers": 1}
  ],
  "dependency_health_at_start": {
    "payments-api": "degraded",
    "inventory-api": "ok"
  },
  "network_errors": ["POST /payments 503 after 30012 ms"],
  "agent_steps_diff_vs_last_pass": [
    "skipped: open_cart",
    "added: search_product"
  ]
}

Every field in that bundle points at a bucket. A degraded payments API points at noise, a failure with eight workers followed by a pass with one points at a test defect, and a changed step sequence on a healthy environment points at an agent error. When the signals conflict, as they do in this example, the bundle shows the conflict instead of hiding it. A person reading this bundle can usually name the bucket quickly, and so can a decision model.

Route Failures by Label and Confidence

Once the evidence exists, the classifier’s job is narrow, and keeping it narrow is what makes it safe to automate.

, Co-Founder and CEO of , which builds AI SRE agents for incident investigation, shows how far that labeling can go once a team has the evidence to support it. His team tracks across its agent investigations. Those labels separate tool access problems from reasoning errors, omitted steps, and unfinished runs, because a status that only says the agent responded tells the team nothing about whether it did useful work.

Most CI teams do not need 51 labels on day one, but Anver’s taxonomy shows that the label set should grow as the evidence gets richer. A decision model makes that growth cheap, because a choice question over four labels or forty costs about the same to run. The harder design question is the rule for acting on each answer. The code below sends a failure straight to its owner only when the model is confident, and puts everything else in a human triage queue.

LABELS = ["product_defect", "environment_noise", "agent_error", "test_defect"]
OWNERS = {
    "product_defect": "feature-team",
    "environment_noise": "platform-team",
    "agent_error": "agent-owners",
    "test_defect": "test-authors",
}
AUTO_THRESHOLD = 0.90

def route(evidence_bundle, classify):
    """classify() wraps the team's decision model or classifier."""
    label, confidence = classify(state=evidence_bundle, options=LABELS)
    if confidence >= AUTO_THRESHOLD:
        return {"label": label, "route_to": OWNERS[label], "automatic": True}
    return {"label": label, "route_to": "human-triage", "automatic": False}

The threshold should come from the team’s own data and not from a vendor’s claim. Public write-ups on Jev note that most claims about the model come from TypeSafe itself and that no calibration results have been published yet. So run the classifier in for two weeks, keep human labels for the same failures, and check whether answers given at 90 percent confidence are actually right about 90 percent of the time.

from collections import defaultdict

def calibration_report(predictions):
    """predictions is a list of (confidence, predicted_label, human_label)."""
    buckets = defaultdict(lambda: [0, 0])
    for confidence, predicted, actual in predictions:
        bucket = min(int(confidence * 10), 9) / 10
        buckets[bucket][0] += 1
        buckets[bucket][1] += predicted == actual
    for bucket in sorted(buckets):
        total, correct = buckets[bucket]
        upper = bucket + 0.1
        accuracy = correct / total
        print(f"{bucket:.1f}-{upper:.1f}  n={total}  accuracy={accuracy:.2f}")

If the 0.9 bucket comes back at 0.70 accuracy, the model is overconfident on this team’s failures. In that case, raise the threshold or improve the bundle before letting it route anything on its own.

treats the classifier as the last step of triage, not the first. “A model can sort failures faster than anyone on the team, but only if the pipeline kept what that model needs to see,” he says. “Start by labeling a month of failures by hand. Once your own engineers agree on the buckets, a classifier has something real to learn from and something real to be checked against.”

The first week of this work needs no model at all. Pull the last month of failed and flaky tests, label each one by hand as a product defect, environment noise, an agent error, or a test defect, and note which piece of evidence decided the label. Then make the triage job attach those pieces of evidence to every new failure, run a decision model in shadow mode against the hand labels, and switch on automatic routing only for the labels where its confidence matches its accuracy.

items.title: Mozilla to Shut Down Solo, Deleting Users' Websites and Data
items.author: BeauHD
items.content: Mozilla is shutting down Solo, its AI-powered website builder and hosting service, on November 30. A notice on the Soloist.ai homepage reads: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026." The Register reports: Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. Some 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them -- complete with custom domain names. Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ, users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images. The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com, with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code.

items.title: Microsoft's Global Outage May Be Worse Than Amazon's Or Crowdstrike's, Expert Says
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: A global outage taking down a wide range of Microsoft 365 services remains ongoing Friday morning. The outage started midday Thursday, impacting users of Microsoft email, cloud, and AI services. Microsoft has documented the full list of services impacted by the error, while moving early Friday morning to protect customers around the world from losing emails during the extended disruptions. "Recovery actions are ongoing," the Microsoft 365 Status account confirmed on X. "To help preserve delayed mail during this event, we've extended email timeout to 48 hours."
 
Similar to recent world-shaking outages of widely used tech like Amazon Web Services and CrowdStrike, the Microsoft disruption looks like "one of the biggest outages of all time," Ciaran Martin, the former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, told NBC News. Possibly even "worse," he suggested.
 
Businesses, hospitals, police departments, and schools were among those scrambling to work around the outage. In Japan, it disrupted government IT infrastructure, according to deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki. NBC's report documented various harms, noting that "few public bodies were immune from the outage." In some cases, doctors couldn't send patients "important" updates on medication changes or follow-up care. The financial sector suffered, too, with people blocked from making bank transfers since they couldn't receive verification codes.
 
Justice systems were also hobbled. The Supreme Court in the Philippines saw its legal work derailed, NBC reported. And one US sheriff's office in Colorado reported that the outage made it difficult for people to post bond for prisoners' immediate release. It's unclear how many users were affected, but Microsoft estimated in January that the total number of paid Microsoft 365 commercial subscriptions exceeded 450 million. Microsoft's most recent updates confirmed that it's seeing "broader improvements in North America, sustained improvements across much of Europe, and encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific."
 
"Some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as mitigation continues across remaining affected infrastructure," Microsoft said. "Our focus remains on stabilizing recovered infrastructure, completing mitigation in remaining impacted areas, and reducing delayed email queues and backlogs while we validate service consistency across connection methods."

items.title: Comparing Six AI Video APIs by Cost, Concurrency, and Reliability
items.author: Nica Furs
items.content:
Most AI video work still starts in a browser tab: type a prompt, wait, download. That breaks down once a team needs 200 product clips a week, a video step inside an app, or an agent that renders drafts overnight. Video APIs move generation into code. In this article, we: how the requests work, a short working example, what matters once real traffic arrives, six APIs side by side, and the automation layer on top.

How API Video Generation Works

A video takes anywhere from under a minute to a few minutes to render, so no provider keeps an HTTP connection open until the file is ready. Every major video API follows the same three-part pattern.

  1. You send a POST request with the model, prompt, and settings. The API answers right away with a request ID and a status URL.
  2. You poll the status URL, or register a webhook and wait. The job moves from queued to in progress, then to a terminal state such as completed or failed.
  3. The completed response holds a URL to the MP4. Download it to your own storage, because providers delete outputs: Replicate after one hour by default, Higgsfield after at least seven days.

The names change from provider to provider. fal calls them requests, Replicate calls them predictions, and Runway calls them tasks. The shape stays the same.

Step-by-Step Example: A Text-to-Video Request in Python

The example below uses the Higgsfield API and Seedance 2.5. The same submit, poll, and download loop works with any provider. Only the URL, auth header, and field names change.

Step 1: Set your credentials. Create an API key in the console and export the key ID and secret.

export HF_API_KEY_ID="your-key-id"
export HF_API_KEY_SECRET="your-key-secret"

The idempotency key lets you resend the same request after a timeout without paying twice.

import os, time, uuid, requests

AUTH = {"Authorization": f"Key {os.environ['HF_API_KEY_ID']}:{os.environ['HF_API_KEY_SECRET']}"}
job = requests.post(
"https://api.higgsfield.ai/bytedance/seedance-2.5/text-to-video",
headers={**AUTH, "Idempotency-Key": str(uuid.uuid4())},
json={
"prompt": "A cinematic tracking shot along a sunlit coastal road",
"resolution": "720p",
"duration": 5,
"aspect_ratio": "16:9",
"generate_audio": True,
},
timeout=30,
).json()
print(job["request_id"], job["status"])  # -> queued
Step 3: Poll until the job ends. Four statuses are terminal: completed, failed, nsfw, and canceled.
TERMINAL = {"completed", "failed", "nsfw", "canceled"}
while True:
result = requests.get(job["status_url"], headers=AUTH, timeout=30).json()
if result["status"] in TERMINAL:
break
time.sleep(5)
Step 4: Download the video.
if result["status"] == "completed":
clip = requests.get(result["video"]["url"], timeout=120)
with open("clip.mp4", "wb") as f:
f.write(clip.content)
else:
print("Job ended with status:", result["status"], result.get("error"))

The official Python SDK (pip install higgsfield-client) wraps steps 2 and 3 into a single subscribe() call. In production, replace the polling loop with a webhook: add an hf_webhook query parameter with your URL-encoded HTTPS endpoint, and Higgsfield sends a POST when the job reaches completed, failed, or nsfw.

What Matters in Production Workflows

A demo needs one successful call. A production pipeline has to survive timeouts, rate limits, moderation rejections, and bills that grow with every retry. Four areas decide how much work that takes.

Every provider caps parallel jobs. Higgsfield allows 20 concurrent requests, fal allows 2 to 40 on self-serve accounts, Runway allows 1 to 20 depending on usage tier, and MiniMax allows 30 in-flight H3 jobs. Put your own job queue in front of the API, such as a database table or a Redis list, so a batch of 500 renders waits its turn instead of failing.

Retry network errors and 5xx responses with exponential backoff. Never retry 4xx validation errors, since the same input will fail again. Send an idempotency key with each submission so a resent POST does not start a second paid job. Treat webhooks as at-least-once: Higgsfield, fal, and Replicate can all deliver duplicates, so deduplicate by request ID. Keep a polling fallback in case a webhook never arrives.

Billing on Failed Generations

Failure rules differ more than prices do.

  • failed, timed-out, and NSFW-rejected requests are refunded automatically.
  • 5xx server errors are free; 422 invalid-input errors can still be charged if a GPU already worked on the request.
  • failed runs on public models are free; canceled runs on official models may be billed.
  • credits come back when an error on Runway's side fails a job, but input moderation rejections are not refunded.

Validate inputs before you submit. A broken image URL or an unsupported duration is the cheapest bug to catch.

No single model wins every shot. Kling 4.0 handles long takes, Seedance 2.5 handles reference-driven scenes, and MiniMax H3 delivers 2K at a low rate. Calling each vendor directly means separate keys, balances, rate limits, and response formats. Platforms such as Higgsfield, fal, Replicate, and Runway Dev put multiple models behind one key and one balance, so switching models means changing one model ID. The trade-off is dependence on the platform’s pricing and model coverage.

Prices are list rates per second of 720p video (768p on MiniMax), checked in late October and early November 2026. Promotions are excluded.

Refunded on Runway-side errors

Sync call or background mode

Google shut down the three Veo 3.1 preview models in the Gemini API (veo-3.1-generate-preview, veo-3.1-fast-generate-preview, and veo-3.1-lite-generate-preview) on October 22, 2026, and points developers to Gemini Omni Flash instead. The generally available Veo 3.1 models remain on Google Cloud’s Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

Pick Higgsfield when you want top models plus production tools like consistent characters and camera control behind one key, or fal for a broad open catalog. Replicate fits teams that also deploy custom models. Runway Dev makes sense when Gen-4.5 and Aleph editing sit at the center of the pipeline. The Gemini API suits chat-style edits on Google's own model, and MiniMax wins when 2K output at a low per-second rate matters most.

Automating Video Generation

A cron job or a cloud scheduler, such as GitHub Actions, Google Cloud Scheduler, or AWS EventBridge, can read tomorrow's briefs from a sheet or database, submit one job per row, and write the finished URLs back. Pair it with webhooks so the scheduler never sits idle polling.

Both connect to any video API through a generic HTTP step, with no custom node required. In n8n, a typical flow runs Schedule Trigger, then HTTP Request to submit, then a Wait node set to resume on a webhook call, then a download and upload to Google Drive or S3. Pass $execution.resumeUrl as the provider's webhook URL so the workflow wakes up when the video is ready. In Make, one scheduled scenario submits jobs through the HTTP module, and a second scenario that starts from a Custom webhook receives results and files them.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets an AI assistant call outside tools directly. Higgsfield's MCP server connects to Claude, ChatGPT, Claude Code, and other MCP-compatible clients, and gives the agent 30+ image and video models with no API key. A marketer can ask the assistant to make three 9:16 hook variants of a product shot and get the files back without writing code. Agents work best on drafts and one-off requests. Scheduled pipelines still handle volume better.

Which AI video API is the cheapest? Per second of output, Wan 3.0 on Higgsfield starts at $0.020, MiniMax H3 runs $0.08 at 768p, and Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash costs about $0.10 at 720p. Count retries too: a cheap model that needs four takes costs more than a pricier one that lands in one.

Do I need webhooks, or is polling enough? Polling every 5 to 10 seconds works at low volume. As job counts grow, webhooks cut wasted requests. Keep polling as a fallback either way.

How long do providers keep generated videos? Not long. Replicate deletes API outputs after one hour by default, and Higgsfield keeps them at least seven days. Copy each file to your own storage as soon as the job completes.

Can I spend web app credits through the API? Usually not. Higgsfield and Runway both bill API usage from a separate prepaid balance, apart from app subscriptions.

items.title: Nvidia Employees Petition For Jensen Huang's Return
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Some Nvidia employees are calling for Jensen Huang's return even after his multiple reported extramarital affairs and abrupt resignation, according to internal correspondence reviewed by WIRED. An internal "suggestion box" post submitted before Huang's resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company's board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang.
 
"If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss," wrote one anonymous commenter. "We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance," wrote another. One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang's exit. "I stand by Jensen," the staffer wrote. "Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us."
 
[...] It's been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang's resignation left many employees stunned. In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn't identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation. One employee who has been at Nvidia for a couple of years and wasn't authorized to speak publicly says they perceive the desire for Huang's reinstatement as widespread. They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back. "Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen," the employee tells WIRED.
 
Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion-box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment "about Jensen's continuing as our CEO." Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. Staffers are seeking to better understand why. "If America fails the man who helped build its future," the employee in the companywide email stated, "then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang."

items.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.content:
Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day.

On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System, which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System.

Turning a Windows defense against itself

The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates.

items.title: Parents and Teachers Decry Google Pledge To Yank Search If Schools Block AI
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Guardian: Parents and teachers across the US are criticizing Google's announcement that schools choosing to block AI tools could also lose access to Google Search. Google announced last week a range of new AI tools for schools and classrooms, alongside options allowing teachers and administrators to restrict their use. The company said schools should have control over whether students use AI in the classroom, but that schools that choose to block Google's AI tools will also lose access to its search engine. [...] Parents and teachers across the country raised concerns to the Guardian about AI's potential to weaken students' critical-thinking skills and the growing influence of big tech in education. Some called on schools to consider alternative search engines, while others argued that students should be taught how to use AI responsibly rather than prevented from accessing it altogether.
 
Jen Atay, a 51-year-old teacher in Hawaii, lambasted Google's approach, saying: "When the software is free, you are the product, and it is inappropriate for Google to test or develop AI with minors. This should not be allowed at all." A 44-year-old father of two boys in Amissville, Virginia, said he worries that "AI will weaken people's ability to think critically. I use AI in my work, but it would not be effective if I did not have well over a decade of experience under my belt. Even the best models are often flat-out wrong in their responses." [...] Others questioned why schools should depend on Google at all. An 84-year-old retiree and mother in Maryland, said: "Google decided to follow the evil path to riches. When they started, they were great. Today they are simply evil money grubbers Schools should tell Google to go pound sand and simply have kids use DuckDuckGo or one of the other search engines There is nothing Google offers that is not available from some other source." [...]
 
Not everyone believes blocking AI is the answer. Some argued that schools should focus on teaching students how to use the technology responsibly. A 67-year-old emerging technology teacher in Texas said: "I do not blame Google. AI is not going away. I've been very frustrated this year trying to teach AI literacy with AI blocked. Schools need to teach how to properly use AI, not block it." A California resident echoed that view, arguing that schools could use Google's AI tools to teach students to question the information they receive. "Google Search has existed since the 90s and it's crazy of them to completely remove it instead of just removing Gemini. That being said, I would like to see schools actually permit the use of Gemini and use it as an opportunity to show students how its sources aren't always valid and you can't trust everything an AI tells you," they said.

items.title: Building a Multi-Agent Website Launch Validator With OpenMinion
items.author: Alan De Bortolo
items.content:
I run a small web agency. We build and host websites for small businesses in the US and Brazil, and every launch has the same floor: a title and a description, a canonical URL, Open Graph tags, JSON-LD, icons, a sitemap, a 404 page that really returns 404, an , and a that does not lock AI search crawlers out. For years we checked that list by hand, one tab per item.

For Cortensor Hackathon 5, I turned the checklist into an agent called , built on OpenMinion 0.1, the agent SDK from the Cortensor ecosystem. It answers one question: is this site ready, ready with warnings, or blocked? The code is MIT-licensed at github.com/DesignMaster-Solutions/golive-gate and there is a 2-minute demo at youtu.be/tVH-x62QV3I.

This post is about the one design decision that made it trustworthy, and about what it looks like to run an agent on open, swappable inference instead of one vendor's API.

The rule: the model never fetches anything

The tempting version of this agent is one prompt: "here is a URL, tell me if it is ready". That version hallucinates. It will tell you a sitemap exists because sites usually have one.

So Go-Live Gate is split in three agents with different powers:

  1. It can call three read-only tools: , and . They are plain with 15-second timeouts and they return facts only (title length, which Open Graph tags exist, which bots blocks, the HTTP status of a random missing path). If the model skips a tool, the gap is filled deterministically, so the next step never guesses.
  2. It gets the raw facts and must return a pydantic-validated : a verdict plus one row per check with the evidence and the fix. The judge has no tools at all. It cannot fetch, so it cannot invent.
  3. A third agent must call , a tool marked . OpenMinion routes that call through a human approval callback (an interactive y/N, or for CI). If the human says no, nothing is written.

Every run writes next to . A reviewer can open both and check the model's verdict against what the tools actually saw. That file is the whole point: the agent is only as honest as the layer under it, and that layer has its own offline tests against a local HTTP server.

class Check(BaseModel):
    name: str
    status: Literal["pass", "warn", "fail"]
    evidence: str   # the fact from a tool result that justifies the status
    fix: str = ""

class GoLiveReport(BaseModel):
    site: str
    verdict: Literal["ready", "ready_with_warnings", "blocked"]
    checks: list[Check]
    summary: str

Why this matters for decentralized inference

When the facts live in code and the model only reasons over them, the model becomes replaceable. That is what makes open inference practical for a business tool.

OpenMinion talks to any OpenAI-compatible provider. Our recorded runs used a free open-weight model (nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free through OpenRouter); the same project is set up for the Cortensor Portal with one command (setup --provider cortensor-portal). I did not have to rewrite prompts or tools to switch. The judge's output is validated by a schema either way, so a weaker or slower node fails loudly instead of quietly writing a wrong verdict.

If you are building on a decentralized inference network, you cannot assume the same model, the same latency or the same token limits on every call. Designing the agent so that the model is the least trusted part is how you get repeatable results anyway.

The hackathon asked for building blocks tested and lessons learned, and these were the useful ones:

  • Read-only tools still asked for confirmation. A tool tagged and still came back as "Policy confirmation required ... reply yes", because the decorator default wins over the tags. Declaring fixed it.
  • The first request of every turn was not my agent. It was the automatic memory extractor, carrying the whole system prompt but exposing only one tool, . A model replaying that request alone said "the inspection tools are not available", and I spent an hour thinking my tools were hidden. A top-level "brain": {"auto_fact_extraction": {"enabled": false}} in removes that round trip.
  • One turn did not fit a free tier. With default tools, the main turn sent about 17k characters of system prompt plus eight built-in tools. Groq answered at 8,683 tokens. Free tiers also need pacing the SDK does not have (its retry waits 300 ms; the rate window is 60 s), so I wrapped the adapter to stay under 6.5k tokens per minute.
  • is not enforced on the model. The judge once answered with a markdown table. A JSON schema at the end of the instructions changed nothing; the same schema inside the user message worked on the first try.
  • in the same session lost the first message, so retries now resend the facts.

And one bug was mine. The first live run flagged a 697-character title on a client site whose real title is 63 characters. My parser was concatenating the elements inside inline SVG icons. The agent repeated what the tool reported, which is exactly why the facts layer has regression tests and the model does not get the last word.

On capegraniteconnection.com, a site we built, the gate returned with 11 checks: title 63 characters, description 149, canonical present, all four Open Graph tags, 12 JSON-LD types including LocalBusiness and FAQPage, , both icons, no AI crawler blocked, a sitemap with 44 URLs, a 3,902-byte , and a real 404. On a free model the investigator took 232 seconds and the judge 355. Slow, but it runs unattended before every launch, and it is cheaper than the hour of tabs it replaces.

python3.12 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
.venv/bin/python -m unittest test_checks -v
.venv/bin/python gate.py yoursite.com --auto-approve yes

The lesson I would carry to any agent on open infrastructure: let code collect the facts, let the model reason over them, put a schema on the answer and a human in front of anything that writes. Then the model can come from anywhere.

items.title: AARO Solved Iraq's 'Jellyfish' as Balloons. Alaska's Jellyfish UFO Still Lacks the Data
items.author: Anomaly Detection
items.content:
A June sighting in Anchorage went viral in November. Two witnesses, one camera, a rainbow, a military base somewhere behind the treeline, and far more questions than verified answers.

A Rainbow, a Treeline and an Object With Tentacles

At about 10:13 p.m. Alaska Daylight Time on June 15, 2026, Sara Jane Osborn was photographing a rainbow from a car on Sixth Avenue in Anchorage when she noticed a dark, black-and-silver shape above the trees. Her husband, Pete, pulled into an empty downtown parking lot so she could shoot unobstructed. Osborn described dangling appendages that seemed to move independently as the shape turned side to side, and said it was visible for roughly three minutes before it "disappeared almost as quickly as it came," according to IBTimes UK, which drew on a November 10 Daily Mail interview.

The couple then searched a nearby park for a kite flyer and drove toward Arctic Valley, looking for about 30 minutes without finding an operator or another witness. That fruitless search is part of their testimony. It is not proof that a kite was impossible. Asked who knows what she saw, Osborn offered: "Only God and the government." She also allowed, "maybe it's a drone-type thing."

Two eyewitnesses are named: Sara Jane and Pete Osborn. Only Sara Jane is credited as the camera operator. Coverage that says the couple "captured" the object does not establish two independently operated cameras.

The defensible public count as of November 12: one witness, one phone, several still photos taken in quick succession, followed by one video, per IBTimes UK. No outlet we reviewed published the video's length or the total number of stills. The clips circulating on X and Instagram, including an X post by Mario Nawfal and a screengrab WION credits to X user @digijordan, appear to be reposts, crops or excerpts of the same encounter. Counting reposts as independent sightings would be misleading.

No verified second-angle recording was located. Nor was an original uncompressed file, complete EXIF metadata, camera specifications, verified geolocation or an authenticated radar track. WION says plainly that it "cannot independently verify the authenticity" of the footage.

five months between capture and publication is a long time for a file to travel through messaging apps and social platforms, each of which strips metadata and recompresses video. Provenance standards like C2PA can, in principle, ride along with a file, but provenance metadata is only useful if it survives, and as Paul Krause argues on HackerNoon, records attached to a file can simply be stripped. The single most valuable artifact in this story is still the original file on Osborn's phone.

Was It Over Military Land? The Map Matters

The couple believed the object sat toward Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson (JBER). Pete estimated it was within about three miles. IBTimes UK notes that neither the distance nor any link to the base or military airspace has been verified. An object visually aligned with military land may be much closer to the camera. Without a reliable range, azimuth and camera position, no one can say whether it entered restricted airspace.

The published still adds a useful constraint. In the frame, the object hangs in front of a sunlit, forested mountainside, not against open sky (see the feature image). Whatever it was, it was nearer to the camera than that slope. That fits a modest-range object at least as well as a giant distant one.

The Sun Was Up, and Behind Them

"10:13 p.m." sounds like night. In Anchorage in mid-June, it isn't. Sunset that week falls around 11:39 p.m. at an azimuth of about 328 degrees, and civil twilight runs all night. Using the standard NOAA solar-position approximation, we estimate the sun sat roughly 6 degrees above the horizon in the northwest at the time of the sighting.

Two things follow. First, a rainbow always forms opposite the sun, so Osborn was facing generally east to southeast, toward the Chugach front range, which is consistent with a sightline toward the eastern reaches of JBER and Arctic Valley. Second, a low sun behind the camera front-lights everything in view. That helps explain a "silver" sheen on a dark object. Reflective fabric, foil or Mylar would flash brightly in exactly that light.

It also rules out one famous lookalike. A "space jellyfish" is a rocket exhaust plume lit by the sun high above a ground observer who is in twilight darkness. Osborn was standing in daylight, and the object was in front of a mountainside, not 100 miles up.

Does It Really Look Like a Jellyfish?

Visually, yes, at a descriptive level. A domed upper mass with thin dangling projections evokes a jellyfish drifting through water, and the resemblance strengthens when the appendages flex and the body rotates. But resemblance is not taxonomy. Helium decorations, show kites, balloon bundles, fabric, debris and compression artifacts can all produce organic silhouettes.

Real jellyfish move by contracting a bell to push water. The Anchorage object has not been shown to pulse in a matching locomotion cycle, and the available clips do not establish its speed, altitude or any controlled acceleration. "It looked alive" is a witness impression, not a biological or aerospace finding.

The Best Ordinary Explanations, and What Each Would Need to Prove

Long fabric streamers and wind-driven rotation fit the silhouette. Inflatable octopus and jellyfish show kites are commercial products, sold in sizes like an 8-meter octopus. A visible tether, an identified operator or a weather-consistent trajectory would strengthen the case. Note that under the FAA's Part 101 rules, kites flown high or near an airport require notice to air traffic control, and Anchorage has several airports, including JBER and Merrill Field. The couple's failure to find a flyer does not eliminate the explanation, and Osborn's own reasoning ("why would you only fly it for, like, three minutes?") is a fair question rather than evidence.

Balloon cluster or novelty balloon. A buoyant object can drift and rotate while ribbons swing on their own. Close-ups showing seams or strings, or a reconstruction against wind data, would test it. This is the explanation that resolved the most famous previous "jellyfish" (see below).

Mechanically possible, but there is no evidence of a drone, operator, motor noise or flight record. Since March 2024, the FAA has fully enforced its Remote ID rule, which requires most drones to broadcast identification and location. A compliant drone would have been detectable by any nearby receiver at the time; no one has reported such a capture.

Digital manipulation or AI generation. Possible in principle, but no forensic analysis of the original file has been published either way. As HackerNoon contributor Matthew of Technology News Australia observes, despite ubiquitous cameras no one has produced one clear, independently verified photograph of an alien craft. Blurry phone footage keeps both the believers' and skeptics' cases unfalsifiable.

Perspective and apparent size. The couple recalled an aircraft that looked much smaller than the object. That comparison cannot establish size unless both distances are known. The Pentagon's AARO paper on forced perspective and parallax explains why apparently huge or fast objects routinely mislead observers.

As of November 12, no aerospace engineer, meteorologist, imaging-forensics specialist or AARO investigator has publicly authenticated or solved this recording. Claims of expert confirmation should be treated with caution. IBTimes UK states explicitly that the object's identity, location and link to the base remain unverified.

The base rate is worth knowing. AARO's FY2025 annual report, summarized by New Space Economy, counted 319 new reports. Of the 114 incoming cases it closed, 60 were balloons and 44 were satellites. The Pentagon's 2024 historical UAP review found no verified evidence of extraterrestrial technology and noted that many unresolved cases simply lack adequate data. Neither is a determination about this video.

Al Taqaddum Air Base, Iraq, October 23, 2017. The infrared "jellyfish UAP" that Jeremy Corbell released in January 2024 was filmed from a force-protection aerostat over the base. In September 2025, AARO assessed with high confidence that it was a cluster of fully and partially inflated balloons drifting with the wind at roughly 4 to 14 mph and 850 to 2,200 feet, with no heat signature from motors. It is a separate case with a different sensor and does not corroborate Anchorage, but it is the closest precedent: dangling strings, apparent shape-shifting and a military backdrop, all resolved as balloons once the full footage and geometry were analyzed. The Metabunk forum thread documents how independent analysts reached the same answer.

Stroud area, England, February 10, 1989. Drivers near the A46 reported a jellyfish-like aerial object, according to a recap citing the Swindon Star's front page. The account rests on old newspaper reports, with no comparable imagery.

Fresno area, California, April 2023. A tentacled object drew comparisons to sci-fi creatures until zoomed footage showed strings consistent with a novelty kite, per the same recap. A useful cautionary counterexample, not a debunking of Anchorage.

What Could Actually Settle the Alaska Story

The useful next steps are concrete: obtain Osborn's original phone files and full photo burst; check capture timestamps and GPS metadata; pin down the exact Sixth Avenue and parking-lot positions; reconstruct the rainbow and mountain sightlines (the solar geometry above is a start); identify the lens focal length; pull wind profiles at several altitudes; check FAA records, Part 101 kite notices and any Remote ID logs; request a JBER public-affairs response; and look for other cameras pointed east that evening.

The open question is not whether the silhouette is strange. It is. The questions are whether the object was near or far, how it moved relative to the wind, whether its disappearance was real acceleration or just loss of visibility, and whether anyone else filmed it. Until those are answered, the most precise description is "an unidentified object in one witness's video," not an alien vehicle over a military base.

The Anchorage jellyfish is real as a reported encounter: a named woman and her husband say they saw something unusual, and her imagery surfaced five months later. The viral claims, including giant size, flight directly over JBER, impossible motion, multiple independent films and extraterrestrial origin, remain unverified. The one still in public view places the object in daylight, front-lit by a low sun, in front of a mountainside. The last famous jellyfish turned out to be balloons. This one deserves the same patient analysis, starting with the original file.

items.title: Matt Pocock's 39 Agent Skills Make Your AI Grill You Before It Writes Code
items.author: UserStory
items.content:
Matt Pocock, creator of Total TypeScript, publishes 39 MIT-licensed agent skills that make the AI interview you before it builds. They turn the answers into specs, tickets, tests and code. All 39 are installable from Cuttlefish.MD, HackerNoon's license-checked skills marketplace, and from Matt's own repo.

Plan and interview: 14 skills

Tells you which skill or flow fits your situation

Shared vocabulary for designing deep modules and their interfaces

Builds and sharpens a project's domain model and GLOSSARY.md

A relentless interview that sharpens a plan or design

Grills you about a plan, decision or idea

Grills you on specs for the workflows you want to build

Builds a throwaway prototype to answer a design question

Investigates a question against primary sources and saves the findings in the repo

Shared language for designing a software factory and its services

Turns a decision you can't answer into a questionnaire for someone else

Turns the conversation into a spec on your issue tracker

Breaks a plan into tracer-bullet tickets with their blocking dependencies

Plans work too big for one session as a map of decision tickets

Build, review and hand off: 14 skills

Pursues a long-running goal in one session by coordinating subagents

Hands the conversation to a fresh background agent that picks up the work

Reviews changes since a commit, branch or tag for standards and correctness

Compacts the conversation into a handoff document for another agent

Implements work from a spec or set of tickets

Runs a retrospective on a coding session

Builds features and fixes bugs test-first, red-green-refactor

Moves issues and outside PRs through triage: categorize, verify, respond

Makes the agent stop and check before it carries on

Generates a bash wizard that walks a human through steps only they can do

Repo setup and TypeScript: 5 skills

Writing and teaching: 6 skills

Creates exercise folders with problems, solutions and explainers that pass linting

Teaches you a new skill or concept inside your workspace

Assembles material into beats, defining each term before a beat leans on it

Shapes raw material into an article, paragraph by paragraph

Cuttlefish sorts skills by what they do, so Matt's 39 are spread across five category plugins. Most of them (29) are in Dev Workflow:

/plugin marketplace add hackernoon/cuttlefish-agent-skills
/plugin install dev-workflow@cuttlefish
