items.content:
The FAA is expanding its $875 million AI-powered SMART system to all 22 U.S. air traffic control centers across the country. Since being implemented over Washington, DC, on September 21, the system has helped reroute 180 flights, saving an average of 10 minutes and nearly 80 gallons of fuel per flight. Ars Technica reports: The FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about "weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics" to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft. However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency. Furthermore, the AI-powered SMART system "cannot be used to replace the critical role air traffic controllers play or take over control of an aircraft," the FAA clarified in the September 21 announcement about the initial deployment. Local air traffic controllers can decide whether or not to accept the SMART system recommendations.
 
[...] Following the initial deployment in airspace above DC, the FAA expanded the SMART system's coverage to air route traffic control centers in Atlanta along with Jacksonville and Miami in Florida, according to The Dallas Morning News. The FAA also shared an example with The Dallas Morning News about how SMART recommended a shorter and faster route for a cargo flight arriving at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, although the newspaper noted that the agency did not identify the flight involved and has not provided information about how SMART may have assisted passenger flight traffic.

items.title: Packaging Innovation for Good
items.author: Brian Wallace
items.content:
The European Union has declared an ultimatum against unsustainability: all consumer packaging placed on the EU market must be designed for recycling by 2030.  This mandate was announced by the and formally became law in all 27 EU member states on Aug. 12, 2026.  Since then, the mandate has placed restrictions on synthetic “forever chemicals” (PFAS) in food packaging as part of the “Design for Recycling” (DfR) framework, which will become the baseline by 2030.  It is significantly reshaping how companies design, import and sell products globally.

All packaged products must meet these regulatory changes, not just those manufactured in the EU.  Because many brands prefer to standardize packaging across different nations’ markets, it is probable that PPWR’s influence will reach well beyond Europe as brands change their designs to streamline operations.

Under PPWR, materials will be graded based on their recyclability performance rates through the DfR framework.  Grade A materials are __≥95% recyclable__and meet the highest circular life cycle standards.  Grade B materials are ≥80% recyclable and are still considered to be highly efficient.  Materials graded as C are ≥70% recyclable.  Any material rated below 70% is deemed unrecyclable and will be banned from all markets.

The new rules imply that paperboard is one of the best materials for long-term reuse, reducing and recycling because it combines a high recyclability rate and excellent compatibility with set content targets.  This paper-based material can be recycled 5-10 times into innovative packaging for consumer retailers and their customers.  After it is responsibly disposed of, the cycle starts again for this valuable material.  European waste systems reportedly recover 87% of paper and paperboard packaging for reuse.  This significantly outperforms plastic, which has just a .  Other fiber-based materials help companies adjust to the tightening restrictions and mandates on single-use plastic packaging while simultaneously supporting enduring goals made for resource efficiency and overall recyclability.

The first rising concern about single-use plastics began in the 2010s.  By 2022, the European Commission proposed PPWR to replace the outdated Packaging and Packaging Waste Directive (PPWD) of 1994.  By February 2025, PPWR went into full effect.  In the coming years, the development of secondary legislation will start.  By 2028, mandatory standardized labels will appear on consumer packaging and on all waste sorting receptacles. Later on in the early 2030s, all packaging in the EU, whether locally produced or imported, will officially meet DfR criteria.  Most plastic packaging and plastic parts will meet initial minimum recycled content requirements.  By the end of the decade, all packaging must meet even stricter criteria for recyclability to ensure an even more sustainable world.

The PPWR intends to set a binding packaging waste reduction target of .  Brands that adapt to the DfR mandates from the start by adopting paperboard material and designing for a circular material lifecycle will be better prepared for decades to come.  Additionally, they will also gain an advantage in a competitive market where environmental sustainability is rapidly becoming the criterion.

items.title: GITEX GLOBAL 2026 Puts AI Security, Cyber Resilience and Post-Quantum Readiness in Focus
items.author: Hacker and Technology Events
items.content:
As artificial intelligence moves from experimentation into critical business and government infrastructure, cybersecurity is facing a new set of challenges. Autonomous AI agents, increasingly interconnected systems, and growing concerns around data sovereignty are changing how organizations approach digital security. These developments will take center stage at , taking place December 7–11 in Dubai, UAE. With a dedicated cybersecurity showcase, GITEX is bringing together global cybersecurity companies, government institutions, technology leaders, and industry experts to explore the next generation of digital defense.

GITEX Cyber Valley: Addressing the Next Generation of Cyber Threats

One of the key cybersecurity highlights of this year's event is , which will focus on AI security, dual-use cyber technologies, and post-quantum readiness.

As organizations increasingly deploy AI agents capable of making decisions and executing tasks, questions around accountability, access control, and operational security are becoming more urgent.

The challenge is no longer limited to protecting networks and endpoints. Organizations must also secure the data, infrastructure, and autonomous systems that increasingly power their operations.

GITEX Cyber Valley will bring these conversations together through tailored business meetings and private briefings for global cybersecurity leaders, creating opportunities to examine how organizations can scale AI capabilities while protecting the systems and information they depend on.

Global Cybersecurity Leaders Take the Stage

GITEX GLOBAL 2026 will feature an extensive lineup of cybersecurity companies showcasing technologies and solutions across the security ecosystem.

Confirmed cybersecurity exhibitors include Acronis, AMIVIZ, Cohesity, Commvault, Forcepoint, Forescout, Kaspersky, ManageEngine, NETSCOUT, Netskope, NinjaOne, Proofpoint, SentinelOne / Sentinel Labs, and Trellix.

Their participation reflects the breadth of the cybersecurity landscape, spanning data protection, endpoint security, network defense, threat detection, and enterprise resilience.

The UAE Cybersecurity Council will also participate, alongside other government institutions and public-sector entities, highlighting the importance of collaboration between national cybersecurity strategies and private-sector innovation.

Why AI Is Changing the Cybersecurity Conversation

The growing adoption of AI is creating new opportunities for businesses, but it is also expanding the attack surface.

AI-powered applications, autonomous agents, cloud infrastructure, and connected systems introduce new security considerations. Organizations must account for how AI systems access information, interact with other applications, and operate within critical business environments. At the same time, the emergence of quantum computing is prompting organizations to consider the long-term resilience of their encryption and data protection strategies.

These developments make AI security and post-quantum readiness increasingly important areas of discussion for cybersecurity professionals, technology providers, and government decision-makers.

GITEX GLOBAL's wider focus on sovereign AI, frontier models, agentic AI, and sovereign security provides a broader context for these discussions, connecting cybersecurity with the infrastructure and technologies shaping the next phase of digital transformation.

GITEX Global 2026: A Global Meeting Point for Technology and Cybersecurity

Beyond its cybersecurity programme, GITEX GLOBAL 2026 will bring together more than 6,000 global technology enterprises, government entities, and startups, alongside 1000+ investors representing nearly US$2 trillion in assets under management.

The 2026 edition also introduces a new venue and format. The GITEX Summit will take place on December 7 at Dubai World Trade Centre, followed by four days of exhibitions and conferences from December 8–11 at Dubai Exhibition Centre, Expo City Dubai. Expand North Star, the co-located startup and investor showcase, will run at the same venue.

For cybersecurity professionals, enterprise technology buyers, government representatives, and security innovators, the event offers an opportunity to connect with the companies and decision-makers shaping the future of digital security. As organizations prepare for a new era of AI-driven operations, the conversations at GITEX GLOBAL 2026 will be particularly relevant to those working to balance technological progress with security, resilience, and trust.

items.title: Postgres not using your index? It's counting pages, not rows
items.author: Anatolii Zhadan
items.content:
Slow Postgres, part 1 of 8. The SQL and raw numbers for every test are on GitHub.

You add an index on , run , and Postgres reads the whole table anyway. doesn't change the plan. Someone suggests , the plan finally shows your index, and the query gets slower.

Usually the planner is right. It prices a plan by the 8 KB pages it has to read and by whether it reads them in order or jumps around between them, and once you count pages the same way, you can answer most "why is it ignoring my index" tickets yourself.

One note before the numbers: the AlphaVPS link at the end is a referral link, so I may get a commission at no extra cost to you, and the netcup vouchers come from my own account.

  • Postgres prices a plan in pages, and in my test table a status with 0.9% of the rows sits on 94% of them, so its index saves 12 page reads out of 221.
  • On 5 million rows in RAM, the index beat a full scan up to 10% of the rows when the matches were scattered, and at every share I tried (up to 50%) when they were stored together.
  • Read cold from disk, the scattered lookups at 0.5% and 1% of rows ran 2 to 5 times slower than a full scan, and Postgres still picked them.
  • A 200-row table gets a Seq Scan even when 2 rows match, so a plan from a tiny test copy says nothing about production.
  • Keep out of app code, read before , and if you only query the rare values, index only those rows.

What a B-tree index stores

A regular B-tree index keeps only keys, the values it is sorted by, and next to each key a TID: the row's address in the heap, which is the table's main storage.

A TID is a page number plus a slot on that page. You can see it as the hidden column:

SELECT ctid, id, status FROM orders WHERE status = 'chargeback' ORDER BY id LIMIT 3;

  ctid   |  id  |   status
---------+------+------------
 (7,48)  | 1000 | chargeback
 (14,96) | 2000 | chargeback
 (22,8)  | 3000 | chargeback

Row 1000 is slot 48 on page 7. An index lookup for returns a list of addresses like these, and Postgres then visits each of those heap pages to fetch the row and check that your transaction can see it.

The second step is the one people forget. To fetch one row, Postgres has to read the whole 8 KB page it sits on.

The lab: 30,000 orders on 221 pages

The lab runs on PostgreSQL 17.11 in Docker with default settings. My numbers come from a 4-vCPU, 8 GB cloud VM, but any small VPS or a laptop will do.

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id           bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL,
  amount_cents int NOT NULL,
  status       text NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO orders (created_at, amount_cents, status)
SELECT now() - (30000 - i) * interval '1 minute',
       (random() * 10000)::int,
       CASE
         WHEN i % 1000 = 0 THEN 'chargeback'  -- 30 rows, 0.1%
         WHEN i % 100  = 0 THEN 'failed'      -- 270 rows, 0.9%
         WHEN i % 10   = 0 THEN 'created'     -- 2,700 rows, 9%
         ELSE 'paid'                          -- 27,000 rows, 90%
       END
FROM generate_series(1, 30000) AS i;

CREATE INDEX orders_status_idx ON orders (status);
ANALYZE orders;

SELECT relpages, reltuples FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'orders';

 relpages | reltuples
----------+-----------
      221 |     30000

136 rows fit on a page, so 30,000 rows take 221 pages. I picked 30,000 because samples 300 × default_statistics_target rows, which is 30,000 at the default. On this table it reads every row, so the statistics are exact and your plans should come out the same as mine.

Ask for the most common value and the index goes unused:

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid';

Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..596.00 rows=27000 width=25)
  Filter: (status = 'paid'::text)

221 pages  × seq_page_cost     1.0    = 221
30000 rows × cpu_tuple_cost    0.01   = 300
30000 rows × cpu_operator_cost 0.0025 =  75
                                        ---
                                        596

Cost has no unit you can convert to milliseconds. It only means something next to another plan's cost.

The value you filter on appears nowhere in that formula. Ask for with the index paths switched off and the Seq Scan still costs 596. Only the index path's price moves with the value, so the planner is choosing between a fixed price and a sliding one.

For , every one of the 221 pages holds paid rows, so the index path would read the whole heap plus the index. Force it with and you get a Bitmap Heap Scan at cost 872.

How many pages each status sits on

Selectivity is the share of rows that pass the filter. The usual rule of thumb goes: one row, use the index; 1%, usually; 20%, it depends; 70%, Seq Scan. Here is the same table counted by pages as well as by rows:

SELECT status,
       count(*)                               AS rows,
       count(DISTINCT (ctid::text::point)[0]) AS pages
FROM orders
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY rows DESC;

The rule of thumb says index , and Postgres agrees: Index Scan at cost 235 against 596. Run both with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), though, and the index path touches 209 buffers to the Seq Scan's 221, a saving of twelve page reads.

It still finished faster, 0.19 ms versus 0.93, because checking 270 rows is less CPU work than filtering 30,000. For , 30 rows on 30 pages, the index path needs 32 buffers instead of 221.

Two things decide how rows land on pages. Row width sets how many fit on one, and at 136 rows per page any value much more common than 1 in 136 ends up on nearly every page. Physical order is the other. I spread evenly on purpose. If your failed orders came from one bad deploy on one afternoon, they'd sit on a few neighbouring pages and the index would look great.

Timing it on 5 million rows in RAM

On 221 pages everything finishes in a couple of milliseconds, so for timings I built a bigger table: 5 million rows, 326 MB, about 120 rows per page.

A column holds a random number from 0 to 999,999, so matches 1% of the rows. I loaded the same rows twice, once in random order and once sorted by , and forced each plan with the settings at shares from 0.01% to 50%. was 2 GB, which kept the whole table in memory.

For scattered rows Postgres picked a bitmap scan, which collects all the TIDs first and then reads each heap page once, in page order. Up to 10% of the rows it beat the Seq Scan, 98 ms to 124. At 25% it lost, 174 against 139, and the planner still chose it. A plain Index Scan, one heap visit per row, lost from 5% on.

By 10% the scattered matches sit on every single page, and the bitmap scan still won. It reads all 41,667 pages but checks only the 499,000 rows the bitmap points to, while the Seq Scan checks all 5 million. With the table in RAM a page read costs next to nothing, and the time goes into checking rows.

For clustered rows the index won at every share I tried, even 50%: 123 ms against 142.

The same queries with a cold cache

RAM is the friendly case. For the cold runs I restarted Postgres and dropped the OS page cache before every run, so every page came off the VM's disk.

The Seq Scan got about twice as slow, 250 to 350 ms at every share. The clustered index won everywhere again, 23 ms versus 263 at 5%.

The scattered bitmap scan took 748 ms at 0.5% of rows, to the Seq Scan's 349. At 1% it took 1.27 seconds against 255 ms, five times slower, and that's the plan Postgres picks.

The bitmap scan at 2% read more heap pages than at 1%, 37,939 versus 29,143, and still finished more than six times faster, 190 ms against 1,275. From 2% to 10% it beat the Seq Scan again.

The 2% run touched 91% of the pages, so it was close to one long sequential read. The 1% run touched 70%, with holes in between. My best guess is OS readahead, which prefetches reads that look sequential and gives up when they're full of gaps. I haven't confirmed it yet.

The planner has no way to see that difference. All it has is , a single guess at how much a jump costs next to a sequential read, and it used the same guess for both runs.

Seq Scans on a 200-row table

A 200-row copy shows the other end of the scale, where the table is too small for any index to win.

CREATE TABLE orders_small AS SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id <= 200;
CREATE INDEX ON orders_small (status);
ANALYZE orders_small;

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders_small WHERE status = 'failed';

Seq Scan on orders_small  (cost=0.00..4.50 rows=2 width=25)
  Filter: (status = 'failed'::text)

Only 2 of the 200 rows match, but reading two pages and checking 200 rows costs just 2 + 2 + 0.5 = 4.50. Turn off and the cheapest index plan costs 6.19, because its one index page alone is priced as a random read at . If you check plans on a 200-row test fixture, this is the arithmetic you're looking at, and it tells you nothing about the same query on 30 million rows in production.

"We're on SSDs, set it to 1.1." Fair, and on this table that flips the plan to an Index Scan at cost 2.77. Both versions finish in 10 microseconds or less, so on a table this size it makes no difference.

A partial index instead of enable_seqscan

The one place for is a scratch session, where it shows you what the other plan would cost. It applies to every query in the session, so in app code it also overrides the plans that were right, like 596 against 872 for .

If the queries you care about only ask for the rare values, say a failed-payments dashboard or a chargeback queue, index only those rows:

CREATE INDEX orders_status_not_paid_idx ON orders (status)
  WHERE status <> 'paid';

It holds 3,000 entries instead of 30,000 and takes 5 pages, where the full index takes 28. Paid orders, 90% of the inserts here, never touch it.

Postgres only uses it when it can prove your filter implies the index's , and a literal does. With only the partial index in place, a prepared under a generic plan falls back to a Seq Scan, because the planner can't prove anything about a value it hasn't seen. Generic plans get their own part later in the series.

The planner's statistics in pg_stats

Before adding an index, look at the column in :

SELECT null_frac, n_distinct, most_common_vals, most_common_freqs
FROM pg_stats
WHERE schemaname = 'public' AND tablename = 'orders' AND attname = 'status';

 null_frac | n_distinct |         most_common_vals         |   most_common_freqs
-----------+------------+----------------------------------+------------------------
         0 |          4 | {paid,created,failed,chargeback} | {0.9,0.09,0.009,0.001}

That's what the planner believes about as of the last . If most of your queries filter on , at 0.9, they get a Seq Scan, and no extra index will change that.

A negative means a fraction of the row count. On tables bigger than the 30,000-row sample these numbers are estimates; you can raise the sample with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET STATISTICS.

The same view has a column, the planner's idea of physical order. On my 5-million-row tables it was 0.01 for the scattered copy and 1 for the clustered one, and that difference in physical order is what separates the scattered and clustered lines in both charts.

Before , run the query, and the rows-versus-pages count on your own table. If the value you care about sits on most of the pages and the table doesn't stay in memory, the index won't save you reads.

Run it on your own server

All the numbers above come from one 4-vCPU AMD EPYC cloud VM with 8 GB of RAM, so yours will differ. The SQL, the scripts, the raw output and the chart code are on GitHub. Run them on your own server, and if you get a different picture or think I got something wrong, open an issue or a PR.

My own projects run on netcup (VPS from €2.21 a month) and AlphaVPS (VPS from €2.54 a month). If you need a box for this, either works.

For netcup I have a few €5 vouchers for new customers. Each one works once, so take one and leave the rest for the next person:

36nc179418264998
36nc179418264997
36nc179418264996
36nc179418264995
36nc179418264994
36nc179418264993

Paste it into the "Redeem voucher" field at the bottom of the netcup cart. If they're all gone, message me on LinkedIn and I'll send you a new one.

Good luck with your plans. Part 2 is next: how to read Postgres EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

items.title: Tech Adoption Is a Cultural Problem: Why UX Habits Beat Innovation
items.author: Daria Volkova
items.content:
"You’re using our platform wrong."

Oh no, sweetheart. Culture doesn’t adapt to your technology.

Stop blaming Mercury in retrograde when users refuse to abandon their old habits for your shiny new tool. The pattern is always the same: the best tool in the room loses to the one people already trust. Founders file this failure under pricing, onboarding, or "users who need education." In reality, it belongs under culture.

My name is I help tech companies explain what makes their products different and why they matter. At university, I studied sociology and cultural studies. It taught me to look at people in groups first, and products second.

Look at the current wave of AI: the had stellar backers, deep pockets, and massive hype. It was dead in a year. was a plain text box, and it became the fastest-growing app in history. Same period, same underlying tech, and culture decided which one survived.

In 2020, a Japanese minister went to war on two office objects: the fax machine and the hanko, the small personal seal people stamp in red ink instead of signing.

(Minister for Digital Transformation of Japan) had the power and the better technology. A signed PDF is faster, cheaper, and easier to search than a stamped fax. He got most government offices to agree to drop the seal. Years later, the fax still hums and the seal still sits in the drawer.

The seal survived because in Japan it was never only a tool. It stands for identity and consent. A company, a bank, and a neighbor all read it the same way. A better tool cannot push out a habit the whole country trusts.

In , credit cards never caught on; by 2021 only about 38 percent of adults had one. So people skipped the card and went from cash straight to the QR code.

Today two apps, , handle more than nine in ten mobile payments, from the fruit stall to the temple donation box.

The same thing happens inside companies now. A team gets a powerful new AI tool, and people keep working the old way, because the old way is the one they trust.

How did manage to become so popular and usher in a new era of consumer AI? People already knew how to type a question into a box, the way they type into Google or a chat with a friend.

More than a million people tried it in five days. Around 100 million were using it two months after launch. TikTok took nine months to reach that number. Instagram took more than two years.

ChatGPT did not ask us to adopt a new habit or buy a new device. The company didn't ruin our familiar flow.

Strong tech can still read the room wrong

The launched in 2024 with huge attention. It clipped to your shirt, had no screen, and answered out loud or showed tiny text on your palm. To use it, people had to wear a new device, learn new hand gestures, and talk to their own chest in public.

By the summer, the company was taking back more pins each day than it sold. In 2025, HP bought what was left for 116 million dollars and switched the pins off.

The , another AI gadget from the same year, got the same cold response. Both asked people to build a habit from zero, with nothing pushing them to do it.

Great tech can still misjudge the culture it lands in. In February 2024, added image generation to Asked for pictures of people from history, it often returned images that did not match the record. The reaction was loud and fast. Within days, Google paused the feature for images of people. The fix took months.

Respect the culture, or build a bridge

The temptation for founders and product builders is always to focus on the raw technology: the compute power, the model architecture, the sheer wizardry of what a tool can do. But history rewards the technology that integrates seamlessly into how humans already behave.

If you are building something new, you have only two choices:

  1. Fit into existing culture and routines: Design your product around habits people already practice every single day. Meet them where they live: in the text box, the chat window, or their current workflow.
  2. If your technology requires people to act differently, you must make the transition so effortless and the value so overwhelming that they voluntarily unlearn the old way.

Tech fails when it assumes people will change their culture just to use a clever tool. Culture is stubborn, patient, and deeply rooted. Ignore human behavior, and your brilliant creation will end up abandoned.

💬 Have a story to share or want to add your example of tech product adoption? Let me know in the comments.

items.title: The Digital Euro: Solving Problems You Didn’t Have, With Rules You Don’t Write
items.author: Ras Vasilisin
items.content:
Do you actually need a digital euro because payments weren’t convenient enough already?

I pay for everything with my phone. Instantly. Even when I’m abroad. To be fair, I’m still glad we actually get to live in the 21st century.

And no, it’s not because they want to ban cash. Cash is already quietly fading out of daily use in Europe. It’s certainly not because someone at a central bank suddenly developed a burning passion for transparency and democratisation.

So let’s look at what’s actually being built, who gets to set the rules, and most importantly, why it’s being built at all.

A pilot is not a public launch

(It’s just the rehearsal where nobody gets to leave)

According to ECB Executive Board member Piero Cipollone’s speech on 5 November 2026, they plan a 12-month pilot in the second half of 2027.

It will involve 36 payment service providers, including Deutsche Bank, UniCredit, Revolut, Stripe, and Adyen. Testing will cover ordinary situations: purchases, transfers, and refunds.

Harmless on paper. For now.

2029 is more of a wish than a deadline

According to the ECB, the target for a possible first issuance is 2029, but only if the necessary legislation is adopted by the end of 2026. Only then would the Governing Council decide whether to issue it at all.

Preparing a system and approving its use are two separate decisions. News headlines tend to treat them as the same thing.

These aren’t “your” deposits

It might come as a shock, but the balance you see in your banking app isn’t actually your money. It’s a promise from your local bank that they’ll repay it one day. A digital euro would move that promise even further away, all the way behind the walls of the ECB headquarters in Frankfurt.

Apart from that minor detail, your brand-new digital euro would be almost identical to what you already use.

It would still be worth one euro. It would still appear on your screen as if you owned it. And it would still not be immune to money printing, inflation, or devaluation.

Under the proposed design it wouldn’t even pay the princely 0.05% interest some accounts currently offer. And there would be a limit on how much you could hold. Roughly €3,000 was one of the options analysed, not a final rule.

Europe doesn’t want to depend on Visa and Mastercard

Now, to be fair, there is one legitimate point in favor of the digital euro.

For card payments, Europe still depends heavily on non-European companies, in practice, mainly Visa and Mastercard. A shared European payments infrastructure makes sense as a political and economic objective. The real test is whether regular people actually get enough out of the digital euro to bother switching.

Good luck convincing 450 million people to just switch up their daily habits. Especially when the new system arrives with holding limits, no interest, and a few extra questions about why you’re using it.

Now for the part everyone’s actually worried about: privacy.

For offline payments, the intention is cash-like privacy, personal transaction details known only to the payer and the recipient.

That does not mean the entire wallet would operate anonymously like cash. Anti-money-laundering checks would still apply when depositing, transferring or withdrawing funds.

If losing privacy on offline transactions worries you, online payments are a whole different story. Naturally, the ECB promises to process data so it can’t be traced straight back to you. Your bank or payment provider would still have identification and other legal obligations.

In other words, the ECB says it will not monitor everything you buy. Your local bank will.

The ECB says the digital euro would not be programmable money. The issuer wouldn’t dictate where, when or on what you could spend it. That’s different from a conditional payment you choose to arrange yourself.

So there’s no need for panic about your money expiring or a sudden ban on steak purchases.

There is a good reason to check whether protection against such restrictions remains firmly written into the final rules. A press release is no substitute for a legal safeguard.

The same applies to cash. The ECB says the digital euro would complement it, not replace it. What matters is whether people can actually keep using cash, and whether pulling it out of your wallet is still treated as normal rather than vaguely suspicious.

The digital euro and Bitcoin serve different purposes.

A digital euro would remain a euro, governed by monetary and public institutions.

As I learned the hard way after a single copy-paste mistake sent a test transfer straight into oblivion: with Bitcoin, I don’t need a central issuer to hold or send my money. The catch? If I hold my own keys, protecting them is entirely on me.

Bitcoin isn’t magically anonymous, either. Its public ledger and wild price swings don’t vanish just because we’re fed up with central banks.

I judge the digital euro on whether it actually fixes payments without chipping away at our rights. I judge Bitcoin on its own merits and risks. They’re playing entirely different games.

The digital euro isn’t about easier coffee purchases.

Money is a form of expression. How we spend it, who we send it to, and whether we can do so with a degree of privacy is part of personal freedom. If we trade that for a new shiny digital euro, we may one day discover we have lost both the convenience and the freedoms.

Once the rules are written and the system is live, complaining that “this wasn’t what we signed up for” will be largely irrelevant.

The real question isn’t whether the digital euro happens.

It’s whether we wake up in time to realize our right to use our own money is being quietly rewritten. Politely, step by step, and backed by world-class PR.

items.title: Educational Byte: What Is a Liquidity Pool in Crypto —and Why It Matters
items.author: Obyte
items.content:
To understand this one, let’s first look at the "traditional" processes for exchanging money via digital platforms. We can commonly see two mechanisms: you exchange your currency directly against the exchange or provider’s own funds, or an order book is used. This order book records all buy and sell orders placed by users and provides liquidity based on that activity. The more orders in place, the more liquidity. Well, liquidity pools have come to replace these models in Decentralized Finance (DeFi) protocols.

A liquidity pool in crypto is a supply of tokens locked inside a smart contract on a DeFi protocol. It has the purpose of offering liquidity to other users for swaps, loans, or any financial activity on that specific protocol. The locked funds come from other users who, in exchange for providing this liquidity to the pool, receive rewards in the form of transaction fees and even .

This way, no powerful middlemen are required to safely access financial instruments. It’s the users themselves who provide liquidity in a decentralized environment.

How Does a Liquidity Pool Work?

Typically, a liquidity pool holds two tokens, such as GBYTE and USDC. Liquidity providers are the ones who deposit these token pairs—and they could be anyone with the available funds. Then, those funds help to create a big reserve that traders can use for their own operations, like swaps. The smart contract keeps track of those balances and applies the rules that govern each trade.

comes from the reserves themselves. In a classic Automated Market Maker (AMM) model, a simple formula is used: X × Y = K, where X and Y represent the quantities of the two tokens and K is the constant. When someone swaps, let’s say, USDC for GBYTE, the pool receives one asset and releases the other, changing the balances and thus the price for the next trade. Depending on the available liquidity, a larger trade may create more price impact, which implies that the price could drop by a certain percentage for the next swap.

For liquidity providers, the platform may give them LP tokens as proof of their share of the pool. These tokens can be used to track and redeem that share, including the depositor’s portion of trading fees earned by the pool. Their reward is directly proportional to their contribution to the pool.

Some pools may be rewarded with additional incentives. For instance, in the Obyte-based DEX , all to a few selected pools receive 100 GBYTE every seven days, distributed in proportion to their contributed liquidity. That’s an additional incentive on top of fees.

Why Does This Model Matter?

A healthy financial environment needs liquidity, and liquidity doesn’t come out of nowhere. For trades and other operations to actually happen, funds must be available, and someone must put the funds there. In traditional finance, that someone is often a powerful middleman, like a bank. But cryptocurrencies weren’t created to rely on powerful middlemen; they were created to get rid of them. So, we have liquidity pools instead.

By using this model, everyone can access liquidity without cumbersome requirements or censorship risks. Meanwhile, liquidity providers receive rewards for their contributions in what is, without a doubt, a type of investment that can yield a good and frequent passive return. Of course, the specific rules and the vary from network to network.

uses a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) structure without miners or “validators,” which increases its decentralization and drastically reduces the mere possibility of censorship or blocking. In Oswap.io, each pool has its own parameters and governance, but all are decentralized and open for everyone to participate. That’s the whole idea; that’s why liquidity pools matter: they offer a freedom we can’t enjoy in traditional financial products.

Featured Vector Image by pikisuperstar /

items.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia Exit Is a Wake-Up Call for Startup Founders
items.author: Bruce Li
items.content:
The Unthinkable Happened on a Thursday

I had to read the headline three times.

This morning, November 12, 2026, Nvidia's board said Jensen Huang had resigned as President, CEO, and director, . CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO. The board also named Harvey C. Jones as its , which tells you it had been a one-man show for 33 years.

The board's word is "resigned." Most headlines went with "ousted." Days earlier, CBS had reported the board was to remove him. You decide which word fits.

Here's the short version. A New York Times report alleged multiple affairs, including one with a Singapore data-center executive whom U.S. officials reportedly suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence, at a firm that bought billions of dollars of Nvidia hardware. Another alleged affair was with a senior executive who reported directly to him. Huang had already admitted infidelity in a memo to employees on November 9. Then came national-security questions, demands from lawmakers, and a stock that fell roughly 10%, wiping out hundreds of billions in market value. After that, the end came quickly.

Set the morality aside for a minute, because the board didn't need to settle it. What I want founders to notice is the .

Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in a Denny's in 1993. He bet the company on GPUs, then on CUDA, then on AI, and grew it into a company worth more than $4 trillion. He is about as close to a founder-god as Silicon Valley has.

And he had no structural protection whatsoever.

Nvidia has a single class of stock: one share, one vote. Its board was made up of independent directors plus Jensen, and it could remove the CEO with or without cause by simple majority. Mark Zuckerberg can't be fired. Larry Page couldn't be fired. Jensen Huang, the man who made the AI age possible, could be shown the door in a week.

If that doesn't make every founder reading this check their charter, nothing will.

Why Founders Fall: A Short History of Losing Your Own Company

Founders don't usually lose control in one dramatic boardroom scene. They lose it gradually, through a series of small and individually reasonable decisions.

Act I: One share, one vote. For about sixty years the NYSE refused to list companies with dual-class shares. The idea was that voting power should track economic risk. Ford's 1956 IPO, where the family kept super-voting shares, was the famous exception. Media dynasties like the New York Times Company got a pass on the grounds of editorial independence.

Act II: Google changes the rules. In 2004, Larry Page and Sergey Brin took Google public with Class B shares carrying . The public bought it anyway. Facebook, LinkedIn, Snap, and Alibaba all followed. Hong Kong held out, lost Alibaba's $25 billion IPO to New York, and changed its rules in 2018. By 2021–22, about were dual-class.

Act III: the slow loss of your majority. This is the part nobody puts in the pitch deck. According to Carta's 2025–26 data, founders typically hold:

  • after Series A (thanks, pre-money option pool)
  • after Series C, which is less than the employee option pool

Capital intensity makes it worse. If your company works with atoms (chips, robots, biotech), you burn two to three times the cash of a SaaS company and sell more of the company at every round. Jensen is the hardware founder's cautionary tale: decades of capital-hungry growth, and nothing left to vote with when it counted.

The lesson: you don't lose control when the board votes. You lose it, one term sheet at a time, years before.

Case Study: Apple and the Prodigal Son

Every founder knows this story, and every founder assumes it couldn't happen to them.

In 1985, Steve Jobs was 30, a co-founder of Apple, and the person most responsible for its products and culture. He had no super-voting shares. The Macintosh launched to great reviews and disappointing sales. Jobs's "my way or the highway" style wore everyone out. John Sculley, the Pepsi executive Jobs had personally recruited with the famous "sugar water" pitch, moved to take away his operating authority.

Jobs tried to get Sculley removed instead. The plan leaked, the board backed Sculley, and Jobs, with no structural power at all, resigned and went off to start NeXT.

What followed was a twelve-year slide that brought Apple to within about 90 days of insolvency in 1997. The board, out of options, bought NeXT, mostly to get Jobs back. You know the rest: iMac, iPod, iPhone, and the most valuable company on Earth.

Dual-class advocates like to say that if Jobs had held super-voting stock, Apple would have skipped a lost decade.

Maybe. I'll give you the more uncomfortable version. The Jobs who got fired was probably not the Jobs who saved Apple. NeXT and Pixar humbled him and taught him things, and he came back a better CEO. Getting fired may have been the most valuable thing that ever happened to him, though it's hard to see it that way while it's happening.

The Counter-Lesson: WeWork, or What Happens When Nobody Can Say No

Adam Neumann got the thing Jobs never had: . The board couldn't fire him, investors couldn't overrule him, and he ran the company accordingly.

He bought buildings personally and leased them back to WeWork. He trademarked the word "We" and had his own company pay him for it. (He reversed that after the public backlash, which is a bit like returning the cookie once your mom has already seen the crumbs.)

When the S-1 came out in August 2019, public investors saw $47 billion in lease obligations against $4 billion in committed revenue, plus governance that made Apple's 1985 board look like the Federalist Papers. The IPO collapsed and SoftBank had to fund a bailout. Neumann was out, and in 2023 the company filed for Chapter 11.

Here's the lesson I care about most. Super-voting stock does two things: it protects you from the market's panic, and it protects you from your own mistakes. The first is valuable. The second can kill the company. The same structure that would have saved 1985 Jobs from Sculley also saved Neumann from anyone who might have told him no.

So what should you actually do? Here is the playbook, roughly by stage. If you can, negotiate these terms when you have leverage, which means you need the money.

  • Founder-friendly charter from day one. Authorizing a high-vote Class B institutional money arrives is far easier than recapitalizing later. Musk said he wanted 25% voting control at Tesla and admitted that retrofitting dual-class after the IPO is close to impossible. Don't put yourself in that position.
  • Clean vesting and 83(b) elections. These are boring and they are essential.
  • Board composition is the real cap table. Lock in seats elected by common stockholders. A 2-1-2 board (two founders, one independent, two VCs) holds up much better than a board where you have one seat and keep telling yourself the independent director is on your side.
  • Supermajority to fire the CEO. Make your own termination without cause require a supermajority of the board. That gives you a veto over your own exit.
  • The 2026 NVCA baseline lets a majority of preferred force a sale. Push for a (preferred common) and a , so you can't be forced to sign a deal in which the liquidation preferences consume everything and common gets nothing.
  • These let you take some money off the table in a later round without giving up voting control. A founder who can pay the mortgage makes better long-term decisions.
  • Dual-class with a sunset you choose. Glass Lewis and ISS now recommend voting against directors at companies that IPO without a time-based sunset. Pick your own, seven to ten years, before someone picks one for you.
  • Choose your jurisdiction deliberately. Delaware's new Section 122(18) makes founder consent rights in stockholder agreements enforceable again after . Texas offers friendlier rules for controllers and has a growing business court. (See: Tesla's move after .)
  • Character is part of your governance. No structure would have protected Jensen this week. Nvidia's code of conduct, the national-security issues, and lawmakers demanding briefings would have overridden any share class. Super-voting stock doesn't protect you from regulators, prosecutors, or your own direct reports.

The Balance: Governance as Seatbelt, Not Leash

The academics have a useful framework for this. are the damage a founder does when nobody can stop them; that's WeWork. are the damage investors do when they're in charge: panic, short-termism, and a buyback where an R&D budget should be. That's 1985 Apple.

Law professors Zohar Goshen and Richard Squire argue the right structure of the two. A visionary founder in a 20-year bet like AI, VR, or rockets should get more insulation. A mature company with a founder who has drifted should get less.

The data supports this. Dual-class firms trade at a at IPO, because markets value the founder's vision. Around later, that premium tends to become a discount as the founder's economic stake shrinks while their votes don't.

So the goal isn't maximum control. It's control that fits where your company is in its life: enough insulation to make long-term bets, with a working mechanism for someone to say "stop" if you lose your way.

Jensen had plenty of the first and none of the second, which was fine for 33 years until this week. Neumann had too much of both. Jobs had none, and it took a lost decade to fix.

Here's what I expect over the next five years.

1. The Jensen effect on fundraising. Founders raising in 2027 will bring up Nvidia in every board-composition negotiation, and investors will bring up WeWork. Both are fair points.

2. Trust-based structures as the new middle ground. Anthropic's S-1 shows a new model. The founders hold a Class F share that gives them 50.1% of ordinary votes, while an independent with no economic stake elects a majority of the board. The founders control the shareholder vote, and the trust controls the board. OpenAI's foundation keeps exclusive power over its PBC's board even though Microsoft owns 27% of the equity. These are deliberate checks and balances in a company charter, and you'll see others copy them.

3. Sunsets become standard. Perpetual founder control is ending. Index providers, proxy advisors, and institutional investors all agree on that. Expect seven-to-ten-year sunsets to become the price of a dual-class IPO.

4. The jurisdiction wars continue. Delaware vs. Texas vs. Nevada. Your state of incorporation is now a strategic decision, not a box your lawyer checks.

5. Character as a governance mechanism. This is the uncomfortable one. As founders gain more structural protection, the remaining risks come from conduct: personal behavior, conflicts of interest, national security. Those risks don't care how many votes your shares carry.

My closing advice to every engineer-founder reading this:

Fight for control early, when it's cheap. Protect it with structure, not just goodwill. Give it an expiration date before someone else does. And above all, build a company and a character that a board would never want to fire.

Jensen Huang built one of the greatest companies in history and still lost it in a week. Your share structure can't fully protect you from yourself, so you'll have to manage that part on your own.

items.title: Claude Merged 30,401 Changes in One Day. Git Couldn't Keep Up.
items.author: Sidra Zafar
items.content:
An agent gets a task - fix a flaky test. Before it reads a single line of code, it needs a working copy of the repository.

Under git, that meant waiting 7.1 minutes.

Multiply that wait by tens of thousands of agents a day and you get the problem Anthropic described in its engineering post on 13 October 2026. The code wasn't the slow part any more. Claude could write the fix in seconds; the plumbing built for human engineers (source control, builds, CI) couldn't hand it the repo fast enough.

So Anthropic threw out git for its main repository and built Scion.

January: about 1,000 merges a day

The numbers tell the story better than I can. In January 2026, Anthropic merged roughly 1,000 code changes a day. By May it was about 2,500.

The team tried everything git offers to cope: shallow clones, sparse checkouts, promisor remotes, repository snapshots and several hundred git mirrors. Each one bought time. None of them bought enough, because the main-branch history was close to 100 GB and the compressed working copy was over 25 GB. CI alone ran around 25 million checkouts a day.

The mirrors eventually outgrew their disks. At that point you can split the monorepo (and lose speed) or rebuild source control. Anthropic picked the second option.

9 September: 30,401 merges

By September, Anthropic was merging more than 30,000 changes a day. The peak was 30,401 on 9 September. That's a 12x jump in four months, and most of it came from Claude.

That's the day git stopped being a tool and became a ceiling.

Scion looks more like Subversion than git, and Anthropic says so openly. Git assumes every client is a full copy of history that can work offline. Scion assumes the opposite: clients are always online, so the server does the heavy lifting.

The stack has four layers:

  • , the client that runs on a developer laptop or inside an agent's sandbox
  • , one per machine, which shares cached objects across every job on that node
  • , regional caches that sit between the machines and the source of truth
  • , the authoritative layer, backed by Google Spanner and cloud storage

Anthropic reports a cache hit rate above 99% at every tier. Almost nothing travels all the way to the servers.

The unit of history changes too. A git commit points to a full tree. A Scion lists only the files that changed relative to its first parent, each with a content-addressed pointer to a compressed blob. The server works out trees, history and blame from those changesets when someone asks.

Branches are discouraged, except for main and release branches. Creating a changeset never touches a branch; moving one is a single compare-and-swap on one Spanner row. That's why 30,000 merges a day don't trip over each other.

How Claude ships a change on Scion, step by step

Anthropic's post doesn't publish a single runbook, so this is the flow pieced together from what the team described. Follow one agent and one flaky test.

Step 1: Get a worktree in seconds. Claude asks for a working copy. It doesn't clone anything. The client names the root tree it wants and fetches only the objects it's missing, usually from the local daemon. Checkouts are sparse or virtual: a file lands on disk only when Claude opens it. A new agent worktree went from 7.1 minutes to 5.1 seconds, an 84x speedup.

Step 2: Ask the server questions instead of the disk. Where was this test last changed? Who touched this function? Under git, Claude would run or over local history. Under Scion, history, blame and diffs are server queries exposed through an API. Many jobs never need a local repository at all; Anthropic says its automated bisect and revert pipelines wouldn't be practical at scale without this.

Step 3: Edit, and let status stay cheap. Claude changes two files. The client watches the filesystem rather than rescanning the whole tree, so checking status for an agent fell from 4.3 seconds to under 0.2.

Step 4: Commit straight to the server. A commit creates a changeset on the server, and it's visible everywhere at once. There's no push step and no packfile negotiation. An agent commit dropped from 18 seconds to 761 milliseconds.

Step 5: Open a change request in Antique. Antique is Anthropic's new code review tool, built alongside Scion. Reviewers check the of a change, not every line. Semantic approval rules can tell a comment-only edit apart from one that touches sensitive logic, so the review effort goes where the risk is. Review moved to Antique between May and June 2026; by August almost every merged change went through it.

Step 6: Merge without a global queue. Here's the part that surprised me. Anthropic dropped the old globally locked merge queue, because serialising 30,000 merges a day doesn't work. Changes merge concurrently. When two of them conflict, Claude repairs the conflict.

Step 7: Test after merge, before deploy. With no queue holding everything back, the safety net moves later. Post-merge and pre-deploy testing catches what pre-merge serialisation used to. If something breaks, the same cheap server-side history powers the automated bisect and revert.

Add it all up and the source-control overhead for one change request fell from 34 minutes to 3.7 minutes. Across roughly 22,000 change requests a day, that's a lot of machine time handed back.

The part Claude built itself

There's a loop in this story I find hard to ignore. Claude created the load that broke git, and then Claude helped build the replacement.

Engineers set the architecture, the scaling targets and the invariants. Claude wrote much of the code; the source control and Antique directories received 12,257 changes between January and September. The team's original git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline was hand-written. They gave it to an early internal snapshot of Claude Mythos Preview and asked for a rewrite, with no further instructions. The new version used 20x less memory and ran 4x faster, and it kept the ordering rules the old one relied on.

The team also runs dedicated Claude instances that each watch one component's telemetry and logs (the daemon, the cache, Antique's merge flow). And the engineers' most common job, by their own account, was telling Claude "no"; for example, when it read the commit log instead of querying the review tool.

Scion isn't free. You lose offline work: no server, no source control. You also lose portability, because Scion only makes sense with Anthropic's own review, search and CI systems wired around it.

The results, as Anthropic reports them on its own workload:

Source control per change request

The infrastructure footprint shrank about 200x compared with the git mirror fleet, and CI needed 25% less CPU. These aren't general benchmarks against git, and Anthropic is careful to say so.

You can't. Scion isn't open source, and Anthropic calls it "by no means a suitable replacement for git for general use."

What it does want is for git platforms to borrow the ideas: full server-side APIs, a better fetch protocol, and stronger sparse and shallow support for agent-sized workloads. It credits Google's Piper, Meta's Sapling and the Mononoke server (with its Bonsai data model) for many of the techniques.

If your team runs a handful of agents, git is fine. If you're heading toward thousands, look at where your agents spend their first seven minutes.

That's where Anthropic found 30,000 merges a day.

Sources: Anthropic Engineering, "Redesigning source control at Anthropic" (13 October 2026, updated 15 October); coverage by InfoQ, Simon Willison and Matthews Wong. All performance figures are company-reported.

items.title: The Psychology of Luxury Marketing: Why We Pay More for Less
items.author: yuna
items.content:
Have you ever looked at a piece of bent metal and thought, “Why does this cost as much as a decent used car?”

Recently, I stumbled across a Ferrari metal collar online. It cost . It looked like someone picked up a sheet of basic aluminum, bent it aggressively, painted it red, and said, “Yep, that’ll be two grand and a half, please.”

It made me genuinely sit down and ask: Why the fuck would anyone pay that?

Well, welcome to a niche little world called luxury marketing, which apparently means we add a ridiculous price tag to ordinary items and watch everyone scramble to buy them.

Luxury marketing has three main pillars that conveniently work together to gaslight you into thinking that a tiny bottle of perfume = a down payment for a prime city apartment is a completely reasonable thing to pay for.

The three main pillars of luxury marketing are: I know those sound like really scary terms, but trust me, I’m going to hold your hand and explain how they collectively gaslight you.

I’m not a marketing person. All of this has come from research papers and articles I’ve read, plus whatever marginal bits I actually understood from them. 😭)

When you think something you want is about to sell out, you’re more likely to impulsively buy it, even if you haven’t stopped to think about the pros and cons yet. You see something you like, notice that there is very little stock left, and suddenly you’re buying it without thinking about whether you actually need it or not.

That’s essentially what the illusion of scarcity is: less availability, more wanting, quicker decisions, more impulsive buying, more urgency, and ultimately, more sales.

→ What is the Illusion of Scarcity?

The illusion of scarcity refers to the tactic of creating a perception that a product or service is in limited supply when, in reality, it might not be.

It plays on the psychological principle that people are more likely to desire something they believe is running out or hard to obtain.

  • FOMO [Fear of Missing Out]

It compels people to take action when they believe they might miss out on something valuable or desirable.

The illusion of scarcity uses this fear to make customers more likely to buy to avoid the regret of missing out.

People are more motivated by the prospect of avoiding loss rather than gaining something.

The illusion of scarcity creates a sense of potential loss. Consumers fear losing the opportunity to purchase the product or service. This fear of loss motivates consumers more than the desire to gain, pushing them to act quickly.

When a consumer sees that a product is in limited stock or others are purchasing it quickly, they are more likely to believe the product is valuable and worth buying. The perception is reinforced by the idea that if others are scrambling to buy it, it must be worth having.

(Shameless advertisement: I talk more about this in my July edition, where I talked about how Red Bull used this tactic in the trash can myth. For more info, click here — July Edition.)

In luxury marketing, people aren’t just buying the product; they are buying the perceived social status that the said product provides them with.

In emerging markets (such as the BRIC nations, i.e., Brazil, Russia, India, and China), it was observed that logo-flashy or more easily recognised luxury goods are more widely sought after by people, as they felt the need to separate themselves from the masses and perceive a higher social status, like Look at me, I am richer as compared to you, which is why I am higher on the social ladder as compared to you and make themselves stand out.

Meanwhile, mature markets (such as the United States, Italy, and France) were observed to be moving towards more subtle, less flashy luxury items which aren’t very easily recognisable by someone who doesn’t know about it because they tend to do it for (so-called) internalised-luxury consumption. The term refers to the perception of purchasing luxury goods for themselves or to express themselves better and to integrate themselves into a certain social group.

Mature market, in the above context, refers to markets that have reached a certain equilibrium and are characterised by modest growth.

An emerging market, in the above context, refers to markets that have a chronic shortage of resources and are characterised by inadequate infrastructure but also yield impressive economic growth.

So, in mature markets, people are moving towards a more subtle display of luxury, such as minimalistic or no logos, or a higher emphasis on the craftsmanship of the product. While emerging markets move more towards flashy, easily recognisable logos or/and patterns.

Yet in general, both aren’t buying the product for the utilitarian purpose of the product, but rather are purchasing the product or service to display a certain social status and separate themselves from the masses, such as: I am different from you; I have a higher perceived social status than you; and I’m richer than you, and I have a certain expensiveness that you lack and am living a certain level of luxurious lifestyle that you cannot attain.

Luxury marketing emphasizes the item's perceived social status. And consumers invest in it as they associate a certain sense of self-importance and a separation from the masses and their supposed (*air quotes*) superior social status with the ownership of the product, and therefore are willing to invest more in products that are marketed as a luxury, with the illusion of scarcity, than what might be the actual justified cost of the product solely based on utility if it wasn’t marketed as a luxury good or service.

Heritage is a crucial part of a luxury brand, as it needs to have a modern aspect for the current society yet, at the same time, have a certain historical aspect to it.

It adds an association of depth, authenticity, and credibility to the brand's perceived value and can result in increased brand loyalty and a willingness to accept higher prices.

It marks within itself the strategic cultivation of the brand’s origins, traditions, and values over time. As Heritage builds on permanence, prestige, and authenticity, it gives luxury consumers a narrative and a mythology to associate themselves with, linking back to how they view their perceived social status increasing with consumption of luxury brands’ goods and/or services.

items.title: How I Built an On-Device Trading Card Scanner With Apple Vision
items.author: Evan
items.content:
How the scanner in Foilcase works out which printing of a trading card it is looking at: Vision feature prints for the artwork, text recognition for the collector number, and a strict rule for when to ask instead of guessing. Plus the storage underneath it: an append-only ledger and one daily price file for everyone. Foilcase is my iPhone app for scanning and pricing cards from five trading card games (App Store); the user-facing write-up covers what it does.

Why artwork matching picks the wrong print

Before release I built a harness on a Mac that calls the same Vision APIs as the app: 9,903 cards indexed, 400 queries, half drawn on purpose from collector numbers that more than one print shares. Each query was a synthetic degradation of an official card image (perspective, blur, glare, colour cast, JPEG).

Artwork, top-1 on shared numbers

Artwork, top-1 when given the correct number

The last row changed the design. Even with the right collector number, artwork matching picks the right print 89.5% of the time, because alternate arts and higher-rarity parallels often share one number and one illustration. No embedding separates two prints of one picture, so the app asks which print, as it asks whether a card is foil. And since five candidates nearly always include the right card, the five-card sheet is the main flow, not an error state.

The embedding is VNGenerateImageFeaturePrintRequest, revision 2: 768 floats, about 9 ms an image. One option matters more than it looks:

static func featurePrint(of image: CIImage) -> [Float]? {
    let request = VNGenerateImageFeaturePrintRequest()
    request.imageCropAndScaleOption = .scaleFill
    try? VNImageRequestHandler(ciImage: image, options: [:]).perform([request])
    guard let observation = request.results?.first else { return nil }
    var vector = [Float](repeating: 0, count: observation.elementCount)
    _ = vector.withUnsafeMutableBytes { observation.data.copyBytes(to: $0) }
    return vector
}

static let artworkMatchingAvailable: Bool = {
    let probe = CIImage(color: .gray).cropped(to: CGRect(x: 0, y: 0, width: 64, height: 90))
    return featurePrint(of: probe) != nil
}()

The default, , cuts the top and bottom off a tall card: 82.4% against 93.2% for on the same 1,295-card index. The probe exists because feature prints fail in the Simulator ("Failed to create espresso context"). The app checks once and falls back to the collector number alone, as it would on any device without a usable neural engine.

Distance is not a confidence score

The obvious next step is a distance threshold. Measured, it says almost nothing: median distance was 0.450 when the top match was right and 0.420 when it was wrong. But distance does tell whether there is a card at all: photographed cards sat at a median of 0.459, a phone pointed at a laptop at 0.966. I found that out when the scanner, with no ceiling, turned a browser window into twenty-six confident entries. The ceiling is now 0.80, which keeps 99% of photographed cards and rejects 89% of everything else.

Reading the collector number

The number is unambiguous whenever it is legible, so most of the work went into legibility.

Between a handheld frame and a sharp one, the artwork gained 5.6 points and the collector number 46 (32.8% read against 78.5%). The gate is the variance of the Laplacian on a greyscale buffer of the rectified card. My first version chained Core Image filters, a Laplacian then a multiply blend, and returned negative variances: blend modes clamp and premultiply, they are not arithmetic.

Don't ask Vision to find the card. On iOS, VNDetectDocumentSegmentationRequest returned the card's text box at 0.96 confidence, and VNDetectRectanglesRequest found artwork panels, never the border. So the scanner draws a card-shaped guide, tries three crops around it and keeps whichever embeds closest to the index.

Read in passes, at full size. Downscaling crops is how my first benchmark reported an OCR accuracy of zero. runs over the whole card, then the top and bottom 22% enlarged 2.5 times, then three corners at 4 times if nothing turned up:

private func scan(_ image: CIImage, into found: inout Set<String>, minimumTextHeight: Float = 0.008) {
    let request = VNRecognizeTextRequest()
    request.recognitionLevel = .accurate
    request.usesLanguageCorrection = false   // these are codes, not words
    request.recognitionLanguages = ["en-US"]
    request.minimumTextHeight = minimumTextHeight   // the default floor skips the number
    try? VNImageRequestHandler(ciImage: image, options: [:]).perform([request])

    for observation in request.results ?? [] {
        for candidate in observation.topCandidates(2) {
            found.formUnion(PrintedNumber.extract(from: candidate.string))
        }
    }
}

The recognizer swaps look-alikes (S and 5, O and 0, B and 8), so readings are folded before comparing. That tolerance is what kept producing wrong additions. The fix was two keys: a loose one, padding removed, for candidates, and a literal one, padding and variant marks kept, for without asking. "45/195" fits a catalog "045/195", but it is also what "145/195" looks like with its first digit lost.

When the scanner adds and when it asks

Add without asking only when the artwork's first choice (or a card it can't tell apart from it) and a reading that spells that card's number literally name the same card, and nothing the artwork can't rule out shares that number. Everything else is the sheet. Trimmed from :

func blocks(_ card: CardRef) -> Bool {
    guard card.id != winner.id else { return false }
    guard baseName(card) != baseName(winner.card) else { return true }   // same card, other print
    guard let margin = policy.distinctParallelMargin, let mine = winner.distance,
          let theirs = distances[card.id] else { return true }
    return theirs < mine * (1 + margin)
}
if parallels.contains(where: blocks) { return .ambiguous(candidates: offered, reason: .parallelPrints, numbers: numbers) }
let artworkAgrees = winner.id == candidates[0].id
    || artworkTies(candidates[0], winner, policy.minimumRelativeMargin)
let byNumber = winner.numberMatched && artworkAgrees
    && (spelled(winner.card, literals) || unpadded)
guard byNumber else {
    return .ambiguous(candidates: ordered, reason: winner.numberMatched ? .numberDisagrees : .lowConfidence, numbers: numbers)
}
return .identified(winner)

A different card sharing the number stops blocking only if the artwork puts it at least 15% farther away. lets an old card printed "18/130" match a catalog "018/130", but only when it lands on the artwork's own first pick.

The rule took three rounds of adversarial review to reach, each reported bug reproduced against the real catalogs. The first confirmed 33 defects; the second found 12 new ones, 11 introduced by the fixes. As my commit message put it, a comparison built to candidates was also allowed to one. Adding on artwork margin alone went too: a card missing from the index still has a nearest neighbour that can be clearly ahead and wrong.

Before a silent add, a second text request also counts Han, kana and hangul characters, because artwork and number are identical across languages and each catalog holds one. English cards read 0 to 3, Japanese ones 37 to 188; the cut-off is 8.

Then I measured on 529 real photographs of cards, labelled against the catalog, with all five games installed (62,331 cards in one index) and the app's recognition code running on a Mac. Every silent add was checked by eye:

Added without asking, wrong card

Added without asking, right card

Right card added, or first in the sheet

The gains came from the photos: a picked photo now skips the quality gates, since no better frame is coming; the number is read from the loosest crop when the tightest cut it off; and each crop is also embedded slightly blurred, because a holo's sparkle pulled matches away from the flat scans in the index (right card first: 377 to 397). The live camera path is still unmeasured; for that, the app keeps an on-device calibration log of each attempt and the card the user actually picked.

Keeping a 27,000-card index on the phone

Each game's index downloads separately, quantised to int8 with one scale per pack. On queries perturbed to the distance a handheld photo sits at, int8 and float16 returned the same card 99.8% of the time, for half the bytes. There's no approximate nearest-neighbour library: in the Mac harness, a brute-force scan of the largest index, 26,978 vectors, takes 1.6 ms widened to , but holds 83 MB. So the app memory-maps the int8 bytes and converts 512 rows at a time with and : 5.6 ms, nothing resident. The scan runs only on a steady frame, so four milliseconds is invisible and 83 MB isn't. A pack from a different Vision revision is refused; its distances live in another space.

The index is built on a Mac and lags the catalog, so a clearly read number naming a card the artwork never offered goes to the top of the sheet, asked about and never added.

A ledger that never overwrites, and one price file for everyone

The collection is an append-only table plus an table derived from it in the same transaction. Removal is a tombstone; replays the log. Replay needs an order every device agrees on, and the middle term of the sort key is a bug fix: the scanner adds a card and sets its finish within one millisecond, and a random event id sometimes sorted the edit first.

/// Creation sorts before every edit to the same item at the same instant.
var replayRank: Int {
    if case .added = self { return 0 }
    return 1
}

for record in records.sorted(by: { ($0.timestamp, $0.event.replayRank, $0.eventID)
                                 < ($1.timestamp, $1.event.replayRank, $1.eventID) }) {

It paid off in October. The upstream catalog renamed sets, card ids include the set name, and 1,323 cards in one game got new ids overnight, 222 more across the others. Copies saved under old ids dropped off the collection screen. The fix is an alias table read in memory; the log stays as written.

Prices are one binary file per game, the same bytes for every user, so a request says nothing about what anyone owns. Names are content-addressed and the manifest is written last, so a client never sees half an update. Prices are integer cents, with a sentinel so a $0.00 promo isn't an unpriced card. Each carries the day it was captured, and past PriceProvenance.staleAfterDays (7) the portfolio headline says "These prices are 2 weeks old" instead of presenting an old total as current.

How do you tell apart card printings that share the same artwork?

Mostly not from the image: in my pre-release harness, artwork matching picked the right print 89.5% of the time even when given the correct collector number. Foilcase reads the number with Vision text recognition and, when other prints share it, shows the candidates and asks.

Is VNGenerateImageFeaturePrintRequest good enough for on-device image recognition?

For retrieval, yes, with no model to ship: the right card was in the top five 99.8% of the time on sharp synthetic frames of a 9,903-card index. Use , and test on a device, because it doesn't run in the Simulator.

Do I need an approximate nearest neighbour library for on-device image search?

Not at tens of thousands of vectors. A brute-force Accelerate scan over 26,978 feature prints took 1.6 ms on a Mac in Float, or 5.6 ms as memory-mapped int8, which avoids holding 83 MB in memory.

Can embedding distance be used as a confidence score?

Not between similar images: median distance was 0.450 for correct matches and 0.420 for wrong ones. It does separate cards (0.459) from non-cards (0.966), so Foilcase uses it only as a 0.80 ceiling.

How do you read small printed numbers with VNRecognizeTextRequest?

Lower , turn off language correction, never downscale the crop, and add passes over enlarged strips and corners. Rejecting blurry frames first matters most: it took collector-number accuracy from 32.8% to 78.5% in my harness.

Why store a collection as an append-only ledger?

Nothing is overwritten, so a mis-tap or a bug can't destroy data: removal is a tombstone and the item table is rebuilt from the log. Changed upstream ids resolve through an alias table at read time, without touching user data.

items.title: How I Built a Free Chess Engine That Runs Entirely in Your Browser
items.author: Wajid Ali
items.content:
Most "find the best chess move" websites work the same way: you send a position to their server, an engine analyses it there, and they pay for every second of CPU. That's why so many of them cap free analysis per day or fill the page with ads.

When I built Chess Move Finder, I went the other way. Stockfish 17.1 runs entirely in the user's browser. The server only serves static files. Analysis costs me nothing per user, so the tool can stay free with no account, no ads and no daily limit.

Here's how it works and the tradeoffs I ran into.

  • for the site, tools, blog and translated pages
  • Stockfish 17.1, compiled to WebAssembly, using the build
  • The engine runs in a , so the board and UI never freeze while it thinks

Why the "lite single-threaded" build

Stockfish's WebAssembly builds come in a few flavours, and the choice matters more than I expected.

Multi-threaded builds need SharedArrayBuffer. That means the page must be : you have to send Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy headers. That's fine for a single-page app, but it breaks a lot of normal things on a content site: third-party embeds, some analytics, images from other origins. My site has a blog and other tools alongside the engine, so I didn't want those headers everywhere.

The single-threaded build needs none of that. It works on any page, in any modern browser, on any phone.

"Lite" means a smaller neural network (NNUE) file. The full network is large; the lite one is a fraction of the size. It plays slightly weaker, but it's still far stronger than any human, and the first analysis starts much faster, especially on mobile data. For a "what's the best move here?" tool, a fast first answer matters more than the last few Elo points.

Talking to the engine: UCI over postMessage

Stockfish speaks (Universal Chess Interface), a plain-text protocol. Inside a Web Worker, you send it strings and listen for strings back:

const engine = new Worker('/engine/stockfish.js');

engine.onmessage = (e) => {
  const line = e.data;
  if (line.startsWith('info') && line.includes(' pv ')) {
    // depth, score (cp or mate), and the principal variation
  }
  if (line.startsWith('bestmove')) {
    const move = line.split(' ')[1]; // e.g. "e2e4"
  }
};

engine.postMessage('uci');
engine.postMessage('setoption name MultiPV value 3'); // top 3 lines
engine.postMessage('position fen ' + fen);
engine.postMessage('go movetime 1500');

A few things worth getting right:

  • before sending a position, especially on slow devices where the WASM takes a moment to initialise.
  • Always send before a new search. Users click fast. Without it, results from an old position can arrive after you've shown a new one.
  • gives the top three lines in one search. That powers the "compare the top lines" view, so users can see the best move beats the alternatives.

Quick vs Deep: time-boxed search

Rather than searching to a fixed depth, the tool uses a :

  • Quick: about 1.5 seconds. Enough for most positions on most devices.
  • For sharp tactical positions where a longer search changes the answer.

Fixed depth sounds cleaner, but depth 20 takes wildly different times on a desktop and a budget phone. A time budget keeps the experience predictable, and the engine simply reaches a deeper depth on faster hardware.

Making engine output readable

Raw UCI output isn't something most chess players want to read. The UI turns it into:

  • for the best move
  • : positive favours White, negative favours Black, and means a forced mate is on the board
  • , written as normal chess moves

The UCI score is always from the side to move's perspective, so you have to flip the sign when it's Black to move to show a consistent White-relative evaluation. It's a classic first bug.

Most users arrive with a position from somewhere else: a game on Chess.com or Lichess, a puzzle, a book. So the tool accepts a and also lets you set up the board by hand. Every position can also be , so you can send it to a friend and ask "what would you play here?"

Once the engine was running client-side, adding more tools on top of it was cheap:

  • from a PGN, plus practice from your own mistakes
  • from the Lichess open puzzle database, filterable by difficulty and theme
  • An for 20 openings
  • Play against the computer at several levels

All of it reuses the same in-browser engine.

  • Weaker devices give shallower analysis in the same time. For a move-finder that's acceptable; for deep correspondence analysis it wouldn't be.
  • First load downloads the engine and network. The lite build keeps that reasonable, and the browser caches it afterwards.
  • No server means no central analysis cache. Every user computes their own positions. That's fine at this scale, and it's also why there's nothing to rate-limit.

If you play chess (or just want to see Stockfish running in a tab), give it a go: . Paste a FEN, pick who moves, and see what Stockfish thinks.
