I'd love feedback, especially from anyone who has shipped WebAssembly engines in production. What would you have done differently?

items.title: The Hidden Cost of Adding a CDN to Google Cloud Run
items.author: Nandan Kumar
items.content:
A couple of days ago, we were working on a website and wanted to add a CDN. It sounded like a small change, and in engineering terms, it was. On the bill, it wasn't.

The setup was already fine

Right now, we run the website on Google Cloud Run with request-based instances. The site doesn't get much traffic yet, and with request-based billing you only pay when something actually hits it. The result is a bill of around a dollar a month.

For a site like this, that's usually the sweet spot: nothing idles, nothing needs babysitting, and the bill is small enough that nobody reads it.

Then performance scans suggested we add a CDN for better caching and to reduce load times. Reasonable advice. Static assets served from an edge location load faster than assets served from a single region.

I thought, why not? How much would it cost?

I didn't actually answer that second question before acting.

What a CDN on Google Cloud actually involves

So we set up Google Cloud CDN, with a load balancer and everything. Cloud CDN doesn't sit directly in front of Cloud Run. It hangs off an external HTTP(S) load balancer, and the load balancer is the part with a fixed monthly cost whether you get ten requests or ten million.

The setup looked roughly like this:

  1. Cloud Run service, unchanged.
  2. A serverless network endpoint group pointing at that service.
  3. A backend service with Cloud CDN enabled.
  4. An external load balancer with forwarding rules, a URL map and a certificate.

None of those steps is especially difficult. The problem is that one of them comes with a meter that never stops running.

It’s estimated at around $30 a month.

For context, last month’s bill was about $2. This month it will probably reach $30. That’s a 15x jump.

The cost itself isn’t a problem. What intrigued me was the jump in the bill. Thirty dollars won't break anything. But going from "rounding error" to "a line item" in one change, for a site with very little traffic, is the kind of thing I'd like to know before I click deploy, not after.

Was the latency worth it?

For this site, at this traffic level, the CDN is solving a problem we barely have. Without it, some visitors far from the region wait a bit longer for a page.

I’m okay with 200ms of extra latency there, right?

If I had seen both numbers side by side up front, 200ms on one side and a 15x bill on the other, I could have decided that I don't want a 15x jump in my cloud bill just for adding a CDN.

So I built the thing I wanted

What I wanted was a place where I could put these pieces together, an instance here, a load balancer there, a CDN, and see what they would cost me before provisioning anything. Not after the first invoice.

So I thought, let’s build that.

That's . Whatever you add to it, the cost is calculated across Google Cloud, AWS and Azure. So while you're checking what your setup costs on the provider you already use, you can also see what the same setup would cost on a different one.

The limitations, stated plainly

The prices are static, picked up from publicly available sources, with no live API calls yet. That means they can drift as providers change their pricing.

So don’t take them as absolute, but you can use it to get a general idea of your future cloud costs before making a decision.

  1. "Small change" in architecture and "small change" on the bill are different measurements. Check both.
  2. Fixed-cost components, like a load balancer, hurt most on low-traffic setups, because there's no traffic to spread the cost over.
  3. A performance scan tells you what's faster. It doesn't tell you whether faster is worth it.
  4. Price the setup first. Then decide whether 200ms matters to you.

items.title: I Turned My Personal Website Into a Four-Hole Golf Course With AI
items.author: Sam Brovda
items.content:
I wanted a personal website that wasn’t boring.

Not a resume and a headshot. Something fun to click, with my resume, the stuff I’ve been writing, and the things I actually do with my time.

Now sambrovda.com is a four-hole golf course. Here’s how it came together, built with my AI agents in Grok Bot.

Eight mocks before anything else

I didn’t start with a design. I started with research.

My agents went through standout personal sites people share on X and around the web. Then they built eight mocks. Not pictures. Eight working pages I could click:

  • A desktop with folders and windows you can drag around
  • A flat apartment where every object opens something
  • A grid of widgets with cards that flip
  • A timeline you can scrub through
  • A “now” board that changes its look on Sundays
  • A pixel-art apartment you walk around with the arrow keys
  • A Sunday TV sports desk in golf green, cream, and scoreboard gold

I picked the Sunday desk. It looks like my Sunday. Watching golf is my favorite way to spend one. Fantasy lineups. Movies once the games are over.

The desk had golf on the TV. That TV turned into the whole site. Click it and you tee off.

Each hole is one part of me.

Hole 1, par 4: my career. You drive off the tee and I introduce myself. I come from the sales world and I build software on the side with AI coding agents. The approach shot is my resume, laid out like a yardage book. On the green, my articles are the pins. Each pin opens the full piece on the site.

The tee shot is at a drive-in. There’s a projector beam, a marquee with chasing bulbs, and a clapperboard that snaps when the ball lands. The green ends with two ticket stubs. is my all-time pick. is the 2026 Elizabeth Holmes documentary from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. I saw it recently, and it’s already one of my favorite movies of all time.

You tee off toward a ballpark in Queens, with light towers and a train passing by. Then it plays an illustrated replay of Francisco Lindor’s grand slam in Game 4 of the 2024 NLDS. October 9, Citi Field, against the Phillies. Bottom of the sixth, bases loaded, one out, Mets down 1–0. A 99.4 mph fastball on a 2–1 count. 109.5 mph off the bat, 398 feet into the Phillies’ bullpen. The scoreboard flips to 4. Final, 4–1, and the Mets are on to the NLCS.

On my scorecard that hole goes down as a 2. On a par 5, that’s an albatross.

Hole 4, par 3: dinner in New York. It’s a short shot off a rooftop, over a street full of moving cabs. Neon signs flicker on when the ball lands. The green sits under string lights with three pins: Minetta Tavern, Hillstone, and Peter Luger. Those are my three favorite restaurants in the city.

Then you sign the card. The scores get written in, the birdies get circled, the card gets signed with my name, and there’s confetti. Ten shots, six under. The page is upfront about it: the scores are part of the game, not a real round of golf.

Every hole has a commentator.

“Sam Brovda, on the first tee.”

On hole 3: “Into the Phillies’ bullpen. Grand slam.”

At the end: “From Sam Brovda’s course, that’s the broadcast.”

All of it is original. The lines were written for the site. They’re spoken by an open-source text-to-speech voice trained on public-domain audiobook recordings, and it’s not an impression of any announcer. The crowd is synthesized in code: filtered noise, layered “ooh”s, and hand claps.

The sound is timed to the animations. The ball lands, the crowd reacts.

Browsers often block sound until you interact with the page. When that happens, the mute button turns into a gold “Tap for sound” pill. One tap and it comes in. If you mute it, it stays muted from hole to hole.

There’s no game footage on the site. No broadcast audio, team logos, movie posters, or player photos.

Every scene is drawn in code. The batter on hole 3 wears a generic pinstripe uniform and a blue “SB” helmet. It’s not a likeness of Lindor. The page says it’s an original illustration, not affiliated with the Mets or MLB.

Fun on top, real text underneath

I had one rule for every page: it has to be readable to search engines, not just fun to click.

So the interactive stuff sits on top of real text. It doesn’t replace it. Under the drive-in and the ballpark, each page is plain words: who I am, my favorite movies, the box score.

Every page has my name in the title and the main heading. Each one has its own canonical link, structured data that says who I am, and a spot in the sitemap. That rule covers every new hole too.

It helps people as well. If your device is set to reduce motion, the long animations get skipped. The tee pages show the finished shot, and the greens open with the links already showing.

I clicked through it myself

I’d rather click through something than look at screenshots of it.

So the course got opened live on my Mac, and I played it hole by hole like anyone else would.

The site runs on Cloudflare Pages, for free.

My domain is registered at Spaceship. I switched its nameservers to Cloudflare and waited for it to activate. Once it did, sambrovda.com and www.sambrovda.com both came up.

My writing lives there now too. Every article I publish gets its own page on sambrovda.com with the full text. Medium stays the original, and each copy points back to it.

If you’re building your own

A few things I’d steal from how this went:

Look at a few mocks you can actually click before you pick a direction.

Put real text under the fun stuff.

Click through it yourself before you call it done.

items.title: Agent Skills Compatibility: How Claude Code, Vibe, and Copilot Compare
items.author: Nicolas Fränkel
items.content:
I love Anthropic Claude Code (I have the Max subscription), but I use it so much that I regularly exhaust my weekly quota before the end of the week. When that happens, I usually switch to other free-tier CLIs, , Google Antigravity, GitHub Copilot, and, just last week, Mistral AI's Vibe. I really wanted to try Vibe to evaluate the feasibility of moving away from Claude Code in favor of a more sovereign solution (i.e., an European one).

Vibe only offers a single model by default, Mistral Medium 3.5. It hallucinated results, and they were so bad that I noticed it immediately. When I researched to try to understand what happened, I realized that it hadn't triggered any of the skills that I had previously crafted with much love. The reason is that Claude Code stores skills in custom locations, in opposition to most other assistants.

I went through each assistant's documentation, so you don't get bitten the same way and here is the result:

<project>/.<your-client>/skills/

Your client’s native location

<project>/.agents/skills/

Cross-client interoperability

Your client’s native location

Cross-client interoperability

My conclusion is pretty straightforward. Put skills in and , then symlink and to them. If the folders already exist, move their content to the ones first.

ln -s ~/.agents/skills ~/.claude/skills
ln -s ../.agents/skills .claude/skills        # 1
  1. Run it from the project root

I definitely love Claude Code, but it isn't a good citizen here. It doesn’t abide by the specification. That's one more reason for me to try Mistral AI’s Vibe more seriously and try to definitely migrate from Claude Code to Vibe.

items.title: When Everyone Can Build, the Ability to Sell Becomes the Real Differentiator
items.author: Aditya Vithaldas
items.content:
Last month, Hector Serrano from Wispr Flow put out a video that caught the attention of everybody on the internet.

It wasn't a particularly intriguing topic either. It was about how Wispr Flow can create a win-win with creators in getting out their proposition. Why did it work? He knew exactly who he was speaking to, and he communicated what the value truly was for them, in a calm and composed manner.

And that becomes such a big deal when you look at the market. If you've used Wispr Flow, you'd imagine it's one of the most commoditizable products out there. It has limited virality and limited network effects. It's predominantly about the quality of the transcription, and with the imminent entry of the operating systems and the big labs, it's going to be part of their core feature set.

Clearly, the product needs to be great for it to win. But now, standing out is turning out to be a close contender, just to even be seen.

Similarly, Matt Palmer from Grok is another interesting case. His Grok Bot update videos keep breaking through to his target audience: the one from last week passed 1.7 million views, and his latest crossed 280,000 in under a day. He was already known for creating fantastic content at Replit, and he brought his own distinctive style of presenting with him.

HeyClicky is a similar case. Farza Majeed generated 15 million views for a relatively straightforward product, presented in an interesting way.

Do Hector, Matt and Farza understand what the consumer wants any less than a classical product manager? I would imagine not. And it's not just the marketers. More and more founders are taking a much more public stance, talking about their products directly to their consumers. The skill of selling yourself in an interesting way is starting to be a non-negotiable.

It's not just the product leaders; it's the CEO's job as well. Look at the number of CEOs who have started doing this, whether it's Sundar Pichai posting Google demos himself, Satya Nadella talking up Microsoft's latest, or Tobi Lütke building in public at Shopify. You can see a trend there. In a cluttered market, standing out matters more, and the mindset matters more than ever before.

And it's not about Twitter, Facebook or Substack. To be honest, the channel is completely dependent on where your customers and your target audience sit. It may be G2 reviews, it may be Twitter, it may be LinkedIn, it could be the right forums. Doesn't matter. And it's not about being salesy or constantly trying to push what you have. Sometimes it's about genuinely being helpful in the periphery of the domain you operate in.

Shouldn't good product managers have been doing that anyway?

But shouldn't the product manager have been doing that all along? Well, yes. Technically, a good product manager would have been scouring the customer channels on a weekly or monthly basis and responding to key queries. That said, in a lot of organizations, with the deluge of "stakeholder management" and "prioritization meetings", that genuine customer connect has been deprioritized for more "important" alignment activities. The really good product managers are probably already doing it, but now it has pretty much become a non-negotiable.

So, coming back to it: what skills start to matter more? I trust more and more product managers will need to be comfortable putting their face out there, being able to eloquently present what they have to offer and, well, not be shy.

Clearly, a lot of customer service problems can and should be agentified. Booking did a good job of that. But a reasonable number of jobs need your face out there and your personal touch, because if you're handing over everything you do to a bot, what is your reason to exist anyway?

When building becomes cheap and your customer base is large enough, feedback comes in from every direction. The core role is to stay consistent with a vision and not get distracted by short-term feedback that trades off your long-term vision. That is a big part of orchestrating building right now.

Being a builder is a temporary crutch

Today, there's all the talk about the builder and how that's a must-have skill. But my hunch is that it won't really last. Not because it's not important, it clearly is, but because it'll become table stakes, and then not sufficient, over the next year or two. When everybody can build, building is not what gets you out. True understanding of your customer and their problems, and your ability to articulate and sell it, becomes what really matters.

It's like Excel or Microsoft Word. Sure, there was a point in time when you had to put Microsoft Word on your resume as a skill set, and that was worth something. Today, that's not even a question. You're assumed to know it.

That's why there was a separate post going around saying the ideal job profile is a person who's perennially online and able to generate buzz for the product. That person is rare, and that's the person who's going to be calling the shots.

Visioning, combined with amplification and the ability to cut through the noise to the core, is the skill set to be had.

items.title: Building a Typography Playground With Variable Fonts and Fluid CSS
items.author: sammii
items.content:
Kern is a typography explorer I built for variable fonts, with Next.js, TypeScript and Framer Motion. It has three views: a specimen sheet, a playground for moving the axes of a font and comparing two fonts, and a type scale generator that writes fluid values. This post covers the interface and the maths behind the generated scale.

Every font in Kern is a small config: a name, a CSS family and a list of axes, each with a tag, a label, a minimum, a maximum, a default and a step. Roboto Flex has weight, width, optical size, grade and slant. Fraunces adds softness and a wonky axis to weight and optical size. Playfair Display has weight only.

The slider panel never special-cases any of them. It maps over the list and renders a range input per axis, using that axis's own minimum, maximum and step. A font with one axis gets one slider, and a font with five gets five. Adding a font means adding its config and loading the font file; the panel does not change.

The same list builds the CSS. One function writes each axis as a quoted tag followed by its current value, falling back to the default, joined with commas. That string goes straight into on the preview.

A slider that updates a paragraph can still feel like a form. What helps is that both the letters and the numbers move continuously.

The preview has a short ease-out transition on its font variation settings, so the glyphs change shape smoothly rather than stepping. The readout beside each slider is driven by a Framer Motion spring, so the number eases towards its new value instead of jumping. The preview text is editable, so you can drag the weight axis on your own headline.

For fonts with an optical size axis, the playground shows the same word twice: at your current settings, and with optical size pinned to its minimum, which shows what that axis is doing.

Compare mode puts two panels side by side, each with its own font picker, axis values and reset, rendering the same sentence at the same size. Picking a new font on one side resets that side to the defaults of the new font, because two fonts rarely share the same axes or ranges.

The single-font playground writes its state into the URL. Each change to the font, the size or an axis replaces the query string with all three plus any custom colours, and the page reads them back on load, so a link reproduces the setup.

The maths behind the generated clamp()

The type scale page takes a base size, a ratio, a number of steps, and a minimum and a maximum viewport width. The default ratio is a perfect fourth.

Steps are labelled from xs upwards, and the third step is the base. Each step gets an exponent, its distance from the base: zero for the base, positive above it and negative below it.

The large size, used at the widest viewport, is the base size times the ratio raised to that exponent: an ordinary modular scale. The small size, used at the narrowest viewport, uses three quarters of the exponent. That is the same as a gentler ratio on narrow screens, so headings still step up but less steeply.

Each step then needs a straight line between those two points:

  • The slope is the large size minus the small size, divided by the maximum viewport minus the minimum viewport.
  • The intercept is the small size minus the slope times the minimum viewport.

Both come out in pixels. A vw is a hundredth of the viewport width, so the slope becomes a vw value when it is multiplied by a hundred, and the intercept becomes rem when it is divided by 16, the default root size in browsers. Each step is written as a clamp() with the small size in rem as its minimum, the intercept plus the slope as its preferred value, and the large size in rem as its maximum.

At the minimum viewport the preferred value equals the small size, at the maximum it equals the large size, and outside that range clamp() holds it at the bound it has crossed. Every step is written as a custom property on , ready to paste.

An edge case worth knowing

Below the base the exponent is negative, and three quarters of a negative number is closer to zero. So for the small steps, the narrow-screen size comes out larger than the wide-screen size. When the minimum of a clamp() is larger than its maximum, the minimum wins, so those steps render at one fixed size at every width.

Small text arguably should not shrink on a narrow screen, so the result is reasonable, but it comes from how clamp() settles the conflict rather than from the formula. The label beside each of those steps also shows a size you never see. A cleaner version would skip the damping below the base.

The viewport preview has a similar gap: its container can be resized, but vw follows the browser window, not the container, so dragging rewraps the text without changing the sizes. Container query units would fix that.

  • Describe font axes as data and render the controls from it, so the interface covers the whole design space without special cases.
  • Animate both the glyphs and the numbers, so a drag feels continuous.
  • Write fluid type maths as a slope and an intercept between two known points. It is easier to check that way.
  • Test the edges of a generator, not just the middle.

items.title: I Run a One-Person Company With AI. Here's What I Won't Let It Do
items.author: sammii
items.content:
In one week in October, 565 changes went into my code. 143 of them carry the signature of an AI co-author. I am the only person in the company.

I want to start with that number because most writing about AI and work is either a sales pitch or a eulogy, and the truth of it, for me, is neither. It is just how I work now.

I don't have a team. I can't afford one. That is the honest reason, and I would rather say it plainly than dress it up as a philosophy.

What AI changed is not that I have help. It is that my ideas stopped being limited by my skills. Before, every idea came with a reading list. If I wanted to build something I had never built, I first had to learn the language, the framework, the edge cases, and by the time I had learned enough, the idea had usually gone cold.

Now I can go from an idea to a working version at a speed that still surprises me. Without AI I would not have built half of what I have, and nowhere near this quickly.

But speed is not the interesting part. The interesting part is what I still have to bring. I have enough base knowledge to know when the AI is building something properly and when it is building something that only looks right. That knowledge is the difference between moving fast and moving fast in the wrong direction.

The ideas are mine. The instructions are mine. And the part I have come to think matters most: finding the gaps. Noticing what is missing, what does not fit, what the system confidently did that nobody asked for. An agent will happily build the thing you described. It is much worse at noticing that you described the wrong thing.

If I had to say what authorship means now, it would be that: deciding what should exist, and noticing when what exists is not it.

What I would not hand over

When people ask what I would never let AI do, they expect a striking answer. Mine is: not much, really. I am overwhelmed most of the time. I run several products, the content for several accounts, and the systems that hold it all together. I want AI to take as much off my shoulders as it possibly can.

But I did draw one line, and I drew it into the systems themselves, not just into my head.

A proposal is not an approval.

My agents can draft, suggest, cut, render, schedule. They can propose a post, a reply, a change to something already queued. What they cannot do is publish in my name without me. That rule is written into the tools: a proposal goes into a store, and it stays a proposal until I say otherwise. The same goes for a validation check passing. Passing a check is not the same as being approved.

I did not do this because I distrust the tools. I did it because my name means something only if I stand behind what goes out under it.

The oldest lie on the internet

People have always lied online. "I made this much money last month, buy my course." "I have this many followers, pay for my thing and you will too." That last one is the easiest sell there is, because everyone wants more followers.

And it works, if followers are all you want. Growing a number is easy when the number is the point. The people who struggle are the ones trying to turn that attention into anything else, because attention built on a lie does not hold weight.

For my brand I always want the truth. I want to be trustworthy. Lying to get what I want is against my morals, because anything I built that way would be built on false pretences, and I would know.

AI makes that choice more important, not less. Every tool I use can now invent a moment, a quote, a result, a screenshot, in seconds and at no cost. So I wrote a second rule into my content system: never invent an event. My tools can retell something that really happened to me, in new words. If a moment is not in my real history, it did not happen, and it does not go on screen. Even when a made-up moment would perform better. Especially then.

People want me to pick a side on AI. Will it end in doom or create something like a utopia? Should we be worried?

I am very much in the middle. I build with it every day, and I can see both futures from where I sit.

What I have noticed is that the future is not decided only by the people training the biggest models. It is also decided, quietly, by the millions of us deciding what we let these systems do in our own small corners. What we let them publish. What we let them invent. Whether a proposal counts as an approval.

Those decisions are small. But they are the ones I can actually make. So I make them, and I write them down, and I build them into the tools so they hold even on the days I am too tired to check.

items.title: Euclid Mission Data Release Spans More Than 900 Million Galaxies
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
The European Space Agency has released the largest dataset yet from its Euclid space telescope, containing 1.7 petabytes of observations covering more than 900 million galaxies. "The data unveiled on Thursday covered a survey of the sky equal to about 9,500 times the size of the moon as viewed from Earth," reports Reuters. "The mission's goal is to complete the "largest-ever three-dimensional atlas of the cosmos, spanning more than a third of the sky, in 2031." From the report: "It marks a major milestone for ESA's Euclid mission and for everyone involved," said astrophysicist Valeria Pettorino, ESA's Euclid project scientist. Euclid, launched from Florida in 2023, is gathering data on how the universe has expanded and how its structure has formed over time while amassing information about the nature of dark energy and dark matter and the role of gravity on large scales.
 
"Euclid will not just take images of galaxies in the sky, in two dimensions, but will also measure their distance, the third dimension. This will tell us where galaxies are in space and time, across 10 billion years, and in all directions beyond our galactic plane," Pettorino said. "Galaxies cluster along filaments, surrounded by empty space, and form a network that we call the cosmic web. Euclid will reconstruct the cosmic web and how it has grown over time. This is important because the exact configuration of the cosmic web, how many clusters or voids are there, how fast it changed, depend on the properties of dark energy and dark matter," Pettorino said.
 
[...] Previous Euclid data releases covered only a few days of observations. The newly released dataset includes more than a year of data and still spans only 14% of the total sky area Euclid is due to survey in visible and near-infrared light over six years. This data release will be completed next year with the first results on dark energy and dark matter.

“Companies entering digital assets aren’t just looking for a vendor. items.title: Lagarde Is Leaving the ECB Early. Bitcoin Never Has to Choose a Successor
items.author: The Bitcoin Act
items.content:
Christine Lagarde will step down as president of the European Central Bank on 7 February 2027, before her term of eight years has run its course.

In Europe, the story is mostly about legacy and succession. For bitcoiners, it raises a more basic question. What does independence actually mean for an institution that sets the price of money, when the future of a currency can turn on the timing of one person’s exit?

An Outsider Who Beat the Skeptics

She later admitted she had accepted the job believing the mandate lasted five years. It lasts eight.

Seven years on, her record is stronger than her critics predicted. Her tenure covered a pandemic, two energy shocks and the worst inflation spike in the history of the euro zone. Willem Buiter, an economist and former Bank of England official, described her time at the ECB as broadly good, pointing out that the bank brought inflation down faster than its counterparts in Britain and the United States.

The ECB under Lagarde launched emergency bond purchases that stabilized markets as COVID-19 spread. After Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, it carried out its fastest series of interest rate hikes. The bank later acknowledged that it had been slow to recognize the full impact of surging energy prices.

Inside the institution, she worked to build consensus among the euro zone’s 21 national central bank governors. Her predecessor, Mario Draghi, had governed in a more centralized way that left some hawkish northern European colleagues resentful.

When One Sentence Moves a Bond Market

The clearest lesson of her tenure came early. In March 2020, as the pandemic shook sovereign debt markets, Lagarde told a press conference that the ECB was “not here to close spreads” between Italian and German borrowing costs.

Bond markets sold off immediately. She had to walk the comment back.

That episode says more about discretionary money than any textbook. A central bank can command an enormous balance sheet, yet a single phrase from its president was enough to move the borrowing costs of a member state. The system depends on credibility, and credibility depends on words chosen in real time by people under pressure.

Her career before the ECB carried a similar lesson. As head of the IMF in 2018, she backed a record $57 billion lifeline for Argentina in support of then President Mauricio Macri. The program did not prevent a currency collapse or a deep recession, and it left the IMF tied to its most troubled debtor.

Bitcoin was designed around the opposite assumption. There is no press conference and no forward guidance to parse. Its issuance schedule is fixed and published in advance, and every node enforces it. Nobody at a podium can change it with a careless sentence.

Independence Protects Decisions, Not Appointments

The timing of the exit is where the political questions start.

By leaving early, Lagarde gives European Union leaders the chance to choose her successor before next spring’s French election. Opinion polls suggest that Marine Le Pen, the candidate of the far right, will win that election and replace President Emmanuel Macron.

The reaction among central bank watchers has been sharp. Paul De Grauwe, a professor at the London School of Economics, said the move damages the institution and follows the political calculations of the French president.

Neither Lagarde nor Macron has responded to that criticism directly. Lagarde has said she will not run for the French presidency, but that she intends to defend European values in her home country in whatever role she judges most effective.

Read as a matter of institutional design, the episode exposes a seam that usually stays hidden. Central bank independence, as it is commonly built, shields monetary policy decisions from political instruction. It does much less to shield the question of who holds the office. Appointments remain political acts by design.

That means independence can be shaped at the point of entry, and the timing of a departure decides who controls that point. Whether this particular exit protects the ECB or weakens it is a fair debate. What it shows beyond dispute is that the calendar of an election can matter to the leadership of a central bank.

Frederik Ducrozet, head of strategy and macro research at Pictet Wealth Management, observed that Lagarde was put in place to be more political than her predecessor, and that she largely succeeded. Her willingness to engage in politics surfaced again this January, when she walked out of a World Economic Forum dinner in Davos during a speech by US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick that criticized Europe.

Bitcoin is not free of politics. Debates over changes to the protocol can be long and bitter. But no election, no appointment and no departure date alters its monetary policy. There is simply no chair to fill.

What the Successor Inherits

Whoever takes over on February 7 will face strains in French bond markets ahead of next year’s election, along with a Middle East conflict that threatens a fresh round of inflation.

Bitcoiners do not need to predict who gets the job or how that person will handle it. The point is structural. The next president will exercise broad discretion at a moment of inflation risk and political stress, and every choice will rest on judgment made in real time.

Under a fixed rule, there is nothing to forecast.

A Paradox Worth Remembering

Lagarde’s tenure proved that political skill can steer a central bank through historic shocks. Her departure shows that the same political instincts can shape how and when that institution changes hands.

In a monetary system that runs on trust in individuals, both things can be true at once. Bitcoin exists for those who would rather not depend on either.

For sharp analysis of Bitcoin law, policy and regulation twice a week, subscribe to The Bitcoin Act.

items.title: How I Built a Data-Driven Portfolio That Takes 30 Seconds to Update
items.author: sammii
items.content:
Adding a new project to my portfolio takes 30 seconds. No component changes. No new routes. No layout adjustments. Just 4 lines of JSON and an image dropped into a folder.

I got tired of the typical portfolio maintenance cycle: build something cool, then spend an hour wiring it into your portfolio site, adjusting layouts, making sure the new card doesn't break the grid. So I designed mine to be completely data-driven from the start.

The Single Source of Truth

Every project on my portfolio lives in one file: . Each project is an object with exactly 4 fields:

{
  id: 'crystal-index',
  title: 'Crystal Index',
  techStack: 'TypeScript, Next.js, Prisma, SQL, GPT4, React 3 Fiber',
  info: 'Custom CMS for cataloguing crystals with structured filters for colour, chakra, and properties, and GPT-4-generated descriptions.',
}

That's it. Four lines. The entire portfolio renders from an array of these objects.

The field is where the design gets interesting. It's not just an identifier. It serves three purposes simultaneously:

  1. The portfolio constructs repository URLs by appending the ID to a base GitHub URL. becomes https://github.com/sammii-hk/crystal-index. No separate URL field needed.
  2. An auto-generated image map resolves the ID to the correct image file and extension. maps to /assets/images/crystal-index.jpg. No manual image path configuration.
  3. The ID serves as the unique key when mapping over the array. Standard React pattern, but it comes free because the ID already exists for the other two purposes.

One field, three jobs. This means there's no redundant data, no fields that can fall out of sync, and no opportunity for a GitHub link to point to the wrong repo because the image and the link derive from the same source.

For projects under a GitHub organisation, the ID includes the org path: . The image utility handles this by splitting on and taking the last segment for the filename lookup, while the full path constructs the correct GitHub URL.

I didn't want to manually track whether each project screenshot is a or . So I wrote a build script that scans the images directory and generates a JSON map:

import { readdir, writeFile } from 'fs/promises';
import { join } from 'path';

const imagesDir = join(process.cwd(), 'public', 'assets', 'images');

async function generateImageMap() {
  const files = await readdir(imagesDir);
  const imageMap = {};

  files.forEach(file => {
    if (file === 'sammii.png') return;
    const name = file.replace(/\.(jpg|png)$/, '');
    const ext = file.endsWith('.png') ? 'png' : 'jpg';
    if (!imageMap[name]) imageMap[name] = ext;
  });

  const outputPath = join(process.cwd(), 'app', 'common', 'utils', 'image-map.json');
  await writeFile(outputPath, JSON.stringify(imageMap, null, 2));
}

generateImageMap();

The output is a simple lookup:

{
  "crystal-index": "jpg",
  "lunary": "png",
  "succulent": "png",
  "day-lite": "jpg"
}

Then a utility function resolves any project ID to its full image path:

import imageMapData from './image-map.json';
const imageMap = imageMapData;

export const getImagePath = (projectId) => {
  const projectBaseId = projectId.split('/').pop() || projectId;
  const extension = imageMap[projectBaseId] || 'jpg';
  return `/assets/images/${projectBaseId}.${extension}`;
};

Drop an image in the folder, run the script, done. The portfolio picks it up automatically.

The portfolio has two completely different view modes: a responsive grid with click-to-expand modals, and a full-screen vertical carousel. Both consume the exact same projects array.

The grid view maps over the array and renders cards:

{projects.map((project) => (
  <div key={project.id} onClick={() => setSelectedProject(project)}>
    <ProjectItem project={project} isGrid={true} />
  </div>
))}

The carousel view maps over the same array and renders full-width slides:

<Carousel
  items={projects}
  renderItem={({ item, isSnapPoint }) => (
    <CarouselItem key={item.id} isSnapPoint={isSnapPoint}>
      <ProjectItem project={item} />
    </CarouselItem>
  )}
/>

accepts an prop that switches between compact card layout and expanded layout. Same component, same data, two presentations. Adding a project to the array means it automatically appears in both views with no additional work.

When I finish a new project, here's what I actually do:

  1. Drop it in as
  2. Run node scripts/generate-image-map.mjs
  3. Add 4 lines to

The portfolio rebuilds and the new project appears in both views, with the correct image, the correct GitHub link, and the correct layout. Five steps, thirty seconds, zero component files touched.

This isn't just about saving time on a portfolio. It's a pattern I use everywhere.

My astrology app Lunary has a grimoire with over 2,000 articles. They're stored as structured data and rendered through shared components. Adding a new article about a crystal or a tarot card doesn't require touching any UI code.

My publishing tool Spellcast manages multiple social media accounts and platforms. Account configurations are data objects. Adding a new platform means adding to the config, not rebuilding the interface.

The principle is always the same: separate data from presentation. Make the data structure do the heavy lifting. Keep the components generic enough that they never need to know about specific content.

If you're spending more time wiring new content into your portfolio than building the projects themselves, you've got the architecture backwards. Make your portfolio work for you, not the other way around.

items.title: SpaceX To Invest $74 Billion Into Data Center Construction Projects In Texas, Arizona
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from the Hill: Elon Musk's SpaceX plans to invest more than $74 billion into building two data centers in Texas and Arizona, the company announced Thursday, marketing them as projects that will boost local communities amid backlash surrounding such facilities. "These investments will expand local tax bases, generate substantial new revenue for schools and public services, and create economic opportunities that extend far beyond the facilities themselves," the company said in a release. SpaceX said it will put more than $24 billion into a new project in Texas's Rio Grande Valley, expanding the company's headquarters in Starbase -- a coastal town the tech giant established in 2025 in a previously unincorporated area of Cameron County. In Arizona, SpaceX will invest around $50 billion in Cochise County, a rural area east of Tucson bordering Mexico and New Mexico.
 
SpaceX pledged the new projects will be created cooperatively with the surrounding communities and will be environmentally conscious. The company said the project in Texas would generate its own power and invest $220 million to expand the water supply in nearby Brownsville. While in Arizona, it vowed to work with local electric cooperatives and "potentially" reduce electric bills, saying the site would use dry cooling without water consumption. "They require strong partnerships with local communities, responsible environmental stewardship, and stable, competitive policies that give companies the confidence to make long-term investments," the company said in a release. Both sites promise hundreds of permanent jobs even once construction is complete.

items.title: Whoop Launches a Social Network Where Every User Has a 'Verified Heartbeat'
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Whoop has launched Humans, a social network built into its fitness app where every account is a real person with a "verified heartbeat." The wearable company claims its platform is "entirely human," unlike other social media platforms that are "saturated with artificial intelligence, automated accounts and bots, and manufactured content." The Verge reports: Starting Thursday, Whoop members can share their data from its wearables on the app's new Whoop Humans social network. Users can make their metrics, activities, and achievements visible to other Whoop wearers, post Story-like "Moments" with photos and captions, and add comments and reactions on other members' posts. [...]
 
In the Community tab in Whoop's app, users can scroll through Moments from people they're following, like tapping through your Stories feed on Instagram but with your friends' fitness tracker data. In one of Whoop's examples, swiping up on a user's Moments post with a photo from their run shows a map with their route and details like their pace and distance. The Community tab also shows cards for people in your "community" with their sleep, recovery, and strain scores.
 
Whoop says users choose which activities, achievements, and metrics they want to share on Humans, including Recovery, Strain, Sleep, HRV, and resting heart rate. Any activities marked as sensitive aren't shared by default. There's also an option to keep Moments posts private and a "Stealth Mode" for temporarily hiding health and performance data without changing your sharing settings.

items.title: Nintendo Takes Down Switch Emulators, Mod Chip Firmware in Massive GitHub DMCA Sweep
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Nintendo has issued four DMCA takedown notices targeting two Nintendo Switch emulators, Yuzu and Citron Neo, along with mod chip firmware such as Picofly, SX Core and HWFLY. As a result, 144 repositories containing firmware used to circumvent the console's copy protections have been removed by GitHub and replaced by a DMCA takedown notice. IGN reports: GitHub has posted Nintendo's November 6 DMCA notice, which says, "The Nintendo Switch console and video games contain technological protection measures ('TPMs') that permit the Nintendo Switch console to interact only with legitimate Nintendo video game files. This process protects Nintendo's copyright-protected video games, (...) by preventing users from playing pirated copies of Nintendo's video games on the Nintendo Switch console and by preventing users from unlawfully copying and playing Nintendo's video games on unauthorized devices."
 
However, while this takedown has effectively wiped out a ton of repositories with mod chip firmware, it seems like it's still being hosted elsewhere on the site, according to TorrentFreak. It's possible, though, that Nintendo isn't finished yet; back in 2024, Nintendo effectively took down 8,500 copies of Yuzu by issuing a takedown that targeted 12 different mirrors of the emulator. This particular takedown also comes a few days after emulators were able to run the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on PC, so this could be a sign that Nintendo is winding up its lawyers to crack down on emulation once again.

items.title: AI Is Dividing Product Designers: Exploring vs. Building
items.author: Andrii Bondar
items.content:
The AI split in product design

A week ago, I attended in Munich, Europe's largest conference on product design and user experience, featuring speakers from Anthropic, Wise, Google, IKEA, n8n, and other prominent organizations. On my way home, I kept thinking about one recurring theme: product design teams are approaching AI from fundamentally different perspectives.

Some are cautiously experimenting with AI while trying to fit it into established processes. Others have already integrated it into their daily workflows, connecting research, prototyping, design, and code with fewer handoffs. The difference goes beyond tool adoption. It reflects how teams understand their work, organize collaboration, and measure product value.

The trap of "AI everything."

highlighted a fundamental problem with the way organizations approach AI:

"Most efforts start with tools, copilots, and automation, and mistake faster cycles for value. The result is a pile of pilots nobody adopted, and a lot of people wondering what happened to the work they were good at. The alternative: to build something that fits, lasts, and makes an organization better at what it already does well. That starts by refusing the AI first, AI everything instinct."

I think this captures one of the central challenges in product design today.

Adding AI to an existing workflow can make individual tasks faster without improving the product or the way a team operates. Organizations can accumulate tools and experiments while leaving the underlying processes unchanged.

Meaningful adoption starts with understanding where teams lose time, which handoffs create friction, and where AI can improve how products are researched, designed, built, and validated.

Expanding Designer Ownership

For years, product design and software development operated as distinct stages. Designers worked in Figma, documented interactions, prepared specifications, and handed their work to engineers for implementation. This division made sense when building and testing functional interfaces required substantial engineering resources. AI-assisted development is changing that relationship.

After years of designing fintech and blockchain-based products, I kept encountering the same limitation: I could design an experience without having full control over how it was implemented.

Working closer to production code lets me build, test, and iterate on interfaces directly, with fewer handoffs between design and engineering.

For product teams, this opens up several possibilities:

  •  Research, UI design, prototyping, implementation, and validation can become more continuous.
  •  Designers can participate more directly in implementation and take responsibility for more of the product experience.
  •  AI can reduce coordination overhead and help smaller teams explore and ship functional products.
  •  Designers can connect product development with disciplines such as SEO, GEO, and ASO.

This doesn't mean every designer needs to become a full-time software engineer. Deep specialization remains essential, particularly in complex products. However, designers can work closer to implementation and contribute beyond the traditional boundaries of their roles.

Another exciting development is how AI is changing prototyping. Think about how difficult it used to be to create an interactive prototype for a specific device, such as an Apple Watch or an in-car infotainment system. Even without writing production code, designers can now use AI to build interactive prototypes tailored to specific hardware and explore how their ideas work in real-world contexts.

From faster execution to lasting value.

As AI makes prototyping, coding, and exploring alternatives easier, the focus of design work is shifting toward decision-making and product quality. Understanding whether it solves the right problem, meets user needs, and works reliably requires experience and critical judgment.

This is where faster workflows can create lasting value. Teams have more opportunities to test assumptions, explore alternatives, and identify problems before committing significant resources to a solution. However, individual productivity gains aren't enough. Organizations need to connect design, engineering, and product teams around shared workflows, clear quality standards, and meaningful evaluation of AI-generated output.

I'm particularly interested in how this can shape an AI-first product culture. The goal is to encourage experimentation while maintaining the technical rigor, security, and reliability that deep tech products demand.

Many designers argue that AI-generated product experiences lack quality. Are they right? Sometimes. Can the results improve? Absolutely.

AI-assisted research and discovery can produce shallow or generic results, especially when designers rely on AI without applying their own expertise and critical judgment. The quality of the outcome depends on how thoughtfully people guide, evaluate, and refine the process. Julia Bastian from Alasco explored this challenge in a session on AI discovery slop, examining how to recognize and address low-quality AI-generated research and insights.

The PUSH UX conference reinforced how differently the design community is responding to AI. Some teams are still finding their footing, while others are already changing how they work. My own experience has made me more comfortable working across design, product strategy, and engineering, but every team will need to find its own approach.

The important shift is to reconsider established workflows, explore where new capabilities can make a difference, and take greater ownership of business outcomes.

items.title: Singapore Says US Not Helpful On Investigation Into Suspected Spy's Company
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Singapore says U.S. authorities provided limited assistance in its investigation of Megaspeed, the company run by Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence suspects is a Chinese spy and whose relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has drawn scrutiny. According to Singapore, authorities held Alice Huang's passport from June 2025 until February while investigating "potential false declarations," but ultimately released her with a "stern warning" and barred her from re-entering the country. The New York Times reports: The statement raises new questions about the response of the Trump administration to the case and why the U.S. government did not more forcefully intervene. According to the timeline in the statement, Singaporean authorities had been holding Ms. Huang's passport well after President Trump was briefed last fall about her relationship with Nvidia's chief executive and the belief that she was a Chinese intelligence asset. The New York Times has reported that Taiwan began monitoring Ms. Huang in 2024 at the guidance of the U.S. government.
 
In its statement, Singapore said that it had sought information from an American server maker and close Nvidia business partner, Supermicro, but that the company had provided "limited cooperation." Supermicro, a firm that packages Nvidia's A.I. chips onto servers that can be used in data centers, has been at the center of a number of chip smuggling investigations across the globe. Supermicro was a supplier to Megaspeed, a company incorporated in Singapore and run by Ms. Huang, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.
 
Singapore said in the statement its authorities raised Supermicro's "limited cooperation" with the U.S. Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation in July 2025 and "requested their assistance in securing the company's cooperation." "Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company," the statement said.

items.title: Microsoft Outlook Goes Down Nationwide [UPDATE]
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Microsoft is suffering a major Microsoft 365 outage that's disrupting Outlook, Teams, Copilot and SharePoint for users across the Americas, with more than 129,000 problem reports logged on Downdetector shortly after the disruption began. Microsoft blames the connectivity problems on an unexpectedly large number of unavailable servers that overloaded the remaining infrastructure. The company says it's redistributing traffic and restarting affected systems. From a report: Microsoft was not providing an estimated time by which it expects service to return. Both individual Outlook users and those on enterprise accounts experienced problems logging in to the service. The outage also affected other Microsoft services, including Microsoft Teams, the Copilot 365 AI service and SharePoint Online. "Users may be unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 services," the company said on its Service Health Status page. 
UPDATE 11/12/26, 19:50 UTC: From Microsoft 365 Status: "We're testing a configuration change to address a problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable. In parallel, we've initiated a restart of all affected servers and are monitoring health as they return to service. More info under EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center, as well as http://status.cloud.microsoft if the admin center is not available to you." 
UPDATE 11/12/26, 20:19 UTC: From Microsoft 365 Status: "We've not identified any recent change correlated with the start of impact; however, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health. We've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being impacted while we work to return the affected servers to service. More info under EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center, as well as http://status.cloud.microsoft if the admin center is not available to you.
 
UPDATE 11/12/26, 20:29 UTC: "According to https://downdetector.com/, much of the major services are down," writes Slashdot reader xocmot2. "AWS, Microsoft, Meta, on and on. Clearly not a Microsoft thing."
 
UPDATE 11/12/26, 6:17 UTC: Microsoft is still struggling to resolve the outage, which is confirmed to be global with disruptions reported across 74 countries and territories. The outage has disrupted businesses and government services in countries including Japan, Singapore, India, and Australia, while OpenAI and Anthropic have also reported related problems.
 
Microsoft says its recovery efforts have produced some improvements, but the fixes are not delivering "sustained recovery." Microsoft has ruled out a cybersecurity incident, and experts warn that the prolonged disruption could result in significant economic losses. 
UPDATE 11/13/26: Microsoft's most recent updates confirmed that it's seeing "broader improvements in North America, sustained improvements across much of Europe, and encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific."
 
"Some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as mitigation continues across remaining affected infrastructure," Microsoft said. "Our focus remains on stabilizing recovered infrastructure, completing mitigation in remaining impacted areas, and reducing delayed email queues and backlogs while we validate service consistency across connection methods."
 
Further reading: Microsoft's Global Outage May Be Worse Than Amazon's Or Crowdstrike's, Expert Says

items.title: Google Pushes Privacy Angle As Gemini-Powered Smartglasses Debut
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Google is launching its first Gemini-powered smart glasses, with Samsung supplying the computing hardware. Given their built-in 12-megapixel camera, Google is emphasizing privacy protections, including a tamper-resistant recording light, automatic face redaction, and restrictions on real-time facial recognition and livestreaming. The company also promises not to use captured photos or videos for AI training or targeted advertising. Ars Technica reports: Google says the frames all weigh about 41 grams, which is not terrible but is definitely near the top for glasses generally. They will, naturally, weigh much more when you account for lenses. That will also determine the final pricing. So far, we only have the starting prices for these devices, including non-prescription lenses.
 
The setup here is similar to the Ray-Ban Meta glasses we've seen for a few years. There are no screens in the lenses, but you can interact with the AI system via voice or by activating the integrated camera. The experience should be similar to using Gemini Live on your phone, but it will be a lot easier to fire up the AI. You can say "Hey Gemini" or tap a touch-sensitive area of the frame to start interacting with the robot.
 
Since this is the same chatbot that operates across the Google ecosystem, it has access to your data and preferences. You can ask questions and get personalized answers, have Google Maps guide you by voice, or just talk with the AI to kill time. The glasses use custom open-ear speakers to limit distractions for those around you. Google notes the directional microphones should not pick up speech from other people, either.
 
Adding the camera feed is where things get interesting. When the AI can see what you see, it has the potential to do more work on your behalf. Google suggests asking Gemini for recommendations when looking at a bookshelf or glancing at an event poster to have the AI add it to your calendar. The glasses will also support Gemini Guided Vision, which provides conversational audio descriptions for people who are visually impaired. The new frames are available for preorder today starting at $395.

items.title: Iconic First Image of Black Hole Holds Up To Scrutiny
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Conversation: On April 10 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) Collaboration revealed the first picture of a black hole. The object is at the centre of a galaxy known as M87, about 55 million light-years away. The iconic ring structure instantly became one of the most recognized scientific images of the modern era. It showed a black hole "shadow" outlined by light from swirling hot gas -- just as predicted by Einstein's theory of general relativity. The result supported the long-standing idea that the centers of galaxies house supermassive black holes. However, scientists have since had some disagreements on whether the details and structure of the ring in the original publication were accurate. Our new research, published today in Nature, used new techniques to investigate the original datasets. Not only do our results validate the original work, but they also provide a fresh perspective on the ring structure. Our independent results enhance confidence in one of the most significant modern scientific results. And we bring the image of a black hole millions of light-years away back into focus.
 
[...] When compared directly to images from the EHT collaboration, our result is consistent in diameter and overall orientation. Naturally, there are some differences in the fine details of ring width and surface brightness along the circumference, but the overall structure matches. This provides a fresh perspective on the iconic black hole ring while also resolving previous discrepancies. To prove this success didn't depend solely on advanced machine learning, we also developed a complementary imaging method based on traditional statistical techniques. This entirely different method also validated our structure using the new closure invariant data we produced. Overall, our work delivers a strong independent validation of the supermassive black hole structure at the centre of galaxy M87. And it could do more in the future. Our technique could also be useful in other situations where data from multiple sensors are combined to map unknown structures -- such as medical imaging or mapping earthquakes.

items.title: 138 Open Source OCR and PDF Parsers Ranked by GitHub Stars: PaddleOCR, MinerU, Tesseract and More
items.author: Text Mining
items.content:
Every RAG pipeline eventually hits the same wall: the PDF. Before a language model can answer anything about your contracts, papers or invoices, something has to turn pixels and layout into clean text. The tools for that job are splitting into two camps. In HackerNoon's comparison of OCR and vision LLMs, template-based OCR breaks when layouts shift, while vision LLMs read documents more flexibly but cost more at volume. The author's verdict: "It could mostly be a hybrid approach."

Meanwhile, the vision models are shrinking. Xiaomi-OCR-0 handles text, tables and formulas with 0.8B parameters, and TeleOCR does structured document parsing with 1.2B. This list is the "show me everything" version of that landscape.

The Text Mining directory tracks the 3,141 most-starred open source text mining projects on GitHub (100+ stars, no forks or archived repos). Its filter tags 321 of them, which together hold about 1.24M stars. We kept repos with (161) and removed 23 that are tagged OCR but aren't really OCR or document tools: generic AI course repos, an inference framework, a clipboard syncer, and captcha solvers, which we chose not to promote. That leaves . Star counts are from the directory's November 11, 2026 snapshot.

A few patterns stand out in the full category:

  • 158 of the 321 OCR repos are Python. Next are C++ and TypeScript (21 each).
  • The licenses are mostly permissive. 111 are MIT and 80 are Apache-2.0. But some heavy hitters are copyleft, including PyMuPDF (AGPL-3.0) and paperless-ngx (GPL-3.0), so check before you ship.
  • The new wave is "PDF to LLM-ready Markdown." MinerU, opendataloader-pdf, liteparse, zerox, chandra, Dolphin and GLM-OCR all describe their output as data for AI, not just text.
  • Translation is a hidden OCR use case. Manga, visual novel, game and subtitle translators make up a surprising share of the top 50.

items.title: Critical Apache HTTP/2 Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code Remotely
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
A critical flaw in Apache HTTP Server's HTTP/2 module could allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code and potentially take control of affected server processes. Tracked as CVE-2026-119618, the vulnerability affects Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 when HTTP/2 is enabled and is fixed in version 2.4.71. The Hacker News reports: The vendor's assessment, published yesterday, also says "public research has demonstrated a reliable exploit" against a server in its default configuration with mod_http2 enabled. It does not name or link that research. Security company Wiz said later that day that no exploit was available and that no exploitation in the wild had been reported.
 
HTTP/2 runs only where the Protocols directive turns it on, as the module documentation explains. The directive uses h2 for HTTP/2 over TLS and h2c for HTTP/2 over plain TCP. It can be set for the whole server or for a single virtual host, so admins should check the server-wide setting and every virtual host.
 
Standalone builds of the module, released on GitHub as mod_h2, are affected from version 2.0.8 through 2.0.42. Admins who run the Apache HTTP Server project's own releases should move to version 2.4.71, the fixed release named in its security advisory. That release also fixes a crash in mod_md, rated important, and a one-byte overwrite of stack memory in mod_vhost_alias, rated low.
