items.title: A 23M-Parameter Model Still Wins: 338 Embedding Models Ranked by Real Downloads
items.author: Writings, Papers and Blogs on Text Models
items.content:
all-MiniLM-L6-v2, a 23M-parameter sentence-transformers model, was downloaded 177M times on Hugging Face in the last 30 days. That's 38% of all downloads across the 213 open-weight embedding models tracked by the TextModels directory, and more than the next four models combined. Below are all 338 embedding models in the directory: open weights ranked by downloads, then hosted APIs, Ollama builds and the historical models that started it all.

The sentence-transformers family's lead has a history. As HackerNoon's overview of embeddings for RAG puts it, "Simply said, the BERT model isn't the best for similarity search." SBERT fixed that by embedding each sentence separately so vectors can be computed once and compared fast, and its descendants still dominate the download charts.

What the download data says

  • Small and old beats big and new. The top two models by downloads, all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (23M params) and BAAI's bge-small-en-v1.5 (33M), are tiny. For most production search, "fast and good enough" wins.
  • The market is concentrated. The top 10 open-weight embedders account for 74% of the 470M monthly downloads in this list.
  • Qwen is the newcomer to watch.Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B is already #9 with 9M monthly downloads, and its 4B and 8B siblings both clear 2.4M.
  • Multilingual is mainstream. Five of the top 12 are multilingual: bge-m3, two paraphrase-multilingual models and two multilingual-e5 models.
  • Vector databases ship their own builds. Qdrant's ONNX conversions and sparse models appear nine times, which shows how many teams get embeddings through their database instead of picking a model directly.

Everything comes from the TextModels directory's filter (338 models) as of November 11, 2026. Hugging Face entries are ranked by 30-day downloads pulled from the Hugging Face API. "Verified" means the TextModels directory fetched and confirmed that model's metrics per model. Hosted API models have no public download counts, so they're grouped by provider, alphabetically. Some hosted entries, like OpenAI's 001-series search models, are long retired. They stay in the list because people still search for them when migrating old pipelines.

Part 1: 213 open-weight embedding models on Hugging Face, ranked by 30-day downloads

Part 2: 55 hosted embedding APIs, by provider

These are models you call over an API instead of downloading. The list covers current models and retired ones still found in old codebases.

245. textembedding-gecko@003

246. textembedding-gecko@002

247. textembedding-gecko@001

248. textembedding-gecko-multilingual@001

IBM watsonx / Granite (6)

Part 3: 20 embedding models you can run locally with Ollama

Ollama doesn't publish download counts, so these are sorted from smallest to largest. Pick the smallest one that clears your quality bar.

Part 4: 50 historical embedding models that got us here

Before sentence-transformers there were word vectors, and before RAG there was semantic search. These are the ancestors of everything above.

So which one should you use?

If you need a default today, the download data points to all-MiniLM-L6-v2 or bge-small-en-v1.5 for English, bge-m3 or multilingual-e5 for multilingual, and Qwen3-Embedding for top quality if you have the GPU. Then test on your own data. The model is only half the stack; HackerNoon's guide to choosing a vector database for a production RAG chatbot covers the other half.

To compare all 3,009 text models, including rerankers, classifiers and the LLMs these embeddings feed, browse the TextModels directory.

items.title: GPT-4.5 Fooled 73% of Judges: 20 Turing Tests, Detectors and Fakes to Check Your AI Radar
items.author: Turing Test
items.content:
In a 2025 UC San Diego study, people picked GPT-4.5 as the human 73% of the time, more often than they picked the actual humans. ELIZA, a 1960s chatbot, scored 23%, slightly ahead of GPT-4o without a persona at 21%. Here are 20 tests from the Turing Test directory where you can check whether you still tell human from machine across chat, text, faces, art, voice and video.

The Turing test used to be a thought experiment. Now it's a party game, a research method and a product category. Cameron Jones and Benjamin Bergen's three-party Turing test had 284 participants chat with a human and an AI at the same time and then pick the human. GPT-4.5 with a persona prompt won 73% of the time, and LLaMa-3.1-405B won 56%.

The public versions tell the same story. AI21 Labs' "Human or Not?" game ran more than 10 million conversations, and players guessed right only 68% of the time. They were worse at spotting the bots (60%) than at spotting the humans (73%). And it isn't just chat: in a blind listening study covered on HackerNoon, listeners trying to pick out AI-composed piano music were "essentially guessing," at close to 50% accuracy.

So test yourself. A note on what's included: not everything here is a quiz. Some are games, some are detectors that try to make the call for you, and some are the generators that make the fakes. To understand the Turing test in 2026, you need all three.

Chat: can you tell who you're talking to?

by Indiana University's OSoMe. It scores whether a social media account is a bot. It's a Turing test turned into a classifier. The live version shut down after X ended free researcher access, and the Botometer X archive only covers accounts created before June 2023.

Text: human writer or language model?

(Giant Language model Test Room) from the MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab and Harvard NLP. Paste text and it colors each word by how predictable it was to a language model. It was built in 2019 to spot AI-written text, and it's still the best way to see why AI text "feels" smooth.

This is the AI-writing detector that teachers made famous. Run your own writing through it to see how often humans get flagged. HackerNoon's guide on how to detect text generated by AI explains what these tools measure.

This is the benchmark proposed as a better Turing test. Who does "it" refer to in "The trophy doesn't fit in the suitcase because it's too big"? It's easy for people. For years it was hard for machines.

Faces: real photo or GAN?

This is the generator, not the quiz. Every refresh shows a face of someone who was never born. Look at the ears, teeth and backgrounds to learn the tells.

A commercial deepfake detection platform for faces, video and identity fraud. It's what the professionals use when the stakes are higher than a game.

Art: human artist or image model?

Upload an image and get a verdict on whether it's AI-generated. Try it on your own photos first.

A collaborative image generator where you "breed" images by mixing them. Spend ten minutes making fakes and you'll get better at spotting them.

from MIT CSAIL. A research tool that shows which neurons inside a GAN draw trees, doors or clouds, and lets you switch them off. It doesn't test you. It shows you what's inside the machine you're testing.

Voice and music: who's really singing?

Listen to clips and decide which are human speech and which are AI voice clones. This one matters most in practice, because voice cloning is the deepfake behind phone scams.

An AI music composer. Play its tracks for friends without telling them and see who notices.

The Kaggle competition, organized by Facebook with industry and academic partners, to build automatic deepfake detectors. Its dataset is still a standard for training them.

The deepfake software that started it all. It's on this list because detectors are trained against it.

The pattern holds across formats. People do only somewhat better than a coin flip at spotting AI, and they get worse as models improve. Faces were about 70% in 2019, chat was 68% in 2023, and by 2025 people were choosing GPT-4.5 over real humans. The Turing test has stopped being a bar for machines to clear. It's turning into a skill humans have to practice.

Browse and filter every test by type (Audio, Classic, Game, Modern LLM, Social, Visual), difficulty and access in the Turing Test directory.

items.title: SkyW4lker Exposed: A Growing Microsoft 365 Phishing Threat to American Enterprises
items.author: ANY.RUN
items.content:
(SkyW4lker x365 Sentinel) is an active device-code phishing kit targeting Microsoft 365 users in the United States, Europe, and other regions. By abusing Microsoft’s legitimate authentication process, the kit can give attackers access to corporate accounts without stealing passwords or bypassing MFA. This puts business emails, sensitive documents, and other Microsoft 365 resources at risk of unauthorized access.

The ANY.RUN team identified related to SkyW4lker between June and October 21, 2026, with 46% of submissions coming from the United States. Activity increased from 20 analyses in June to 200 in September, highlighting the growing exposure of organizations relying on Microsoft 365.

  • SkyW4lker is distributed through phishing emails with a password-protected malicious attachment; the password is provided in the email body. After a chain of decoy pages, the victim reaches a page that asks for a Microsoft device code.
  • The kit consists of a PHP backend and obfuscated JavaScript. Its main features are IP-based geolocation of visitors and periodic polling of the backend to check whether the victim has completed authentication.
  • ANY.RUN’s powerful new capability, Related Threat Context, helped analysts accelerate the SkyW4lker investigation by instantly surfacing connections to previous sandbox analyses. This reduced manual correlation work, enabled faster expansion of the campaign cluster, and ultimately helped uncover the phishing kit’s administration panel.
  • As a result, 618 analyses were identified over the past six months (as of October 21, 2026), with monthly submissions growing from 20 in June to 200 in September. They were submitted mainly by organizations in the technology, manufacturing, and government sectors, most often from the United States, India, Canada, and the United Kingdom.
  • SkyW4lker shares its JavaScript modules, landing-URL format, and part of its hosting infrastructure with Gabagool, a credential phishing kit active since April 2026. We assess with high confidence that both kits were built by the same developer.
  • SkyW4lker exploits routine business workflows, using contracts, invoices, and service proposals as phishing lures. By directing employees through familiar platforms and legitimate Microsoft authentication pages, attackers make malicious requests harder to distinguish from normal business activity.

SkyW4lker Threat Overview

Microsoft 365 / OAuth credentials

JavaScript obfuscation (obfuscator.io), Device-Code phishing, Geolocation detection, IP-address detection, CAPTCHA verification

Email attachments (.pdf, .docx, .xls/xlsx and others), redirection links and lure pages (including Google Maps, Google Images, Miro, Zoom and others)

SkyW4lker (SkyW4lker x365 Sentinel)

URL patterns: /session_public.php?action= /endpoints/confirm_visit.php /js/url_helper.js /js/endpoint.js /js/client_geo.js

SkyW4lker Activity Across US Organizations

The United States accounts for 47% of SkyW4lker-related sandbox submissions, more than twice the share of any other country. With the campaign exploiting legitimate Microsoft authentication processes and routine business communications, these findings raise concerns for US enterprises about how effectively existing security controls can identify suspicious activity before it leads to account compromise.

What SkyW4lker Means for Enterprise Security

SkyW4lker highlights several security risks that organizations need to account for when protecting business-critical systems and employee identities:

  • : Device-code phishing can succeed even when MFA is enabled, raising questions about whether existing authentication policies sufficiently restrict unnecessary access methods.
  • Attackers abuse legitimate Microsoft authentication flows and trusted platforms, making it harder for security teams to distinguish malicious activity from normal employee behavior.
  • Broader organizational exposure: A compromised account could provide access to multiple business applications and create opportunities for further attacks against employees, customers, and partners.
  • : Investigating suspicious authentication activity, identifying affected resources, and containing unauthorized access can increase SOC workload and incident response costs.

Stop account compromise before it disrupts your business.Detect threats earlier and reduce response costs.

Technical Analysis of SkyW4lker

You can examine the full SkyW4lker attack chain in this ANY.RUN Sandbox analysis.

The attack unfolds in three main stages:

  1. The attacker sends the victim a phishing email with a password-protected attachment. Typical subjects involve commercial offers, contracts, invoices, or confidential documents. The attachment is a PDF, DOCX, or XLSX file, and the password is provided in the email body.

  2. The document contains a link to a CAPTCHA page. Some variants include an additional lure page hosted on a legitimate service such as Miro, Google Sites, or Zoom, which redirects the victim to the next step.

  3. Finally, the victim is directed to a phishing page that instructs them to enter a device code on Microsoft’s legitimate authentication page, potentially granting the attacker access to their Microsoft 365 account.

The phishing page relies on obfuscated JavaScript functions and separate script files. Using ANY.RUN’s In-Browser Data Inspection, analysts can examine the page’s DOM and HTTP activity to understand how these scripts operate.

The scripts keep the page in regular contact with the PHP backend and determine the location of the victim from their IP address. Within the page DOM, the main script loads additional modules, sets click handlers on buttons and builds GET requests to the PHP endpoint with the action parameter (start or poll).

With , the script sends the geolocation and IP address of the victim and receives a session ID. After that, it sends a request with every few seconds to check whether the victim has authenticated.

The other modules of the phishing page are listed below:

Determines the location of the victim from the response of one of three services: ip-api[.]com, ipapi[.]co or ipwho[.]is. The location can also be obtained through the PHP endpoint php/endpoints/client_geo.php.

Base script with helper wrappers for URL handling, such as building GET parameters and appending slashes.

Each phishing page has its own backend, so the administration panel is likely to be hosted on the same domain. Further analysis of the Threat Intelligence Lookup results and data from other sources revealed an administration panel at .

The CSS styles () suggest the following capabilities of the kit:

  • Dashboard with victim statistics based on the client_geo.js module

Further investigation revealed another important finding: SkyW4lker shares several technical components with Gabagool, a credential phishing kit.

A search in ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence for the unique module paths of SkyW4lker url:”/js/client_geo.js” or url:”/js/url_helper.js” or url:”/js/endpoint.js”) also returns sandbox sessions tagged gabagool. The SkyW4lker investigation reveals several technical indicators and attack patterns that security teams can use to identify related phishing activity. For organizations, these findings also highlight opportunities to strengthen identity security and reduce the impact of potential account compromise.

For SOC Analysts and Threat Hunters

  • Hunt for SkyW4lker’s technical fingerprints. Look for requests to /session_public.php?action=start and repeated /session_public.php?action=poll calls. Check the JavaScript modules and URL patterns identified in this research to uncover related infrastructure.

  • Connect phishing activity with suspicious sign-ins. Singapore, Singapore, November 12th, 2026/Chainwire/-- and , the Binance-backed crypto travel booking platform, today announced AVA 3.0, accompanied by a roadmap that reinforces AVA token utility on Travala.

As the AVA token’s primary commercial application, Travala is the focus of the new plan, which builds on AVA 2.0 and emphasises real-world travel products, transparent buybacks, and measurable member value.

AVA 3.0 leads with existing products. The AVA Smart Program has more than 180,000 members, who lock AVA to save up to 13% on travel and receive other perks. Members can also pay for discounted travel with AVA and receive AVA rewards through the , which is live on BNB Chain in collaboration with Binance Pay.

Backing the program is a monthly buyback. Each month, the AVA Foundation buys back AVA to replenish member giveback rewards, and Travala matches it and locks its share in the AVA Strategic Reserve. The scales Travala’s match between 1x and 3x as AVA givebacks grow, with a total monthly buyback potential of up to 4x AVA givebacks. More bookings generate more givebacks, and more givebacks mean bigger buybacks.

To date, 5,604,414 AVA has been bought back by the Foundation, with 779,691.92 AVA (representing 1.1% of circulating supply) permanently locked in Travala’s AVA Strategic Reserve. 17.5% of AVA’s circulating supply is locked as the ecosystem targets a long-term goal of 30%.

Two launches are next. Increased AVA lock levels for new Smart members are expected in November, while existing members keep their current locks and can use the new Smart Boost feature to increase their AVA locks and potential rewards. follows, with the launch expected in Q1 2027. It will allow partner projects to lock AVA for their tokens to be accepted as payment on Travala.

The Foundation is exploring several further ideas for 2027 and beyond, including AI booking agents that recognise Smart membership tiers to apply membership benefits, curated travel specials available exclusively in AVA, and VIP travel concierge access based on AVA holdings.

“Through every market since we started, one thing has held true: AVA is at its best when it's used,” said Juan Otero, Travala CEO and co-founder, and Steven Hipwell, Travala co-founder and AVA Foundation Lead Contributor. “AVA 3.0 isn’t about grand promises; it’s about evolving what already works.”

The AVA token and all existing memberships, locks, and rewards continue as normal. Partnerships beyond Travala will be assessed where they deliver clear commercial value.

items.title: Jensen Huang Resigns As Nvidia CEO
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO of Nvidia after 33 years leading the company, with CFO Colette Kress taking over as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement.
 
"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," said board chair Harvey Jones in a release announcing the news.
 
The abrupt departure follows revelations about Huang's affairs, including one with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes was a Chinese spy. CNBC reports: Huang, 63, apologized on Sunday for being "unfaithful to my wife," though he provided no details about the affair with businesswoman Alice Huang, who has worked for a Chinese company and Nvidia customer called Megaspeed. Late Wednesday, The New York Times reported that the Nvidia CEO also had a separate affair, this one with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at the chipmaker. Later that afternoon The Times and other outlets reported that Nvidia's board met to discuss the company's future.
 
Jensen Huang denied allegations that he had compromised national security or Nvidia secrets after reports of the Alice Huang affair. The news sparked concerns that Nvidia knew companies based in Singapore and Malaysia had been evading U.S. export controls in accessing its technology. The board said on Tuesday that it had hired Wachtell Lipton to investigate the intelligence allegations.

items.title: I Used AI Coding Tools for 30 Days. Here’s What Made Me Faster (And What Didn’t)
items.author: Yashpal Waghela
items.content:
A few weeks ago, I caught myself spending 40 minutes writing a form validation schema I had written a dozen times before. I wasn’t learning anything. I was just typing.

That was the moment I decided to run an experiment: for 30 days, I would use AI coding assistants on every project I touched, and I would log what saved me time and what quietly wasted it.

I expected a magic productivity boost. What I got was more nuanced. Some habits made me noticeably faster. Others made me slower while feeling productive, which is the worst combination.

This is the honest breakdown, including the mistakes.

I mostly build web apps with React and Node.js, with the occasional Python script for automation. During the experiment, I worked on three things:

  • A client dashboard (React + Express)
  • An internal automation script (Python)
  • An older codebase I joined mid-month and had to understand quickly

I used ChatGPT, Claude, and GitHub Copilot alongside VS Code. To keep myself honest, I kept a plain notes file with three columns: the task, my estimate without help, and the actual time taken. It isn’t scientific, but it was enough to spot patterns.

1. Handing off the boring parts first

The biggest win was boilerplate: config files, validation, CRUD endpoints, regex, date formatting. I know exactly what I want in these tasks, but typing them out is tedious.

Here is a real example. I needed to validate a signup request. Writing it by hand meant checking the docs for the right syntax, handling each field and then writing error messages. About 15 minutes.

“Express 4, Node 20. Write a validation middleware for a signup route using Joi. Fields: name (2-50 chars), email, password (min 8, at least one number). Return 400 with a clear message for each failure.”

I got a working first draft in under a minute, reviewed it, tweaked two messages and moved on. Total: about 3 minutes.

const Joi = require('joi');
const signupSchema = Joi.object({
 name: Joi.string().min(2).max(50).required(),
 email: Joi.string().email().required(),
 password: Joi.string().min(8).pattern(/\d/).required()
});
function validateSignup(req, res, next) {
 const { error } = signupSchema.validate(req.body, { abortEarly: false });
 if (error) {
 return res.status(400).json({
 errors: error.details.map(d => d.message)
 });
 }
 next();
}

The rule I settled on: if I can explain the task in two sentences and I’d be bored writing it, hand it off.

2. Writing prompts like bug reports

My early prompts were lazy: “fix this error.” The answers were generic and often wrong.

Then I started including four things every time:

  • The language, framework and version
  • What I expected to happen
  • What actually happened, with the exact error message
  • Only the relevant code, not the whole file

Compare these two prompts:

“I’m using Express 4 with Node 20. This POST route returns a 500 when the body is empty. Here’s the handler and the error log. I expect a 400 with a validation message.”

The second one gets a useful answer on the first try almost every time. Good prompting turned out to be the same skill as writing a good bug report, and that skill makes you a better teammate even without any tools.

3. Understanding code I didn’t write

This surprised me the most. When I joined the older codebase, I pasted unfamiliar functions and asked, “Explain what this does, what its inputs are and what could break it.”

I still read the code myself afterwards, but having a first explanation to check against cut my onboarding time from what I estimated would be a week to about three days. It also helped me find a function that silently swallowed errors, which nobody on the team knew about.

4. Finding edge cases I would have missed

I’m not great at imagining how my own code will fail. Asking for “10 edge cases for this function that might break it” gave me inputs I wouldn’t have tried: empty arrays, null values, unicode characters, extremely large numbers, duplicate entries.

Three of those edge cases exposed real bugs in a date-range function I thought was finished.

5. Rubber duck debugging, upgraded

Explaining a bug to someone often solves it. These tools work like a duck that talks back. Half the time, I found the answer while typing out the question. The other half, the reply pointed me in the right direction.

1. Trusting output without reading it

In week two, I accepted a generated function without a careful review. It looked clean and passed my quick test. It also had an off-by-one error that affected pagination, and it took me almost an hour to track down two days later.

Generated code sounds confident even when it’s wrong. Now I treat it like a pull request from a junior developer: useful, but it always needs review.

2. Asking for a whole feature at once

When I asked for an entire module in one prompt, the result was messy, inconsistent and hard to modify. Naming didn’t match my project, error handling was different in every file and some parts duplicated logic that already existed.

Smaller pieces worked far better: one function, one component, one query at a time.

3. Skipping the thinking step

This was the hidden cost. When I jumped straight to prompting, I skipped the design thinking. I ended up with code that worked but didn’t fit the rest of the system, and I paid for it later during refactoring.

Now I spend five minutes writing the approach in plain text before opening any tool: what the inputs are, what the output is, where the code will live. It saves far more time than it costs.

4. Using it for things I was trying to learn

When I was learning a new concept (database indexing, in my case), copying answers meant I didn’t actually learn anything. A week later, I couldn’t reproduce it without help.

For learning, I now ask for hints and explanations, then try to write the solution myself first.

5. Outdated or invented methods

A few times, I got suggestions that used library methods which don’t exist or were removed in newer versions. The code looked perfectly reasonable. It simply failed at runtime.

Anything version-sensitive now gets checked against the official documentation.

Here is the rough summary from my log:

A net gain of roughly 14 hours over a month. That is real, but it’s much smaller than the hype suggests, and it only came from using the tools deliberately, not constantly. The weeks where I used them for everything were not my most productive weeks.

After 30 days, this is the routine that stuck:

  1. Write the approach in a few lines, without any tool.
  2. Delegate the boring parts. Boilerplate, tests, repetitive transformations.
  3. Stack, version, expected result, actual result, error.
  4. One function at a time.
  5. Read it, run it, test it.
  6. whenever versions or APIs matter.

Advice for Beginners vs Experienced Developers

If you’re just starting out, be careful. These tools can make you feel like you understand something when you don’t. Use them to explain, to give hints and to review your code, not to skip the struggle that builds skill.

If you’re experienced, the value is in removing friction: the repetitive work, the first draft, the edge-case checklist. Your judgment is still the part that matters, and no tool replaces it.

These tools don’t replace understanding. They reward developers who already know what they want and can judge the result.

The people getting the most out of them aren’t the ones who use them the most. They’re the ones who know exactly when to use them, and when to close the tab and think.

If you try your own 30-day experiment, I’d love to hear what you find. What worked for you, and what quietly wasted your time?

items.title: 17 Agent Skills Analyze Single-Cell RNA-seq So You Don't Have to Script It
items.author: Homology Technology FTW
items.content:
GPTomics' bioSkills includes 17 MIT-licensed single-cell skills that cover the whole analysis: preprocessing, doublet detection, clustering, annotation, batch integration, trajectories and cell-cell communication. They work across Scanpy, Seurat and SingleCellExperiment, and they tell the agent which method fits the data, such as Harmony versus scVI or CellTypist versus SingleR.

The 17 single-cell skills

Integrates samples or batches with Harmony, scVI/scANVI, Seurat CCA/RPCA, fastMNN, Scanorama or BBKNN

Annotates cell types from references with CellTypist, SingleR, Azimuth or scANVI

Runs dimensionality reduction and graph-based clustering in Scanpy or Seurat

Infers copy-number changes to separate malignant from normal cells

Reads, writes and converts AnnData, Seurat and SingleCellExperiment objects

Rebuilds lineage trees and clones from CRISPR scars and barcodes

Analyzes Perturb-seq and CROP-seq single-cell CRISPR screens

Handles QC, ambient RNA, normalization and feature selection

Analyzes single-cell ATAC-seq with Signac, ArchR or SnapATAC2

For the full run from Cell Ranger output to annotated cell types, the scrnaseq-pipeline workflow skill chains these together.

All 17 come with the Data & Science plugin, along with the rest of the 562 bioSkills:

/plugin marketplace add hackernoon/cuttlefish-agent-skills
/plugin install data-science@cuttlefish

For Codex CLI or another agent that supports the standard, clone the repo and copy plugins/data-science/skills/ into your agent's skills folder, such as .

items.title: Upwind Unveils Upwind Response to Stop AI-Driven Cloud Attacks Within Seconds
items.author: Kevin John
items.content:
, the Cloud and AI security platform, has announced Upwind Response, a new capability that the company says stops AI-driven attacks within seconds of detection and keeps attackers from moving deeper into a customer's environment. According to Upwind, the company introduced Response on November 12, 2026, and it is available now to all Upwind customers.

Response is built for speed. When Upwind sees an attacker attempting to exploit a cloud application, Response cuts off that attacker's access to the targeted service and halts the kill chain. It does this without waiting for a person to step in. Security teams still set the rules: they decide which threats Response mitigates on its own and which ones require their approval. Every action Response takes is temporary and can be rolled back.

Why Upwind Built Response

Defenders, in many cases, are starting the race after it has already begun.

AI is a major factor in that acceleration. AI agents can probe an environment from hundreds of angles, chain dozens of small weaknesses into a breach, and keep working around the clock until they succeed. JPMorgan Chase described the imbalance in , writing that "vulnerability discovery and attack automation are moving at warp speed. Remediation is not."

Upwind's position is that finding risks and detecting attacks remain the foundation of cloud security. The challenge lies in what comes after. When a new flaw can be used within hours, a scan-and-patch cycle cannot close the window quickly enough. Meanwhile, backlogs of risky settings and unused permissions keep growing, and each one represents a possible way in.

That gap between finding a problem and fixing it is where Response is designed to operate.

Automatic remediation has been considered as an answer for some time. Many security teams, however, have resisted it. Their concern has been that false positives or over-reaching responses would lead to ongoing problems, with automated tools disrupting the very operations they are supposed to protect.

That hesitation has left many organizations relying on people to act on every alert, even as attackers have automated more and more of their own work.

Upwind designed Response to address that concern directly. It unifies signals across cloud, runtime, code, and identity to understand the full picture of a threat before it acts. That context is what allows Response to separate an actual attack from activity that only looks suspicious.

When Response spots an attacker carrying out a malicious activity, such as an attempt to exploit a vulnerability or take remote control of a server, it blocks the attacker's access point from reaching the specific service under attack. The block works at the cloud network level and takes effect in seconds. Normal customer traffic keeps flowing, because the action targets the attacker and the affected service rather than the application as a whole.

Response escalates only as far as the situation requires. If an attacker gets further, it can terminate a specific malicious process and keep that process from starting again. This avoids large disruptions to regular operations while removing the attacker's foothold.

Response can also limit what a compromised machine can reach. It does this by trimming that machine's cloud identity so it loses access to object storage and databases, cutting the path to the data an attacker is likely after.

As a last resort, Response isolates the machine completely. The machine is taken off the internet and the rest of the network, while a secure tunnel into it is kept open so the team can still work on it.

Taken together, these steps form a clear escalation path. The lightest action comes first, and heavier measures are held back until an attack has progressed far enough to call for them.

Control Stays With Security Teams

The rollout model is gradual by design. Teams can begin by requiring approvals before Response takes action, then allow it to act on its own as they gain confidence. Every action is temporary, visible, and can be easily rolled back, which gives teams a clear record of what happened and a simple way to reverse it.

Approval mode also lets teams see how Response would act in their own environment before giving it more independence.

Amiram Shachar, Co-Founder and CEO of Upwind, framed the launch around the speed of modern attackers.

"Finding risk will always matter, but against attackers that move at machine speed, defense has to be active," said Amiram Shachar, Co-Founder and CEO of Upwind. "Because Upwind sees what is actually happening on the servers running our customers' applications, we know exactly which address sent the attack and which service it hit. That precision is what makes automatic blocking safe. Every blocked attempt costs the attacker time and money, while our customers' business keeps running."

Response is also meant to make the industry more resilient overall. According to Upwind, each attack it encounters is cataloged, anonymized, and added to the knowledge of the Upwind Platform. The company says this allows customers to benefit from the collective experience of their peers.

This turns individual incidents into shared protection. The more attacks Response handles across the customer base, the more the platform knows about how those attacks unfold.

That shared knowledge grows with every customer that turns Response on.

Upwind Response is part of the and builds on the detections customers already use. According to the company, admins can enable it today within the console. Because Response uses cloud- and AI-native primitives, there is no extra firewall to deploy and no new infrastructure to manage.

Upwind says Response is available to all Upwind customers. Those who want to learn more or request a demo can visit Upwind Response.

items.title: XAUH: A Swiss Boutique Bets Gold's Next Buyers Will Carry It in a Chat App
items.author: Sanya Kapoor
items.content:
Gold has traditionally been associated with physical ownership, secure vaults and long-term wealth preservation. However, blockchain technology is changing how investors access and transfer traditional assets. XAUH, a gold-backed digital token issued by Panama-based Herculis Tokens SA, is attempting to bring physical gold into the everyday digital economy.

Each XAUH token represents one gram of 999.9-fineness physical gold held in Switzerland. Built as an asset-backed payment token, it combines exposure to physical bullion with blockchain-based transferability. The project's broader ambition is to make gold accessible to smaller investors through familiar digital platforms, including Telegram.

XAUH Digital Gold: Bringing Physical Gold to Telegram Users

XAUH is the first gold-backed token launched by the tokenization arm of Herculis Group, a Swiss investment boutique established in 2009. Its issuing entity, Herculis Tokens SA, focuses on structuring and tokenizing real-world assets (RWAs).

Introduced in 2025, XAUH was originally developed on the JAMTON.NETWORK protocol. The idea emerged from the founder's interest in gold tokenization, which initially began during the 2016 ICO boom. However, the project gained momentum in late 2024 after discussions with the team behind Jamton.

The collaboration offered access to TON and Polkadot ecosystems, along with an opportunity to reach Telegram's large global user base. With millions of users already familiar with cryptocurrency wallets, Telegram presented a potential distribution channel for making tokenized gold more accessible.

Unlike traditional bullion products that may require significant upfront investment, XAUH aims to reach smaller savers, particularly individuals in emerging markets looking for alternatives to local-currency savings.

The project's distribution strategy includes Telegram's AdsGram network and educational content designed for TON wallet users. Its long-term vision extends beyond simply purchasing gold, with plans to support a broader financial ecosystem where users can buy, earn, borrow and spend.

Those interested in the project's gold-backed digital asset model can learn more through the official XAUH website.

XAUH Coin: The Business Behind the Digital Asset

XAUH operates within a group structure that Herculis describes as deliberately conservative. Six entities cover different business functions, including asset management, fiduciary administration, gold trading, vaulting and tokenization.

According to the company, its experience in physical bullion operations provides an important foundation for its digital asset offering. Its gold trading and vaulting activities reportedly predate the token by more than a decade.

The company also identifies three custodians responsible for holding bullion: Herculis House, Brink's and Loomis. These arrangements are intended to provide additional separation between the token issuer and the physical assets backing the token.

Insurance and custody arrangements are also central to the company's operating model. Herculis argues that combining traditional bullion infrastructure with blockchain technology can help address some of the trust concerns associated with digital assets.

The central feature of XAUH is its one-to-one relationship with physical gold.

Each token represents one gram of Swiss LBMA 999.9 fine gold. It can also be divided into smaller units of 0.01 gram, allowing users to access fractional gold ownership without purchasing a traditional bullion bar.

Physical redemption is available starting from 500 XAUH, equivalent to 500 grams of gold.

The company identifies four important components of its reserve structure:

●        Bullion is refined by PX Precinox SA, an LBMA-listed Swiss refinery.

●        Gold reserves are distributed across Herculis House, Brink's and Loomis.

●        Holdings are insured at fair-market value.

●        On-chain reserve information is made available through Chainlink and can be checked through the XAUH website.

This combination of physical custody and blockchain-based verification is intended to make the token's underlying gold easier to monitor.

XAUH Gold: Why Independent Verification Matters

For any gold-backed digital asset, the existence of physical reserves is one of the most important factors affecting investor confidence.

Herculis engaged KPMG SA in Switzerland to perform agreed-upon procedures under Swiss Auditing Standard 920. According to its report dated August 28, 2026, KPMG physically compared bullion with 18 PX Precinox certificates, matched selected bar and certificate serial numbers, and reported the presence of 15.5 kilograms of gold.

The reported reserve figure also corresponded with market data published by CoinGecko in September 2026. At that time, the platform reported a circulating and total supply of 15,500 XAUH, equivalent to 15.5 kilograms under the one-token-per-gram structure.

However, token supply and market information can change, making it important for users to consult current market data and reserve disclosures.

Regulatory classification is another important consideration. Herculis states that XAUH is an asset-backed payment token rather than a security under Swiss or Panamanian law. It also states that Herculis Tokens SA is reportable to Panama's Financial Analysis Unit (UAF). These represent the issuer's stated legal position and should not be interpreted as an independent regulatory determination.

Herculis Gold Coin: Understanding Fees and Redemption

Accessibility is not determined by the purchase price alone. Transaction costs, redemption requirements and custody arrangements also influence whether a tokenized asset is practical for everyday users.

Herculis has published the following fee structure for XAUH:

●      Tokenization of existing LBMA bullion:  0.3%.

●      Transfers on the Jamton protocol:  0.02% per transaction.

●      Redemption of one kilogram or more:  1%, plus transportation costs.

●      Redemption at the minimum 500-gram threshold:  3%, plus transportation costs.

●      Recurring custody and storage fees:  None once tokens are minted.

The redemption structure is particularly relevant for investors who want the option of converting digital holdings into physical bullion.

XAUH is also available across multiple blockchain networks and trading venues. CoinGecko identifies token contracts on Ethereum, TRON and TON.

The token trades on centralized exchanges BTSE and Biconomy.com, alongside decentralized platforms such as STON.fi on TON and Uniswap V2 on Ethereum. Fiat and stablecoin on-ramps are available through Wert.io.

Herculis has also outlined plans to collaborate with Frankencoin, a Swiss franc stablecoin, and Morpho, a decentralized lending platform. These partnerships could expand the token's potential role within decentralized finance.

XAUH Token: Expanding Beyond Gold Into Other Real-World Assets

For Herculis, XAUH is intended to be the beginning of a broader real-world asset tokenization strategy.

The company's roadmap includes potential tokenization of silver and fine art already held in Herculis vaults. The founder describes silver as "gold for the poor," highlighting its potential to appeal to buyers who want exposure to precious metals at a lower price point.

The strategy is to reuse the existing infrastructure for custody, insurance and verification rather than build separate systems for every asset category.

This approach reflects a wider shift in financial markets. Major institutions, including BlackRock and JPMorgan, have shown growing interest in tokenized real-world assets, bringing greater attention to blockchain-based representations of traditional financial and physical assets.

For Herculis, tokenized gold could provide an accessible entry point for people who are new to digital finance. Unlike more complex financial products, gold is already familiar to consumers across different markets.

The Future of Tokenized Gold and Digital Ownership

The growth of tokenized assets will depend on more than blockchain technology. Investors will also consider the quality of underlying reserves, transparency of custody arrangements, redemption terms, regulatory clarity and the reliability of trading infrastructure.

XAUH represents one approach to combining established bullion operations with digital asset distribution. By connecting physical gold held in Switzerland with blockchain networks and Telegram's user ecosystem, Herculis is attempting to make gold ownership more flexible and accessible.

Whether this model achieves wider adoption will depend on its ability to maintain reserve transparency, deliver reliable redemption and build user confidence over time.

As the real-world asset sector continues to evolve, projects such as XAUH highlight how traditional assets may find new forms of ownership and distribution in an increasingly digital financial landscape.

items.title: Making Agent Harnesses Readable Lets Teams Edit Agent Behavior Without Breaking It
items.author: Tencent
items.content:
Harness Handbook: Making Evolving Agent Harnesses Readable, Navigable, and Editable

Ruhan Wang, Yucheng Shi, Zongxia Li, Zhongzhi Li, Yue Yu, Junyao Yang, Kishan Panaganti, Haitao Mi, Dongruo Zhou, Leoweiliang (Tencent Hunyuan)

1]Tencent HY LLM Frontier 2]Indiana University 3]University of Maryland, College Park 4]University of Georgia 5]National University of Singapore \contribution⋆Work done at an internship at Tencent Seattle †Lead Project Collaborator. \headercontenthttps://ruhan-wang.github.io/Harness-Handbook/

The capability of a modern AI agent depends not only on its foundation model but also on its harness, which constructs prompts, manages state, invokes tools, and coordinates execution. As models, APIs, execution environments, and application requirements change, the harness must be continually modified to add capabilities or adapt existing behaviors. Before a human developer or coding agent can make such a change, they must identify all code locations that implement the target behavior. This is difficult because production harnesses are often large, tightly coupled, and behaviorally distributed across files, functions, execution stages, and state transitions, whereas modification requests describe what the system should do and repositories are organized by files, functions, and modules. Existing approaches to code search, repository indexing, and long-context processing make code easier to inspect, but they still leave developers and coding agents to recover this mapping themselves. Behavior localization is therefore a central bottleneck in harness evolution. We introduce the , a behavior-centric representation synthesized automatically from a harness codebase through static program analysis and LLM-assisted behavioral structuring, which organizes implementation knowledge around system behaviors and links each behavior to the corresponding source code. We also introduce Behavior-Guided Progressive Disclosure (BGPD), which guides coding agents from high-level behavior descriptions to relevant implementation details and verifies candidate locations against the current source. We evaluate Harness Handbook on diverse modification requests from two open-source agent harnesses. Handbook-Assisted planning improves behavior localization and edit-plan quality while using fewer planner tokens. The largest gains appear for changes involving scattered implementation sites, rarely executed code paths, and cross-module interactions. These findings indicate that evolving complex agentic systems depends not only on generating edits, but also on determining where those edits should be made.

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have accelerated the development of agentic systems [1, 2, 3]. These systems extend model capabilities by interacting with tools, APIs, and complex execution environments [4, 5, 6, 7]. Such interactions are not governed by the foundation model alone. They are coordinated by the harness, which constructs prompts, manages state, invokes tools, and controls execution across system components. The harness therefore determines how model capabilities are translated into system behavior. As models, APIs, execution environments, and application requirements evolve, the harness must be adapted accordingly. Harness evolution has consequently become a recurring engineering challenge in modern agent development [8, 9, 10].

In practice, harness evolution requires changes that add capabilities, adapt existing behaviors, or refine execution workflows [11, 12]. Traditionally, human developers make these changes by reading the repository, tracing the relevant behavior, and editing its implementation. Coding agents are increasingly expected to perform the same work from natural-language requests [7, 13, 10, 14]. However, a modification request describes what behavior should change, but it does not identify where that behavior is implemented. Whether the modification is performed by a human developer or a coding agent, the first step is therefore to locate all relevant implementation sites.

Finding every relevant implementation site is difficult in production-scale harnesses [15]. A large harness may span hundreds of functions across many files, with execution logic distributed across stages and connected through shared state. As a result, a single behavior may depend on several nonadjacent implementation sites.

We refer to identifying all implementation sites associated with a behavioral request as . In a large and structurally complex harness repository, this task is costly for both human developers and coding agents. Human developers must invest substantial time and effort in building a mental model of the system and tracing behavior across files and execution stages. Coding agents face an additional constraint from limited input context, which prevents them from examining all relevant code at once. They must therefore explore the repository iteratively and may still overlook scattered or rarely executed paths [16, 17].

Existing approaches to repository understanding make codebases easier to explore. Repository maps, code search, code summarization, repository memory, and long-context editing help coding agents find, inspect, and retain relevant code [16, 18, 19, 17, 20]. However, these approaches organize information around files, functions, and modules, whereas a harness modification request describes a desired behavior. They may identify individual pieces of relevant code, but they do not show how those pieces work together to produce the behavior or whether every affected location has been found. The coding agent must still connect these pieces and infer how the requested behavior maps to the underlying implementation. This missing connection is the gap we address.

We address this gap with , an operational behavior representation that connects system behavior to source code. Instead of organizing implementation knowledge by files and functions, the Handbook organizes it by what the harness does and links each behavior to the code that implements it. Developers and coding agents can therefore identify the relevant behavior first and then navigate directly to the corresponding code. We construct Harness Handbook instances automatically using static program analysis and LLM-assisted behavioral structuring. To evaluate whether the Handbook improves harness modification, we use realistic requests from two open-source agent harnesses and compare Baseline and Handbook-Assisted planning on the same tasks. Handbook-Assisted planning improves behavior localization and edit-plan quality while using fewer planner tokens. These results show that making the connection between behavior and implementation explicit can make harness evolution more accurate and efficient. Our contributions are as follows:

  • We define as finding all code locations that implement the behavior described in a modification request. This step is necessary before a complete edit can be planned.
  • We introduce , which organizes implementation knowledge by what the harness does and links each behavior directly to its source code. We also develop an automated framework that builds Handbook instances from existing codebases using static program analysis and LLM-assisted behavioral structuring.
  • We introduce Behavior-Guided Progressive Disclosure (BGPD), a workflow that guides coding agents from high-level behavior descriptions to relevant implementation details in stages.
  • We evaluate on diverse modification requests from two open-source harnesses. We compare Handbook-Assisted BGPD planning with planning without Handbook access on the same tasks. Handbook assistance improves behavior localization and edit-plan quality while using fewer planner tokens.

Our work is closely related to three research directions: agent harnesses, harness evolution, and repository representations for coding agents. We briefly review each direction and discuss how Harness Handbook differs from existing approaches by introducing an explicit operational behavior representation for behavior localization.

Recent work has increasingly recognized the agent harness as a first-class software abstraction that extends foundation models into deployable agentic systems. Rather than treating prompting, tool use, memory, and execution logic as implementation details, formalizes the harness as an executable and stateful software layer supporting reasoning, acting, feedback, and coordination [15]. Complementary surveys and engineering efforts further characterize the harness as the runtime infrastructure responsible for prompt construction, state management, tool invocation, control flow, and interactions with external environments [21, 22]. This abstraction has been widely adopted by modern agent frameworks and production systems. Frameworks such as AutoGen and OpenHands expose modular runtime components for agent orchestration, tool execution, environment interaction, and multi-agent collaboration [23, 13]. Industrial systems such as Claude Code and Codex similarly emphasize harness design as a key factor in building reliable long-running coding agents [24, 25]. While these works establish the importance of agent harnesses, they primarily focus on harness construction and system design rather than understanding and evolving existing production-scale harnesses.

As coding agents become increasingly capable, software engineering efforts are gradually shifting from manually implementing functionality to automatically evolving the underlying harness [7, 13]. Recent work has begun to investigate harness engineering, adaptive harness optimization, and automated harness repair [10, 14, 8, 26, 27, 28]. These approaches improve the capability and reliability of agent systems by constructing, adapting, or repairing harness implementations. Our work addresses a complementary problem. Rather than directly modifying harness implementations, we study the prerequisite challenge of harness evolution: behavior localization. Harness Handbook enables developers and coding agents to identify where behavioral changes should be made before reasoning about how to modify the underlying implementation.

2.3 Behavior Representations

Recent work has proposed various representations to improve repository understanding for coding agents, including structural repository representations, repository indexing, repository memory, and natural-language artifacts [29, 18, 19, 30]. These representations improve repository navigation, code retrieval, and editing by organizing implementation knowledge into more accessible forms. However, existing representations remain fundamentally implementation-centric, organizing information around source code, repository structure, or execution infrastructure. They do not explicitly capture how system behaviors emerge across distributed execution stages, functional modules, and shared states. In contrast, Harness Handbook introduces an operational behavior representation that explicitly bridges behavioral requirements and their underlying implementation, enabling behavior localization before repository exploration.

Harness Handbook has three parts for understanding and modifying an agent harness. The organizes source around runtime behavior (Section 3.1). The pipeline builds this representation from a repository (Section 3.2). The workflow uses the handbook to guide code changes and automatically resynchronizes it after every non-empty repository diff (Section 3.3).

3.1 Harness Handbook Representation

Source repositories show where code is stored, but they do not directly show how a runtime behavior unfolds. One behavior may cross several files, execution stages, and shared states. Harness Handbook reorganizes this information around behavior while preserving links to the source. As Figure 1 shows, it contains an L1–L3 document tree and a complementary state-register view .

Figure 1: Overview of the Harness Handbook representation. Its three-level hierarchy progresses from a system-level overview to stage-level component overviews and source-backed unit details. The navigation pane provides component and state indexes for direct access and cross-stage tracing.

A reader normally starts at , which summarizes the architecture, execution model, major stages, and global data flow. The reader then moves to for the responsibilities, inputs, outputs, dependencies, and local state of a selected stage. Finally, links that stage to source-grounded implementation entries. The complementary view records state relationships that cross stage boundaries.

Two rules keep the representation useful. means that readers move from L1 to L3 only when a task requires more detail. Behavior–implementation alignment means that every active L3 locator must still resolve to the current repository. If a locator cannot be revalidated, its entry is frozen and excluded from localization until it is refreshed. The repository therefore remains the authority for implementation details.

3.2 Harness Handbook Construction

Construction builds a handbook from a repository . The leaf mode g∈{function,file}, which remains fixed for the lifetime of the handbook, determines the granularity of L3 entries: in function-as-leaf mode each L3 entry covers a whole function or one or more contiguous regions, whereas in file-as-leaf mode each L3 entry represents a file.

The two modes differ in how the stage skeleton is obtained. function-as-leaf starts from a seed skeleton containing the stage and state-register definitions; we use it when a trustworthy seed skeleton that faithfully reflects the harness’s execution stages is available and function-level L3 entries fit the available budget. file-as-leaf instead infers the stage skeleton rather than starting from a seed; we use it when no such seed is available or when function-level organization would exceed the available budget. Both modes produce the representation described in Section 3.1, and Algorithm 2 defines the two branches.

Once g is chosen, construction proceeds in three phases, illustrated for the function-as-leaf branch in Figure 2.

Figure 2: Construction pipeline for Harness Handbook. Static analysis extracts source-linked facts, behavioral organization maps source units to execution stages, and hierarchical synthesis builds the L1–L3 handbook.

  1. Language-specific adapters parse the repository and extract functions, named external boundaries, source locations, signatures, and call edges. The program graph keeps only calls that resolve to an internal function or a named boundary. Unresolved calls are logged rather than assigned guessed targets. This phase is deterministic and makes no LLM calls.
  2. The pipeline organizes source units into the execution-stage skeleton according to the selected leaf mode. • The pipeline uses source and call-graph context to propose function-to-stage assignments, which are refined through iterative review. A function can be assigned to one or more execution stages, either as a whole or as contiguous regions when it serves multiple behavioral roles. Accepted assignments and revisions update the stage skeleton . • The pipeline summarizes the scanned files as cards and combines them with the program graph to infer the stage skeleton . It then organizes the files by execution stage. An optional proposal-and-review process iteratively refines this structure, while uncovered files and unresolved organizational issues remain explicitly recorded in . Appendix A provides the full organization procedures and validation checks for both modes.
  3. Hierarchical Synthesis and Packaging. This phase converts the stage skeleton and source organization from Phase II into the L1–L3 document tree and cross-stage state-register view. Each L3 entry is linked to a statically identified source location and validated against the current repository. This keeps the handbook traceable to the source. Finally, the pipeline renders and packages the structured data needed for source localization and future resynchronization.

3.3 Handbook-Guided Modification and Resynchronization

After construction, the handbook serves as a behavior-oriented guide for modifying the repository. Given a request q, the workflow uses the handbook together with its corresponding repository . The leaf mode g remains unchanged throughout the process.

The workflow consists of four steps. First, Behavior-Guided Progressive Disclosure (BGPD) localizes the requested behavior through coarse-to-fine handbook navigation. It progressively reveals relevant information, follows it to candidate source locations, and verifies those locations against the current repository. This process produces a set of source-grounded evidence for planning. Second, the planner converts the evidence into an edit plan and action declarations Γ. Third, a separate executor applies to the repository. Finally, any non-empty diff triggers handbook resynchronization. Algorithm 1 summarizes the complete workflow.

Handbook-Guided Modification with Automatic Resynchronization

3.3.1 Behavior Localization with BGPD

Rather than treating all source locations equally, BGPD uses the handbook to identify candidate sites from coarse to fine. It then verifies these sites against the current repository.

Localization begins at the level of execution stages. BGPD first uses L1 and L2 of to identify the stages directly relevant to the request. It then follows to include stages coupled through shared state. This step captures mutually dependent stages even when they are structurally distant. Within these stages, BGPD selects the most relevant L3 entries and retrieves their source locators.

BGPD then expands the candidate set along call relations. In function-as-leaf mode, it uses the function-call graph; in file-as-leaf mode, it uses the induced file-call graph. External boundary nodes provide context but are never returned as edit sites.

Up to this point, BGPD operates on the handbook. It then opens the current repository , resolves the candidate locators, and retains only the sites that remain relevant to q. This yields the verified evidence \widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{q}. Each record contains a file path, an optional function or region anchor, and a current source excerpt. The handbook thus guides the search, while the repository remains the basis for the edit plan.

3.3.2 Edit Planning and Execution

The planner converts \widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{q} into an edit plan . Each edit block specifies where the change should be made, which source evidence supports it, and what should change. The block records a target file, an optional function or region anchor, a current source excerpt, and the intended change.

For each edit, the planner also records an action declaration containing the target file, optional anchor, and one of three action types: , , or . The resulting declarations are collected as Γ=(Γmodify,Γadd,Γremove). A rename is represented as one removal and one addition.

The executor applies to and produces the updated repository . The resulting diff is \Delta=\mathrm{Diff}(\mathcal{R},\mathcal{R}^{\prime}). Because Δ is the factual record of what changed, it drives handbook invalidation. By contrast, Γ is used only to check whether execution followed the plan.

3.3.3 Handbook Resynchronization

Every non-empty diff Δ triggers Resyncg. Whenever possible, the procedure updates only the affected parts rather than rebuilding the entire handbook.

it reparses the changed source, refreshes the program graph, and aligns the old and new versions to identify added, removed, and modified units: in function-as-leaf mode, it matches functions using fingerprints that do not depend on line numbers, and in file-as-leaf mode, it matches files using file-set differences and content hashes.

it determines the update scope. If the stage skeleton remains valid, only the affected entries and their enclosing structure are refreshed; otherwise, Algorithm 2 is rerun on with the same leaf mode g and stored configuration Θ.

content that cannot be parsed or classified is handled conservatively: it is frozen or recorded in the coverage record rather than guessed.

Once the update completes, the new pair (\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}) becomes the starting state for the next request. Within resynchronization, model calls are limited to four semantic steps: classification, file assignment, within-stage organization, and description revision. All other operations are deterministic.

We evaluate Harness Handbook on two open-source agent harnesses around three research questions, describing the experiment setup in Section 4.1 and reporting results in Section 4.2.

  • Does handbook-guided localization improve plan quality while reducing planning cost?
  • With the handbook, can a weaker planner match the implementation-site localization of substantially more capable models?
  • Do these gains persist across request types and localization difficulty levels?

Figure 3: Plan quality and planner token usage on Codex and Terminus-2. (a) Overall win rates aggregated across the three judges. (b) Win rates reported separately by GPT-5.5, Opus 4.8, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro. (c) Average number of planner tokens per request; lower values indicate greater efficiency.

Figure 4: Per-judge win rates for three evaluation dimensions. Rows show results for Codex and Terminus-2, while columns show Localization, Scope Control, and Reasoning.

This experiment evaluates localization and edit planning in the modification workflow. Given a natural-language request, a read-only planner built with NexAU [31] and powered by produces an edit plan , and we score the quality of directly.

We compare two arms: the explores the repository directly, whereas the arm locates relevant source code under handbook guidance using a BGPD-consistent navigation policy. Apart from handbook access and navigation, the two arms are identical in requests, model, repository, tool permissions, and decoding settings. The handbook used in the Handbook-Assisted arm is built from the same source.

Plan quality is judged independently by three models: , , and .

Figure 5: Win rates by (a) modification request type and (b) localization difficulty. Q, CF, and SH denote Query, Cross-file, and Search-Hostile requests.

Benchmarks and Modification Requests.

We evaluate [32] and [25], two open-source agent harnesses that adopt the two leaf modes from Section 3.2: Terminus-2 uses function-as-leaf because it has a reliable seed skeleton, and Codex uses file-as-leaf to infer the hierarchy at repository scale.

Each harness contributes 30 behavior-driven modification requests. They are grouped by type into , which modifies existing behavior without revealing target locations; , which adds an end-to-end capability spanning files or modules; and , which places relevant implementations in locations that are hard to recover by keyword search. Requests are also labeled , , or by localization difficulty.

We evaluate plan quality, localization accuracy, and planning cost.

Three independent judges score each plan on three dimensions: (whether the edit sites are accurate), (whether the plan stays focused, with less scope bloat), and (whether the rationale and supporting evidence are adequate). The weighted score is

S=0.5S_{\mathrm{Loc}}+0.25S_{\mathrm{Scope}}+0.25S_{\mathrm{Reason}},

on a 0–100 scale, with Localization receiving the largest weight. Handbook-Assisted and Baseline are declared the winner when their scores differ by at least δ=3 points; otherwise the comparison is a tie. The for any reported slice is the number of wins divided by the number of valid judge–request comparisons in that slice.

We compare each predicted edit plan with independent reference plans from Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5, reporting Recall, Precision, F1, and Wrong at file and symbol granularity. Wrong is the share of valid requests with zero overlap against the reference; lower is better.

We report the average number of planner tokens per request, including the handbook and source context consumed during localization and plan construction.

The results show three consistent patterns. Handbook guidance improves plan quality without increasing planner token use. It also helps a weaker planner produce file- and symbol-level predictions that more closely align with reference plans from stronger models. These gains persist across request types and localization difficulty levels. The following subsections examine each finding in turn.

4.2.1 Better Plans at Lower Token Cost

Figure 3 summarizes plan-quality win rates and average planner token use. The Handbook-Assisted arm achieves a higher overall win rate on both harnesses: 38.3% versus 28.3% on Codex and 45.6% versus 26.7% on Terminus-2. The improvement is consistent across all three judges: the gap is 10.0 percentage points for every judge on Codex and ranges from 13.3 to 26.7 points on Terminus-2. Thus, the direction of the result does not depend on any single judge.

Figure 4 decomposes these judgments by dimension. Averaged across the three judges, the Handbook-Assisted arm has higher win rates for Localization, Scope Control, and Reasoning on both harnesses. The respective gains are 12.2, 6.7, and 4.5 points on Terminus-2, and 2.2, 1.1, and 3.3 points on Codex.

The quality gains are accompanied by lower planner token use. Average use falls from 0.102M to 0.089M tokens per Codex request (12.7%) and from 0.058M to 0.053M tokens per Terminus-2 request (8.6%). The simultaneous increase in win rate and decrease in token use shows that the improvement is not explained by a larger planning-token budget.

4.2.2 A Weaker Planner Matches Stronger Models

To assess whether handbook guidance helps a weaker planner approach stronger models in implementation-site localization, we compare its predicted edit sites with independent reference plans from Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 (Table 1).

Table 1: Reference-plan localization metrics (%). Predicted implementation sites are compared against independent reference plans generated by Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 at file and symbol granularity. Metrics are macro-averaged across valid requests; missing outputs and planner errors are excluded. Wrong indicates zero overlap with the reference plan at the reported granularity, so lower values are better.

Across both harnesses, both reference models, and both granularities, all 24 Recall, Precision, and F1 comparisons are higher for the Handbook-Assisted arm, with F1 gains ranging from 5.0 to 18.8 points. Recall and precision increase together, so the improvement is not explained by returning more candidate sites at the expense of focus.

The absolute agreement is highest on Terminus-2. With handbook guidance, the weaker planner reaches file-level F1 scores of 84.7% and 89.3%, and symbol-level scores of 77.1% and 89.3%, against the Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 references, respectively. Precision reaches 93.3% against GPT-5.5 at both granularities. The consistent direction across two independent references shows that the improvement is not specific to one reference model.

Handbook guidance also reduces complete localization failures. Wrong, the share of requests with zero overlap against the reference, never increases and falls by as much as 25.9 points. Thus, the gains include fewer complete misses, not only better overlap among already plausible plans.

4.2.3 Consistent Gains Across Requests and Difficulty

Figure 5 stratifies the win-rate results by request type and localization difficulty.

All six harness-by-type comparisons favor the Handbook-Assisted arm, with gains ranging from 16.3 to 33.3 percentage points. Codex improves most on Query requests (26.7 points), whereas Terminus-2 improves most on Search-Hostile requests (33.3 points). Cross-file requests improve by 16.3 and 20.0 points, respectively. The gains therefore span existing-behavior changes, cross-file capabilities, and requests that are difficult to localize through keyword search.

All six harness-by-difficulty comparisons are also positive, ranging from 3.7 to 33.3 points. Codex improves most on Easy requests, whereas Terminus-2 improves most on Medium requests. Because the gains are not monotonic in labeled difficulty, the difficulty label alone does not explain their variation.

This work identifies behavior localization as a central challenge in evolving production-scale agent harnesses and introduces Harness Handbook, a behavior-centric representation that links behavioral descriptions to their distributed source implementations. Harness Handbook reorganizes repository knowledge around runtime behavior, constructs this representation directly from source, and supports modification through behavior-guided progressive disclosure and automatic resynchronization.

Our experiments demonstrate the value of this representation along three dimensions. First, handbook guidance improves plan quality while lowering planning cost: on Codex and Terminus-2, overall win rates rise by 10.0 and 18.9 percentage points, while planner token use falls by 12.7% and 8.6%, respectively. Second, with the handbook a weaker planner matches the implementation-site localization of substantially stronger models, improving all 24 file- and symbol-level Recall, Precision, and F1 comparisons against two independent reference plans. Third, these gains persist across request types and localization difficulty levels. Together, these results indicate that making the relationship between behavior and implementation explicit can improve both modification planning and localization efficiency without requiring a larger planning-token budget.

The utility of Harness Handbook extends beyond modification planning. As a behavior-centric repository representation that stays synchronized with the code, it can also support broader uses such as behavior auditing and regression-impact analysis. Our next step is to apply it to harness self-evolving: using the handbook as a shared behavioral memory, an agent can autonomously close the loop of localization, planning, execution, and resynchronization as the repository evolves, moving the harness toward self-improvement.
