items.title: Unicode Normalization and Exact-Match Validation for Redemption Codes
items.author: Digital Field Notes
items.content:
A customer copies a short code from a message and pastes it into a redemption form. The code looks right, but the server rejects it. A support agent types what appears to be the same characters and gets a different result. The first instinct is to “clean up” the input before comparing it. That can be reasonable for a search box. For a value-bearing code, it can create an accidental alias.

The issue is that a code is an identifier with an issuer-defined alphabet, not free-form prose. Two strings that look alike may contain different Unicode characters. Conversely, a broad normalization step can map distinct strings to the same result. The correct behavior depends on the contract for the particular code format.

One example; three inputs

Take the fictional code . The second string below uses fullwidth Latin letters and digits. The third ends with a zero-width space.

import unicodedata

expected = "AB-12"
samples = [
    "AB-12",
    "\uFF21\uFF22-\uFF11\uFF12",  # fullwidth A, B, 1, 2
    "AB-12\u200B",                  # zero-width space
]

for value in samples:
    print(
        value == expected,
        unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", value) == expected,
    )

The three output pairs are , , and . NFKC folds the fullwidth characters into ordinary ASCII but leaves the zero-width space. That behavior is useful in some text-processing contexts. It is not automatically a safe redemption rule. If an issuer never defined fullwidth characters as equivalent, applying NFKC at the point of claim changes which inputs can identify the same value.

Make the alphabet part of the contract

Suppose this fictional issuer specifies exactly two uppercase ASCII letters, a hyphen, and two ASCII digits. In that case the server can reject every other shape. The validator does not guess what the customer intended.

import re

CODE = re.compile(r"[A-Z]{2}-[0-9]{2}\Z")

def parse_code(raw: str) -> str | None:
    if CODE.fullmatch(raw) is None:
        return None
    return raw

assert parse_code("AB-12") == "AB-12"
assert parse_code("\uFF21\uFF22-\uFF11\uFF12") is None
assert parse_code("AB-12\u200B") is None
assert parse_code("ab-12") is None

These tests encode a product decision rather than a universal rule. If the issuer documents that ASCII letter case is ignored, accept lowercase ASCII and map it to uppercase before the lookup. If it documents optional hyphens or spaces, implement those exact exceptions. Do not infer equivalence from what happens to look similar on a screen.

There is a second reason to keep the rule narrow: support needs to explain failures. A generic “invalid code” message tells a customer little. A form can say that the code contains a character outside the published format, while avoiding an echo of the whole code. It can also show the expected pattern, such as , using clearly fictional characters. The server should record a structured error category and a request ID, not the raw code, in routine logs.

Keep presentation separate from authority

A client can help someone enter a code. It might display grouping, highlight unexpected characters, or offer a paste review before submission. Those hints are presentation. The server still validates against the same issuer contract after receiving the value. If two clients normalize differently, the server must not accept one and reject the other by accident.

This separation also matters when codes arrive through APIs. A mobile app, support tool, and web checkout may all send strings to the same endpoint. The documented alphabet and canonicalization rule should live with that endpoint and have tests that cover every client. Otherwise a “helpful” browser-only fix creates a bug that appears only in one channel.

For an existing issuer integration, I would first ask for the actual code specification and a small set of test vectors from the issuer. Then I would test exact matches, documented aliases, visually similar Unicode, invisible characters, and concurrent redemption. A matching input should claim at most once. A rejected input should reveal no balance or ownership details.

The practical lesson is simple: make input forgiving only where the issuer contract permits it. A code comparison protects value. Its normalization rule deserves the same care as the lookup that follows.

items.title: Kalshi vs. Utah: Who Gets to Decide What's Gambling?
items.author: The Bitcoin Act
items.content:
Utah has moved its dispute with Kalshi from the civil courts into the criminal ones.

Prosecutors have filed 14 criminal charges against KalshiEX LLC and its two founders, Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara. The state accuses the company of illegally promoting gambling in Utah.

Kalshi is a federally regulated exchange in the United States. It lets users trade event contracts tied to binary real-world outcomes, such as elections, sporting results, economic data releases, and weather patterns.

The question at the center of this case is old and unresolved. Is a contract on the outcome of a game a financial derivative, or is it a bet?

The 14 counts break down into three categories.

The most serious is a felony count alleging a pattern of unlawful activity. Alongside it sit 12 counts of promoting online gambling and one misdemeanor gambling charge.

The structure tells you how the state is framing the case. A single misdemeanor would treat the conduct as an isolated infraction. The felony count frames it as a course of activity, and the dozen promotion counts give that course of activity its substance.

Naming the founders personally matters too. This is no longer only a dispute about whether a company may operate in a state. Two individuals now face criminal exposure.

The prosecution rests on evidence gathered by an undercover agent from the Utah Attorney General’s Office.

In September, the agent accessed the platform using a local address, a local phone number and a debit card. Kalshi reportedly allowed the agent to place 12 distinct sports wagers.

The state claims those transactions prove the platform is actively promoting illegal gambling within Utah’s borders.

The design of that evidence is deliberate. Every identifier the agent used pointed to Utah. The aim is to remove any doubt about where the conduct took place and to show that a Utah resident could do exactly what the state says its law forbids.

The number of wagers also matches the number of promotion counts. How each count maps onto each transaction is a question the charging documents will have to answer, but the symmetry is hard to miss.

The criminal case did not arrive alone.

Days earlier, Utah’s attorney general filed a civil lawsuit against Kalshi. That suit seeks to stop the company from taking bets from Utah residents and to recover profits it allegedly made in the state.

Running civil and criminal proceedings side by side gives the state two different instruments. The civil case aims at the business itself: access to Utah users and the money earned from them. The criminal case aims at liability for past conduct, including the personal liability of the founders.

For a company, that combination raises the cost of litigating on principle. Every position it takes in one forum can echo in the other.

Kalshi’s argument has been consistent. The company has maintained that sports wagers traded on its platform are not gambling but a type of financial derivative. On that view, they fall under federal regulation by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and should not be subject to state supervision.

Utah and several other states see it differently. They take the position that prediction markets like Kalshi are subject to state gambling laws and state gambling taxes.

Both positions cannot win. If these contracts are derivatives under federal oversight, state gambling statutes may have little room to operate. If they are bets, the federal label does not shield them from state law.

The CFTC has now entered the dispute directly. The agency has sued Utah, arguing that only Washington can regulate these contracts.

That changes the shape of the conflict. It is no longer only a state against a company. It is a federal regulator against a state, each asserting authority over the same product.

The criminal charges sharpen that collision. A state prosecuting a federally regulated exchange, while the federal regulator sues the state, puts the preemption question about as squarely as it can be put.

Several other states, including Arizona, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Michigan and Nevada, have already chosen to file criminal charges, take civil action or restrict access to the platform within their borders.

The scrutiny also reaches beyond Kalshi. Polymarket has faced similar state level gambling allegations.

What emerges is a patchwork. A user’s access to the same contract can depend on which state line they happen to live behind, while the federal answer to the underlying question remains contested in court.

The case leaves several questions open.

The first is preemption: whether federal oversight of these contracts displaces state gambling law, which is the core of the CFTC’s suit against Utah. The second is how the criminal case proceeds alongside the civil one. The third is whether more states follow Utah from civil enforcement into criminal charges.

None of these has an answer yet. What is clear is that the classification of event contracts is no longer an abstract debate among lawyers. In Utah, it now carries criminal stakes.

Author’s note: This article is analysis and commentary for informational purposes only. It is not legal advice, and nothing here is written in a professional capacity. The charges described are allegations, and all parties are presumed innocent unless proven otherwise.

items.title: Your Marketplace's Most Valuable Asset Is Hiding in Its Conversational Data
items.author: Denis Zhurba
items.content:
If your product is a contact-heavy platform (classifieds, rentals, home services, jobs, dating), the richest product signal you have is conversational data. The marketplace, in the broad sense of the word, is the whole family of platforms where strangers transact, and the messenger is where most of those contacts start and end. That makes the messenger the place where AI/ML earns the most.

Growth needs more contacts: more supply, more traffic, a lower-friction "write" button. Quality needs contacts that turn into deals: live listings, responsive counterparts, real intent. The two pull against each other, and usually sit with two owners.

A platform's flywheel spins when buyers and sellers keep buying and selling successfully without paid acquisition pushing them; Every turn goes through a contact. Quantity spins the wheel; quality is what makes the turn count.

The theory behind it: Alvin Roth's market design says a matching market (one where both sides have to choose each other) works only when it is thick (enough participants), uncongested (people can get through their options in time) and safe (no reason to lie, game the timing or take the deal elsewhere). Congestion is what you get when you go thick too fast. A messenger flooded with "Is it still available?" is a congested market, not a busy one.

The two axes are not equally visible. Volume is free to observe: chats, contacts, listings. Quality is not: the deal usually closes off-platform. ML's first job is to make quality observable; its second is to move it.

Three buckets, not one number

A contact becomes one of three things, and each has a different owner:

The label is the product. The hard part is turning a fuzzy human idea ("did they agree?") into reproducible classes: one labelling instruction shared by data science, analysts and the business; a seed set labelled together to find the grey zones, then labelling at volume with a second pass on the disagreements. Then check the classes against the deals you can see: a "sold here" on takedown, a review after a service, a both-sides confirmation in the chat, an in-app payment. That is the ground truth the off-platform majority is calibrated against.

An example: one week, three channels

Every chat gets a class and a reason once a week: rules mark the unanswered, a model classifies the rest. The three buckets are the invariant; the reasons under them are whatever your product needs to act on. "Already sold" and "no deal: price" are supply and pricing problems, "details asked, no decision" is a conversation problem, "no answer" is an onboarding problem.

What to score a chat with

Start cheap and add cost only where the cheap layer is unsure.

Heuristics first. Deterministic rules on metadata, not text: no reply within a window, a call under a few seconds, a first message identical across fifty chats, a listing already closed. Cheap, auditable, and they cover a large share of trash. They also become the first features of the next step.

Then one binary model. One question: did this chat lead anywhere, yes or no. Features: messages per side, reply latency, who spoke last, whether a structured offer was made, the buyer's prior activity on the listing, the seller's reply history, message text only as embeddings. Two classes keep the labels clean; typed labels explode into overlapping categories nobody applies consistently. Set the threshold on precision for the target class, because a false "target" inflates the north star.

Then an LLM, sparingly. It classifies the outcome and the reason the conversation ended: sold, price, terms, no next step, pulled off-platform. Run it on the unsure middle of the score distribution and on a sample for diagnostics. Cost per inference is the constraint, not accuracy.

The trade-off, in one table:

LLM as labeller → small model

a few hundred gold labels

the , new patterns, cold start

bootstrapping labels fast

The binary model wins production because half the signal is not in the text: reply latency, who spoke last, offer made, listing history. An LLM works on text alone, and a call has none. The LLM wins where there are no labels yet (a new market, a new category, a new scam) and where you need the reason, not the score. The combination is the answer: the LLM labels a sample, a few hundred gold labels check it, the cheap model trains on those labels, and the LLM stays on for the unsure middle and a monthly diagnostic sample.

Two disciplines around the model. Recalibrate on a schedule, because behaviour drifts and the thresholds drift with it; a monthly labelling pass on a random sample is the regression test the behavioural metrics cannot be. And log the reply before you trust the metric: if calls are not logged or a channel drops replies, a whole segment scores as trash, and the model learns it.

Seven levers, four places

Once every contact has a class, the score does two jobs. As a metric, it is the number to run A/B tests against: a feature wins when it moves target contacts, not chats. As a signal, it feeds the features themselves: which chat to answer first, which silent chat to nudge, which sender to throttle. The seven levers below use it one way or the other, grouped by where they sit in a chat’s life.

  1. Openers that carry intent. Openers tuned to the listing instead of a blank box (“Can I pick it up today?”, “Would you take X?”): ranked templates, no generation. Easier chat start → more chats → more target contacts if the rate stays. Hinge does the same with a like on a specific photo or prompt.
  2. Throttle low-odds senders. Re-distribute liquidity in search and recommendations towards the users that are responsive, throttle channels that give low-response rates.

At the first message: take the volume off the seller

  1. Help the seller answer the opener. "Is it still available?" is the dominant first message everywhere, and the item usually is. An intent classifier answers it from the listing status; "last price?" and "can you post it?" get a price surface and a shipping quote. Mind precision: a system reply is not a seller reply.

Inside the conversation: get to the agreement

  1. The next step as a chat action. "Make an offer", "Book a viewing", "Buy with delivery" inside the chat. A structured offer is a labelled event; a free-text haggle is invisible. An on-platform transaction plus the chat is the strongest signal.
  2. Close the reply gap. The median seller reply lands over an hour after the buyer writes; most buyers are gone by then. Templates first (most of the value), then ranked templates, then answers retrieved from the listing, never free-form generation.
  3. Make staying safe the easy path. The scam playbook barely varies: pull the buyer off the chat to a "payment" link or a "courier" app. Signals combine into a confidence score; the reaction is graded: allow, warn, hold, block. Warn on a shared phone number; block only high-confidence fraud. And ship the features people leave for (photos, voice, location, in-chat payment).

After the conversation: follow up the ones that can convert

  1. Follow up the conversations that can convert. The deal-probability score says which silent chats deserve a nudge: a follow-up on the seller's behalf when the buyer went quiet on a chat scored "could agree", visible to the seller, switchable off. The same score orders the inbox. Without the score, a nudge to every silent seller moved reply rate a little, deals not at all, and faded within weeks.

Make the target contact your north star: Report teams and ship increments on target contacts, not on contacts or stated intent, and A/B-test every lever against the agreement signal, so a feature cannot win on volume while losing on deals.

items.title: How Switch Mirroring Decisions Create Blind Spots in OT Network Monitoring
items.author: Abdul Khadir Mahamed
items.content:
Your OT sensor is licensed. It's healthy. The dashboard is full of assets, and the alerts are tuned. And the controller that runs your most critical line may still be invisible to it.

Passive platforms learn only from the packets delivered to them. In most plants, those packets arrive through a switch port mirror (SPAN) or a network TAP, placed by someone who had to decide which links mattered. The switch doesn't care about that decision. It forwards frames according to its MAC address table, and a sensor cannot analyze traffic that never crosses a mirrored link.

At a discrete manufacturing site, I compared our monitoring platform's inventory against the PLC projects and the switch MAC tables. Under a quarter of the assets were missing, which sounds tolerable until you ask why. Part of the answer was a vendor's cellular remote-access path: a working connection into the line that never touched the plant network, so no sensor could have seen it. The sensor wasn't broken. It had simply never been shown that traffic.

Try this before you read further. Pick one production line. Count the assets your monitoring platform shows for it. Then open the line's controller project and count every controller, I/O adapter, drive, and gateway in the I/O tree. If the two numbers match, you can skim this article. If they don't, the rest of it explains where the difference went.

The example below is a lab-style scenario with fictional addresses, built from documented switching behavior and common plant-floor designs. Later sections cover redundant topologies, devices hidden behind NAT and gateways, encrypted industrial protocols, and who is allowed to change mirror configuration.

1. How a switch decides what your sensor sees

A switch learns which MAC address lives on which port and forwards each unicast frame only to that port. When two devices hang off the same switch, the frame between them never leaves that switch. A SPAN session copies frames from the source ports or VLANs you define to a destination port. Anything not sourced is not copied.

Most OT monitoring deployments start the same way: the sensor goes in at the distribution layer, near the Level 3 boundary, mirroring the uplinks to each cell or area zone. That position sees north-south traffic well. It sees very little of what happens inside the cell.

Suppose a sensor mirrors only the uplink from a line's access switch:

Reaches a sensor on the uplink?

Engineering workstation (Level 3) to line PLC

Historian collector to line PLC

HMI to line PLC, same access switch

PLC to remote I/O adapters, same access switch

No, unless multicast floods (Section 2)

Laptop plugged into the line cabinet to PLC

The last row is the one that matters most. The most consequential activity in a cell, a program download or a forced output from someone standing at the cabinet, is exactly the traffic an uplink mirror cannot see.

The sensor's configuration tells you almost nothing about its coverage. The switch's forwarding path, and where the copy is taken, decides what the sensor will ever receive.

2. A hypothetical blind spot: Packaging Line 4

The lab has two switches. Distribution switch DS-01 sits at the Level 3 boundary. Access switch AS-L4 sits in the Line 4 control cabinet, connected to DS-01 through port Gi1/0/24. The sensor is connected to DS-01 port Gi1/0/48, and a SPAN session copies both directions of Gi1/0/24 to it.

More on Figure 1: The sensor copies only the uplink. Program downloads, HMI writes, and cyclic I/O are switched locally on AS-L4 and never reach it.

The engineering ground truth for Line 4 is 15 assets: one PLC, four remote I/O adapters, one HMI, one Modbus TCP-to-RTU gateway with six serial VFDs behind it, and two controllers inside an OEM filler skid that sits behind 1:1 NAT.

After two weeks of collection, Figure 2 compares the sensor's view with that ground truth (illustrative values, not captured from a live environment). Only the PLC is fully visible, because engineering and historian sessions cross the uplink. Everything else is missed for one of four reasons:

Learned from ARP broadcasts; its sessions to the PLC stay on AS-L4

Remote I/O adapters .21 to .24

IGMP snooping keeps cyclic multicast I/O on AS-L4

Modbus gateway 10.30.4.60

Seen only when Level 3 polls it

Serial VFDs (unit IDs 1 to 6)

Never on Ethernet; at best implied by unit IDs in gateway traffic

Translated addresses only; the skid network stays behind NAT

The dashboard reports five assets on Line 4. One of fifteen has full protocol visibility. And a laptop plugged into AS-L4 that downloads new logic to the PLC would generate no detection, because none of that traffic reaches DS-01.

More on Figure 2: Graded against engineering ground truth, Line 4 has full protocol visibility on 1 of 15 assets.

A note on the I/O row: if IGMP snooping or the querier is missing, EtherNet/IP multicast I/O may flood every port, including the uplink, and the sensor will see it. That is not good news. It means cyclic control traffic is flooding links it should not touch, which is its own reliability problem.

Step 1: read the mirror configuration

On Cisco IOS-based industrial switches (including Cisco IE and Rockwell Stratix families), the session is visible with:

Confirm the source ports or VLANs, the direction (both, rx, or tx), and the destination. Then list what is not sourced. Syntax differs on Siemens SCALANCE, Hirschmann, and Moxa platforms, but the question is the same: which conversations physically pass through a sourced port?

Step 2: check the destination port for drops

Mirroring both directions of a 1 Gbps uplink can generate up to 2 Gbps of copies toward a 1 Gbps destination port. The switch drops the excess at the destination port, and the sensor is never told. Cisco's SPAN documentation is explicit that an oversubscribed destination can lose packets, and that a frame can be forwarded normally on the production network yet never appear on the monitoring port. Check the destination port's output drops:

show interfaces Gi1/0/48 | include drops

Compare that with the sensor's own ingest and drop counters. Cyclic I/O at short requested packet intervals produces constant packet rates, so oversubscription in OT is often steady, not bursty.

The sensor inventory is not ground truth. The controller project's I/O configuration lists every adapter and module with its address. The access switch's MAC address table lists every device that is physically present:

show mac address-table interface Gi1/0/5

Any MAC in AS-L4's table that is missing from the sensor inventory is a confirmed blind spot. Any adapter in the PLC project that is missing from both is a different problem worth a walkdown.

Step 4: run a controlled observation test

In an approved maintenance window, connect an engineering laptop to a known port on AS-L4 and perform a read-only action, such as going online with the controller without making changes. Then check whether the sensor logged the session. If it logged nothing, the line has no detection coverage for engineering activity that starts inside the cell. Coordinate with operations first, keep the test strictly read-only, and do not run it against safety instrumented systems without the owner's explicit approval.

Step 5: correct the coverage design

Local SPAN on AS-L4 (access ports or the cell VLAN)

Captures intra-cell conversations

Needs a destination port and a path back to the sensor

RSPAN or ERSPAN to a central sensor

Carries cell copies across the network

Adds load to production links; size it, and keep it off control-critical trunks where possible

Passive TAP on the PLC's link

Full-fidelity copy, no switch CPU involved

Insertion needs an outage; confirm fail-open behavior with the vendor

Sensor per cell or area zone

Local visibility without transport

Hardware and licensing cost

Prioritize by consequence, not convenience. The links carrying write-capable protocols to controllers that can hurt people, product, or equipment come first, even if they are the hardest to reach. Whatever you choose, validate it with Steps 1 through 4 before calling the line monitored.

3. Redundancy can quietly take your sensor offline

Plants build redundancy so the process keeps running when a link fails. Ring protocols such as MRP and DLR, parallel networks under PRP, and redundant uplinks all do that job well. None of them consider your sensor.

In a ring, one port is held in a blocking state. When a link breaks, that port opens and traffic takes the other direction around the ring. If your mirror sources the port that used to carry the traffic, the copy stops while the process carries on normally:

More on Figure 3: A single link failure opens the blocked port. Control traffic now bypasses SW-B, and the sensor attached to it receives nothing.

The same pattern appears with PRP. Duplicate frames travel over independent LAN A and LAN B. A sensor on LAN A alone works until LAN A fails, and then it goes blind exactly when something unusual is happening.

Partial capture also degrades analysis. Passive platforms reconstruct sessions to decode industrial protocols. If a sensor sees a Modbus write request but not the response, or sees only one leg of an EtherNet/IP connection, it may misclassify the activity or drop it from protocol analysis.

The practical fixes are modest. Mirror at a point every path converges on, such as the controller's own link, or source the ring ports in both directions on more than one switch. Then test a planned ring break during commissioning and confirm the sensor keeps receiving the same conversations. Alert on a sudden drop in packets from a mirrored source, not only on the sensor's own health status.

4. The devices that sit behind something

Some of the most important assets on a plant floor are hidden by design, and no amount of SPAN tuning on the plant network will reveal them.

More on Figure 4: NAT'd skids, serial segments, and cellular remote access sit outside what any plant-network mirror can copy.

Machine builders often ship skids with a fixed internal address scheme and a 1:1 NAT device, so ten identical machines can coexist on one plant network. The sensor sees the translated addresses. The skid's internal controllers, drives, and safety devices, and every conversation between them, stay inside.

Serial and fieldbus segments. Modbus RTU, PROFIBUS, and similar networks reach Ethernet only through gateways. At best the sensor infers devices from unit IDs or gateway mappings when someone polls through the gateway from above. Wireless field networks such as WirelessHART and ISA100 behave the same way behind their gateways.

OEM cellular remote access. A vendor router with an LTE modem, installed for remote support, can carry traffic from the skid straight to the vendor without ever touching the plant network. No sensor anywhere in the facility will see it. In IEC 62443 terms, it is an undocumented conduit.

These require a different method, not a better sensor:

  • Ask for the skid's internal network drawings and NAT tables at purchase, and make them a contract deliverable.
  • Inventory serial devices from the controller and gateway configurations, not from network traffic.
  • Walk the line cabinets and skids looking for cellular antennas and unmanaged switches.
  • Where the platform supports it, use carefully scoped active queries through gateways, approved by the asset owner, as a supplement to passive data.

5. Mirror configuration is security configuration

Detection rules get reviewed, tuned, and change-controlled. The SPAN session that feeds them usually does not. It lives in the switch config, owned by whoever maintains the network, and it changes whenever the network changes.

A typical failure looks like this. During a planned outage, a technician replaces AS-L4 and moves the uplink from Gi1/0/24 to Gi1/0/23 on DS-01. The process restarts cleanly. The SPAN session still sources Gi1/0/24, which is now empty. The sensor keeps showing every Line 4 asset it learned before, because inventories retain devices for days or weeks. The dashboard looks normal while live coverage of the line is zero.

My position: treat SPAN sessions, TAPs, and the switch ports that feed sensors as part of the security monitoring control, under the same change control as detection rules. In practice that means three things:

  • Add a coverage check to the plant's management of change (MOC) process for any network work touching a monitored zone.
  • Baseline packet volume per mirrored source and alert when it drops sharply, independent of sensor health.
  • Restrict and log who can modify monitor sessions on industrial switches.

This maps directly to the continuous monitoring requirement in IEC 62443-3-3 (SR 6.2) and the monitoring guidance in NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3. A control that silently stops observing the system it monitors does not meet either.

Correctly mirrored traffic may still be unreadable

Getting the packets to the sensor is necessary, not sufficient. Industrial protocols are slowly adopting encryption: CIP Security wraps EtherNet/IP in TLS or DTLS, OPC UA supports Sign and SignAndEncrypt modes, and newer vendor engineering protocols increasingly run over TLS.

That is good for integrity. It also means a passive sensor sees endpoints, timing, and volume, but may not see function codes. It can no longer tell a tag read from a program download.

This is a trade-off security teams create themselves, so document it. Record which flows are encrypted, what the sensor can and cannot decode for each, and what compensates. Useful compensating sources include controller-side change and audit logs, syslog from controllers that support it, engineering workstation logs, and monitoring of controller mode or key-switch position.

6. Validate coverage before claiming visibility

I would not accept an OT monitoring deployment on the strength of an asset count or a sensor health page. The deployment should demonstrate that representative conversations with critical controllers reach the sensor and are decoded. These are the sources for that work:

Switch monitor session config

Which ports or VLANs are copied, and in which direction

Destination port counters

Whether mirrored copies are being dropped before the sensor

Switch MAC address tables

Which devices are physically present on each port

Controller project and I/O configuration

Ground truth for controllers, adapters, modules, and drives

Sensor ingest and drop statistics

What the sensor actually received and processed

Controlled read-only test

Whether engineering activity inside the cell is detected

When the network changed underneath the sensor

Replace the asset count with a coverage measure. For each zone, divide the assets observed with full role and protocol visibility by the assets in engineering ground truth, and weight the result by consequence. Line 4 in this example scores 1 of 15, under 7 percent, while its dashboard showed five healthy assets.

Repeat the validation after any network change in a monitored zone, after a ring failover test, and at least once a year.

More on Figure 5. Coverage validation is a loop, not a commissioning task. Any change under the sensor restarts it.

A passive sensor is only as good as the copy it receives. That copy has to include the right conversations, in both directions, through failover, and in a form the sensor can decode. Miss any one of those and the dashboard stays green while the line goes dark.

So make coverage verification a standing part of design reviews and management of change. Pick a critical controller. List everything that talks to it. Then prove the sensor sees each of those conversations. It's a half-day exercise, and it will find the blind spot before an incident does.

Author’s Note: All IP addresses, device names, and scenarios are fictional illustrations based on publicly documented switching behavior and common industrial network designs.

items.title: From Telecom Expense Management to AI Governance: How IntraTEM Is Expanding TEM
items.author: Sanya Kapoor
items.content:
Photo Courtesy of: IntraTEM

The company that spent two decades finding the technology bills enterprises forgot they were paying is now going after the AI tools nobody approved in the first place.

, according to Gartner research published in 2025. That figure describes close to half the enterprise market operating without a basic answer to a basic question: which AI products is this company actually paying for, and through which team's budget did they get approved. IntraTEM, a leading TEM provider that has spent two decades chasing exactly this kind of invisible spend, is positioning its telecom and cloud audit discipline as the fix. As leading TEM providers including Tangoe, Calero, Sakon, Mindglobal, and IntraTEM expand beyond traditional Telecom Expense Management, the market is increasingly dividing between software-led platforms and fully managed services that take responsibility for acting on what the data reveals. IntraTEM's model centers on human-led execution that does not stop at the dashboard.

From Wireless Bills to AI Seats

IntraTEM was founded in 2005 by Dimitry Malinsky, who started the company by reviewing wireless bills line by line to find costs enterprises did not know they were carrying. The work stayed narrow for years, limited to mobility contracts, carrier invoices, and device lifecycle management under what the industry calls Wireless Expense Management. It broadened as enterprise technology spend itself broadened, into fixed Telecom Expense Management and circuit inventory, and eventually into cloud and SaaS spend as software purchasing moved outside centralized IT procurement.

, with an estimated 25 to 35 percent of that spend occurring entirely outside IT visibility, according to Gartner data reported by enterprise security firm Airia in 2026. A team adopts a coding assistant, a summarization tool, a transcription add-on bundled into a video conferencing app, and the expense lands on a corporate card or a departmental subscription that finance never cross-checks against a master inventory. It is the same blind spot IntraTEM built its original Outsourced Telecom Expense Management practice auditing, wearing a different label.

Why the Old Category Missed This

That distinction matters for how the audit gets done. Finding unapproved software is a detection problem. Finding an AI feature buried inside four hundred already-approved SaaS licenses is an inventory problem, and inventory is the discipline IntraTEM has run since its telecom-bill origins. The company's existing cloud and SaaS management service, built to map what an enterprise licenses against what it actually uses, extends directly to the question of which of those licenses now carry an AI capability nobody separately signed off on. That work requires more than a reporting layer. It requires people who follow through on what the inventory surfaces, which is where the human-led model earns its keep.

Where the Gap Turns Into a Bill

The AI governance conversation usually gets framed as a security problem first, and it is one. A Technology Cost Management perspective on the same finding is more specific. Every AI seat operating outside IT visibility is also a line item nobody is optimizing, negotiating, or cutting when usage drops. A department that adopted an AI writing tool for a six-month pilot and never re-evaluated the seat count carries that cost the same way an enterprise carries a mobile line assigned to an employee who left the company eighteen months ago. IntraTEM's argument is that the two problems, invisible security risk and invisible spend, share one root cause. Both need an ongoing audit that does not stop at the point of initial approval, and both need someone accountable for acting on what the audit finds.

Already in the Conversation

IntraTEM's leadership has already been drawn into the AI governance question from the security side rather than the spend side. Alex Dukhovny, the company's executive vice president, was quoted earlier this year in trade publication REWORKED on the operational effect of AI note-taking tools sitting in on every internal meeting, a version of the same visibility problem viewed through workplace behavior rather than a budget line. The overlap is not a coincidence. A company that spends its days asking which tools an enterprise is actually using tends to notice the same shift security teams are noticing, just from the invoice side rather than the login side.

The Case for Extending the Model

IntraTEM is not entering this category with new technology. Its advantage is two decades of practice treating "we don't know what we're paying for" as an operational failure rather than an inevitability, applied to categories of spend as they emerged, from wireless plans to fixed circuits to cloud subscriptions. AI tools are the fourth category, arriving faster than the previous three and with less internal process built to catch it. The fully managed TEM model that distinguishes IntraTEM from software-only TEM platforms applies directly: visibility without follow-through does not close a budget gap, improve ROI, or resolve a vendor dispute.

AI governance is a natural expansion of IntraTEM's broader Technology Expense Management model because the same questions apply: what is the enterprise paying for, who is using it, what value is it creating, and who is accountable for what happens next. Other TEM services providers are adding AI-tracking modules of their own. Pure security vendors are building AI discovery tools that never touch a budget line at all. IntraTEM's position is narrower than either. It is not trying to police what employees do with AI, only to make sure every seat running one shows up on an invoice somebody is actually reviewing, and that a person is accountable for what happens next.

What is measurable is the size of the gap Gartner and Airia have both quantified, and the fact that closing gaps like it has been IntraTEM's entire business since 2005.

items.title: Avrea’s Faster Runners for GitHub Actions Reflect How AI Coding Is Changing CI
items.author: Ishan Pandey
items.content:
Before any change to a software project can ship, it has to pass continuous integration (CI), the automated builds and tests that run every time a developer proposes an edit. Engineers wait on those checks many times a day, so their speed sets the pace at which a team can ship.

Now AI coding agents are sending a lot more work through those checks. On weekends, when most human engineers are offline, agents and bots account for about one in five of the in-progress code branches being tested in CI, according to CircleCI’s Q3 2026 State of Software Delivery Pulse Report.

Since September 2025, the number of workflows active on a typical day has grown 40% on these feature branches, compared with 17% on the main codebase, where approved changes end up. Testing activity is rising more than twice as fast as activity on the main codebase, and CI has to absorb the extra work.

One of the most practical fixes requires no new CI system at all. Teams keep their existing workflows and move them onto faster machines, often by changing a single line of configuration. Avrea is one of the companies built around that idea. Its main product runs CI checks for teams that use GitHub Actions, the CI system built into GitHub, on machines it says are faster than GitHub’s own, and it saves the results of earlier runs so unchanged parts of a project don’t have to be rebuilt and retested.

The company calls itself a “software delivery platform” and has added newer products, including its own CI engine, which is in beta. Several CI vendors have moved in the same direction in 2026, building tools that cover more of the path from code to production, not just the machines that run the checks.

The pressure on CI comes from three places: volume, repetition and recovery. Volume is the first, and the figures above show how quickly it is rising. The repetition compounds the effect. The CircleCI report says the median team needs roughly five total CI cycles per shipped change. If an agent produces a change, runs tests, revises it and sends it back through CI, each additional cycle consumes more compute and adds another wait. A 20-minute GitHub Actions build becomes especially expensive when the same change has to pass through it repeatedly.

Recovery adds another delay. When a check fails on in-progress work, the typical team now takes almost an hour and a half to get it passing again. The same report found that this recovery time rose from about 80 minutes last September to 86 minutes in August. That delay likely affects coding agents’ workflows as well, because many of them rely on builds and tests to confirm their changes work.

To be fair, plenty of CI runs are fast enough, finishing within a few minutes. The trouble is how many times work has to go through CI and how long it takes to fix failures. The problem is most severe on big projects, where a single build can take 20 minutes or more.

For most teams on GitHub Actions, GitHub’s own hosted runners are the default. They need no setup, but they run on general-purpose machines and bill by the minute, so as AI coding agents push more work through CI, teams wait longer and their bills climb with usage. That has opened a crowded market for third-party runner providers, from Blacksmith, Depot, Namespace and Avrea to newer entrants such as WarpBuild, Ubicloud and StarSling.

Whichever third-party GitHub Actions runner provider they choose, teams usually switch for the same reasons: faster machines, lower usage costs, better caching or more visibility into why a job is slow. Managed runner providers let them make that change without maintaining a fleet of self-hosted machines.

Choosing between Blacksmith, Depot and Namespace for GitHub Actions, or newer options such as Avrea, comes down to what a team cares about most. Blacksmith has built a strong developer brand and community around GitHub Actions, with relatively low ARM pricing, test analytics and Docker integrations. Depot has particularly deep Docker build tooling and now has its own CI engine, Depot CI. Namespace emphasizes premium hardware, debugging capabilities and development environments alongside its runners.

Avrea’s emphasis is on combining high-performance runner hardware with several caching layers. According to Avrea, its build-cache integrations cover tools including Gradle, Maven, Nx, Nix, ccache, sccache, Go, Bazel, Tuist, Xcode and Turborepo. Enterprise customers can also apply an egress firewall that allows or blocks destinations by job. The platform is ISO 27001 certified and SOC 2 Type II attested, with SSO and audit logging available. Those features are not all unique to Avrea. Blacksmith also supports build-tool caching, for example. Avrea works only with GitHub Actions, while newer products such as Avrea CI, the company’s own CI engine, remain in beta.

How to speed up GitHub Actions without rewriting your workflows

For most teams, the quickest way to make CI faster is to change where GitHub Actions workflows run, without rewriting them. Avrea uses the same GitHub Actions workflow model, with migration typically reduced to changing a runner label to runs-on: avrea-ubuntu-latest. Its runners cover Linux on x86 and ARM, as well as macOS and Windows.

The gains come from two places: faster CPUs for compiling and Docker builds, and caching that skips work already done. Avrea claims teams can “build 2x faster than on GitHub-hosted runners on hardware alone, and 10x faster with cache hits.” Its caching covers dependencies, Docker layers, build output and code checkouts as well as integrations with individual build tools.

Independent data gives some support to the hardware side of the claim. As of November 11, 2026, RunsOn’s benchmark ranks Avrea the fastest GitHub Actions runner on ARM at each of the 2, 4 and 8 vCPU sizes tested. On x86, it ranks second to Namespace at most sizes. RunsOn is itself a runner competitor, and Depot is not included in the benchmark, so the results might not tell the whole story.

When a job fails, teams need to see why before they can fix it. Avrea exposes resource usage by step, searchable logs and SSH access to a running job, including through its avr command-line tool.

Avrea AI, currently in beta with access by request, takes that further by identifying and proposing fixes for failing tests, slow builds and outdated dependencies, with changes delivered as pull requests for review. For teams handling more machine-generated changes, reducing recovery time can matter as much as reducing the duration of a successful run.

Is it cheaper to self-host GitHub Actions runners or use a third-party provider?

Cost comparisons became less straightforward after GitHub reduced hosted-runner prices by up to 39% last winter.

Self-hosting can still provide inexpensive raw compute and complete control over the environment. The tradeoff is largely operational, as someone has to provision capacity, patch the machines, secure them and make sure enough runners are available when CI demand spikes.

Managed providers sit between those two models. Many offer cheaper alternatives to GitHub-hosted runners without transferring runner operations to the development team.

Avrea’s pricing page claims “67% lower compute cost than GitHub Actions at list prices, with 2x faster builds.” Part of that saving comes from builds finishing faster, so it makes sense that the real figure will vary from team to team.

Avrea uses per-minute usage pricing with no per-seat fee. Linux x86 starts at $0.002 per minute for a 1-vCPU runner, and its pay-as-you-go plan includes $12 in monthly credit. Actual savings therefore depend on runner size, build duration, cache effectiveness and the amount of operational work a team would otherwise spend on self-hosting.

What CI setup works best for teams shipping AI-generated code

Faster machines are now only part of what these companies offer. Depot made its own CI engine, Depot CI, generally available in March 2026. Namespace, which combines runners with development environments, pitches itself as infrastructure for coding agents. Avrea’s newer products sit alongside the runners that remain its core business.

The reasoning is that coding agents touch more of the delivery path than CI alone. They need somewhere to run code, repeated builds benefit from shared caches, and failed runs still need debugging.

For teams that need to make CI faster now, the simplest step is to move existing GitHub Actions workflows onto faster runners with built-in caching, which for most workflows can be a one-line change. The bigger decision comes after that. A single platform spanning development environments, runners and CI can share machines and caches across each step, but it ties a team more closely to one vendor. Mixing specialized tools lets a team pick the fastest runner, cache or build service for each job, but leaves the team to connect them.

Either way, the checks that once ran mostly for human changes now run around the clock for agents as well, and CI will have to keep pace with both. In 2027, it should become clearer whether teams want one platform for all of it, or the best tool for each step.

Don’t forget to like and share the story!

items.title: Tim Peters, Python User #2 and Prolific Contributor, Dies At 74
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Tim Peters, one of Python's earliest and most influential contributors, died on July 15 at age 74. Known as Python's second real user, Peters created the Zen of Python and Timsort sorting algorithm while contributing to numerous core components. He also served as a Python Software Foundation director from 2001 to 2014. Adafruit remembers Peters in a blog post: He's best known for the Zen of Python, PEP 20, still printed by typing import this. In 2002, he gave Python Timsort, the sorting algorithm he designed for lists, later adopted by Java and Android. He also polished the cyclic garbage collector and the pymalloc allocator, worked on the dict implementation, the float object, the math module and Karatsuba multiplication in longobject, and wrote the first version of doctest, plus difflib, pickletools and tabnanny.
 
He was a director of the Python Software Foundation from 2001 to 2014. Before Python, he wrote compilers at Cray Research and speech-to-text software at Dragon Systems. The thread is full of recollections from core developers about his patient, detailed answers on the mailing lists, signed with his trademark . Python creator Guido van Rossum also paid tribute to Peters in a post on discuss.python.org, writing: "It's hard to overestimate Tim's influence on Python. He's probably best known for writing the Zen of Python (PEP 20), but to me he was a mentor and language co-designer long before that..."
 
Further discussions can be found on Hacker News and Reddit.

items.title: Beyond Fiber Optics: The Hardware Reality of a Decentralized Internet
items.author: Suman Meher
items.content:
In its 2023 report, the digital rights group Access Now documented 283 internet shutdowns across 39 countries. While this figure includes targeted platform blocking rather than just total national blackouts, it highlights a stark reality: various state actors and conflicting parties hold the ultimate trump card. They can simply issue administrative orders to local telecom operators to restrict routing or suspend connectivity.

Web3 developers have spent years bulletproofing consensus mechanisms and peer-to-peer storage. Yet, if the physical fiber-optic cables belong to a state monopoly, software encryption cannot protect network availability. Furthermore, even when physical lines remain active, governments can compel ISPs to execute software-level blocks like SNI (Server Name Indication) filtering. Whether through severing physical connections or enforcing digital filters at the ISP level, access to even the most decentralized dApp becomes severely restricted for average users.

This physical bottleneck highlights the core motivation behind Decentralized Physical Infrastructure Networks (DePIN). Projects in the satellite space, including Spacecoin, are engineering architectures to decouple network access from terrestrial telecoms. However, bypassing legacy ISPs is not an absolute cure for censorship—it merely shifts the battleground from software firewalls to hardware logistics.

The Corporate Chokepoint of Centralized Satellites

Many assume that orbital networks bypass terrestrial laws entirely, but Starlink’s recent legal battle in Brazil illustrates the limitations of centralized physical infrastructure.

After the Brazilian Supreme Court ordered X (formerly Twitter) blocked, Starlink initially refused to comply. After Justice Alexandre de Moraes froze Starlink's local accounts over potential liability for fines owed by X, Starlink notified the telecom regulator that it would comply with the court's blocking order. While Starlink publicly maintained that the asset freeze was illegal, this chronological sequence of events underscores how operating as a centralized corporate entity with a vulnerable financial footprint creates distinct compliance chokepoints.

Web3 infrastructure projects aim to solve this by separating the coordination protocol from physical data routing. However, it is crucial to distinguish between protocol decentralization and physical hardware ownership. According to deployment updates, Spacecoin's CTC-0 nanosatellite launched in December 2024, followed by three CTC-1 satellites in November 2025. These satellites are physically owned and operated by a traditional corporate entity (Space Telecommunications Inc.).

The Spacecoin protocol does not decentralize the physical satellite ownership. Instead, its technical roadmap outlines a separation of capabilities. According to Spacecoin's official updates, its protocol is designed to manage authorization, authentication, and accounting across the decentralized infrastructure, while smart contracts and crypto payments support bandwidth coordination. However, the extent to which these capabilities are operational in the deployed satellite network remains distinct from the protocol's stated design.

On October 1, 2025, Spacecoin claimed a successful demonstration using its CTC-0 satellite to transmit secured data over 7,000 kilometers between Chile and the Azores. While Spacecoin has since announced regional connectivity pilots and commercial partnerships in 2026, a globally resilient, independently accessible satellite internet service remains a different milestone from its initial proofs of concept.

How States Can Still Choke Orbital Networks

Treating orbital networks as an instant bypass for censorship ignores how physical infrastructure is regulated. Moving the internet to an orbital mesh introduces distinct vectors for state control.

1. The Reality of Spectrum Regulation

Space is borderless, but RF (Radio Frequency) spectrum is strictly policed. Transmitting high-speed data to orbit typically involves licensed spectrum, such as Ku, Ka, L, or S bands. Legally utilizing these frequencies requires two distinct regulatory processes: international coordination through the ITU for frequency assignments and orbital positions—including procedures intended to prevent harmful interference—and separate national authorizations granted by local communications regulators within their jurisdictions. If a decentralized project operates outside authorized spectrum allocations or exceeds the technical limits applicable to license-exempt ISM bands, state actors may treat the transmissions as unlawful. Governments do not necessarily need to attack the blockchain; they can confiscate unauthorized hardware or, in specific scenarios, attempt to deploy localized radio jamming equipment to disrupt targeted frequencies.

2. Physical Uplink Detection

While downloading data via a passive receiver can sometimes go unnoticed, two-way satellite internet requires user terminals to transmit data back to orbit. These uplink transmissions emit RF signatures that, with specialized equipment, can potentially be detected and localized. Regimes can outlaw the import and possession of unauthorized satellite terminals. If customs agencies seize the hardware at the border, it can severely restrict network deployment before a single node comes online.

3. Capital and Supply Chain Consolidation

Launching nanosatellites and manufacturing custom RF receivers requires massive upfront capital. If a decentralized network relies on a small number of aerospace launch providers or hardware manufacturers to deploy its infrastructure, those companies become the new chokepoints. A state actor merely needs to apply regulatory pressure on the hardware manufacturers or impose import restrictions to cripple the network's expansion.

Changing the Price of Suppression

Decentralized physical infrastructure does not erase state control. Instead, it forces a shift in the logistics of executing it.

Today, restricting internet access is a relatively straightforward administrative task that relies on legal mandates enforced through local regulators, government agencies, and compliant telecom operators. Censoring a blockchain-coordinated satellite network, however, expands the required enforcement toolkit. It creates a scenario where a state might be forced to strictly police domestic hardware supply chains and import channels, actively track localized RF uplinks, or seize physical terminals.

A decentralized physical internet does not stop governments from using inexpensive software blocks; rather, it introduces a reality where regimes may have to supplement digital firewalls with highly visible, financially exhausting physical enforcement.
